### Summary

Add a way to include text in Streamlit Markdown that shows a tooltip when hovered — for glossary terms, acronym expansions, definitions, or short explanations. There are two complementary approaches:

1. **Footnotes as tooltips:** render standard Markdown footnotes as hover tooltips.
2. **A `:tooltip[...]` directive:** an explicit inline directive for annotating a word/phrase with hover text.

### Why?

It's common to annotate a word or phrase with extra context that appears on hover, without cluttering the main text. Today there's no native way to do this in Streamlit Markdown; users resort to raw HTML (`<abbr>`/`title`), which is limited and not always allowed. First-class Markdown tooltips make docs, dashboards, and explanatory text much richer.

### How?

**Option 1 — Footnotes as tooltips.** Some Markdown parsers support footnotes (see the [Markdown guide](https://www.markdownguide.org/extended-syntax/#footnotes) or [GitHub Markdown](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/basic-writing-and-formatting-syntax#footnotes)). What if we showed them as actual tooltips?

```python
st.markdown("""
Here is a simple footnote[^1].

[^1]: My reference.
""")
```

`remark-gfm` (already used within Streamlit) supports GFM-compatible footnotes: https://github.com/remarkjs/remark-gfm

**Option 2 — A `:tooltip[...]` directive.** A more explicit, inline approach: the bracketed text is displayed and the `text` attribute is shown on hover.

```
The :tooltip[HTML]{text="Hyper Text Markup Language"} specification...

:tooltip[Streamlit]{text="Open-source app framework for Machine Learning and Data Science teams."}
```

Notes:
- The visible text (`[...]`) renders inline; hovering shows the tooltip `text`.
- Works wherever Streamlit Markdown is rendered (`st.markdown`, `st.write`, captions, etc.).
- Consider whether the tooltip `text` itself supports Markdown.

The two options are complementary: footnotes give a standard-Markdown path (and are great for reference-style content), while the `:tooltip[...]` directive is a more explicit, inline way to attach hover text to any span.

### Additional Context

_No response_
issues.title: Support tooltips in Markdown (footnotes-as-tooltips and/or a `:tooltip[...]` directive)

### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Provide a built-in chart command to make it easy to render statistical histogram charts.

### Why?

Currently, users can create histograms using `st.bar_chart`. However, `st.bar_chart` is a general-purpose bar chart and doesn't offer histogram-specific parameters like direct control over binning, density, or cumulative displays. A dedicated `st.histogram_chart` would simplify the process for common histogram use cases, making it more discoverable and efficient for users to visualize data distributions. It would provide a more direct and potentially optimized solution for what is often a manual configuration of `st.bar_chart` or `st.altair_chart`.

### How?

```python
st.histogram_chart(
    data=None,
    x=None,
    bins='auto',
    density=False,
    cumulative=False,
    color=None,
    width=None,
    height=None,
)
```
• data (Anything supported by st.dataframe): The dataset to be plotted.
• x (str): The column name or key from data representing the numerical data to be binned.
• bins (str, int, or sequence): Specifies the number or definition of bins for the histogram.
    ◦ 'auto' (default): Let the charting library automatically determine the bin edges (similar to default behavior in many plotting libraries).
    ◦ int: The number of bins.
    ◦ sequence: A sequence of bin edges.
    ◦ (Note: The bins parameter and its specific values are proposed based on common histogram functionalities and are not directly from the sources but inferrable from the need for a dedicated histogram tool.)
• density (bool): If True, normalize the histogram so that the area under the bars sums to 1 (probability density function). Default is False.
• cumulative (bool): If True, compute a cumulative histogram. Default is False.
• color (str or None): A column name or key to segment the histogram bars by color, useful for displaying multiple distributions (e.g., stacked histograms).

Similar to `st.area_chart`, `st.bar_chart`, `st.line_chart`, and `st.scatter_chart`, this command would be syntax-sugar around `st.altair_chart`. This means it will use the data's columns and indices to infer the Altair specification, making it easier for "just plot this" scenarios while being less customizable than directly using `st.altair_chart`.

### Additional Context

_No response_

### Summary

When a dialog created with @st.dialog(..., on_dismiss="rerun") is opened from within a function decorated with @st.fragment, dismissing the dialog triggers a rerun only of that fragment, not the entire app. This differs from the common expectation that on_dismiss="rerun" causes a full-script rerun. In contrast, dialogs that programmatically call st.rerun(...) inside their button handlers do trigger a full rerun.



### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

@st.dialog("Example dialog (on_dismiss='rerun')", on_dismiss="rerun")
def my_dialog():
    st.write("Inside dialog")
    # No explicit st.rerun call here

@st.dialog("Dialog that forces full rerun", on_dismiss="ignore")
def full_rerun_dialog():
    if st.button("Close and rerun app"):
        st.rerun()  # or st.rerun(scope="app") if your app uses scoped reruns

@st.fragment
def fragment_area():
    st.write("This is the fragment area.")
    if st.button("Open dialog with on_dismiss='rerun'"):
        my_dialog()

    if st.button("Open dialog that forces full rerun"):
        full_rerun_dialog()

st.write("Top of app")
fragment_area()
st.write("Bottom of app")
```

### Steps To Reproduce


Open the first dialog (with on_dismiss="rerun"). Dismiss it via X/ESC/click-outside.
Actual: Only fragment_area() reruns; other parts of the page do not fully refresh.
Expected: Full app rerun.

Open the second dialog and click the button (which calls st.rerun()).
Actual: The whole app reruns and the dialog closes.

### Expected Behavior

Expected: Dismissing a dialog with on_dismiss="rerun" causes a full app rerun, regardless of whether the dialog was opened from within a fragment.

Actual: If the dialog is opened within a @st.fragment, dismissing it causes only the fragment to rerun.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st
import time

st.set_page_config(page_title="st.tabs restart repro", layout="centered")

st.title("Repro: st.tabs does not reset active tab after rerun")

# --- Simulated app state you might reset on restart ---
if "counter" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.counter = 0
if "last_restart" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.last_restart = None

st.caption(
    "Steps to reproduce:\n"
    "1) Click the second or third tab below.\n"
    "2) Click the **Restart Section** button.\n"
    "3) Notice the app reruns and state resets, but the active tab stays where it was, "
    "instead of returning to the first tab."
)

# --- Tabs (no way to programmatically select which one is active) ---
tab_md, tab_io, tab_hist = st.tabs(["tab1", "tab2", "tab3"])

with tab_md:
    st.subheader("tab1")
    st.write("This is the first tab. Ideally the UI would return here after restart.")

with tab_io:
    st.subheader("tab2")
    st.write("Switch to this (or the next) tab, then press Restart Section.")

with tab_hist:
    st.subheader("tab3")
    st.write("Switch here, then press Restart Section to see the issue.")

st.divider()

# --- Some content that changes with state so it's clear a reset happened ---
st.write("**Counter (simulated app state):**", st.session_state.counter)
if st.button("Increment counter"):
    st.session_state.counter += 1
    st.rerun()

col1, col2 = st.columns(2)

def restart_section():
    # Simulate resetting a bunch of session state
    st.session_state.counter = 0
    st.session_state.last_restart = time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
    # Rerun the app; the selected tab remains whatever was active
    st.rerun()

with col1:
    st.button("Restart Section", on_click=restart_section, type="primary")

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Currently, when deploying a Streamlit app to Streamlit Cloud, it’s not possible to prevent overscroll-based page refresh (e.g., accidental pull-to-refresh on mobile) — even when setting the proper overscroll-behavior styles via unsafe_allow_html. This works correctly on local or self-hosted deployments, but not on Streamlit Cloud. A new config option to control mobile overscroll would be highly useful.

### Why?

When deploying to Streamlit Cloud, mobile users often accidentally refresh the page by scrolling up too far — especially in apps with buttons or input forms near the top. This leads to frustration and loss of progress in interactive sessions.

Even applying the following CSS does not resolve it on Streamlit Cloud (but works as expected on a private server):

`
st.markdown("""
    <style>
    html, body, 
    [data-testid="stAppViewContainer"],
    .main,
    .stApp {
        overscroll-behavior: none !important;
        scroll-behavior: auto;
    }
    </style>
""", unsafe_allow_html=True)
`

### How?

Please allow overscroll behavior to be configurable, ideally with a simple addition to config.toml, for example:

`
[ui]
mobile_overscroll_behavior = "False"
`

Alternative solutions might include:
- A st.set_overscroll_behavior("none") command
- Or a documented CSS class that is guaranteed to control mobile scroll handling even on Streamlit Cloud

### Additional Context

- This issue does not occur on self-hosted deployments.
- Streamlit version tested: 1.49.1

Thanks for considering it!
issues.title: Allow control of overscroll behavior on mobile devices via config.toml

### Summary

Right now, `maxUploadSize` in `config.toml` applies globally, which means both `st.chat_input` and `st.file_uploader` share the same size limit. It would be useful to configure them separately (e.g., smaller uploads for chat attachments, larger ones for file uploads) to improve flexibility and user experience. ### Feature Request: Separate `maxUploadSize` configuration for `st.chat_input` and `st.file_uploader`

**Description**  
Currently, the `maxUploadSize` option in `config.toml` is applied globally across all upload-related components. This makes sense for standard file uploads, but it creates limitations when using `st.chat_input` in chat-based apps that also rely on `st.file_uploader`.

For example, in chat applications, users often need to paste or drag in small files/images (like screenshots), while developers may want `st.file_uploader` to accept larger files (e.g., CSVs, PDFs, or datasets). Since both are tied to the same `maxUploadSize`, there’s no way to differentiate these behaviors.


### How?

**Proposed Solution**  
Introduce separate configuration options, such as:

```toml
[server]
maxUploadSizeFileUploader = 200

### Summary

Today, `st.container(..., horizontal=True)` always wraps elements if there are too many to show them in a row. In some situations, it would be good to control whether the elements should wrap or not, e.g. through a parameter `wrap=True|False`. 

### Why?

In some situations, you don't want elements to wrap. 

### How?

- Easiest solution would be a parameter `wrap: bool = True` on `st.container`. 
- We should also think about whether we want to integrate this with scrolling in some way, e.g. by doing `overflow="wrap"|"scroll"|"fit"`. Could then also think through whether we'd need this for horizontal and vertical directions separately. 
- Looking at #6592, maybe we should also allow something like `wrap="phone"|"tablet"|"desktop"` to wrap on different screen sizes, and have the same `wrap` parameter on `st.columns`. 
- We probably also want a `wrap` parameter on a few other elements, such as `st.markdown` to control text wrapping. 
- We also need to look into minimum widths of elements then, to make sure elements don't look weird because they become too small. 

### Additional Context

Related:

- #5003 
- #6592

### Summary

In previous versions, a widget with a key could update its value dynamically based on another widget. For example, a `st.text_area` would change when the selection in a `st.selectbox` changed.

In 1.50.0, this no longer works. If a widget has a `key`, its `value` only reflects the initial `value` provided. Changes in other widgets no longer update it automatically.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

sys_dict = {"key1": "value1", "key2": "value2"}

selected_key = st.selectbox(
    "Key:",
    options=list(sys_dict.keys()),
    key="selected_key",
)

selected_value = st.text_area(
    "Value:",
    value=sys_dict[selected_key],  # depends on selectbox
    height=150,
    key="selected_value",
)

st.write(f"state.selected_key: {st.session_state.selected_key}")
st.write(f"state.selected_value: {st.session_state.selected_value}")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run above code using 1.49.1
2. Observe that changes to the selectbox change the value in the text_area/session_state
3. Upgrade to 1.50.0
4. Observe that changes to the selectbox do not change the value in the text_area/session_state

### Expected Behavior

- If selected_key == "key1", the text_area shows "value1".
- If selected_key == "key2", the text_area shows "value2".

Switching the selectbox causes the text_area to update accordingly.

### Current Behavior

On the first render, the text_area shows the correct value.
After that, changing the selectbox does not update the text_area.

### Is this a regression?

- [x] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

### Summary

We have color in various places:
* A variety of config.toml [theme] settings
* Charts
* Chart columns
* MultiselectColumn

The most modern format for CSS colors uses spaces (and a slash) for value separation instead of commas:
`rgb(255 0 0 / .5)` vs `rgb(255, 0, 0, .5)`.

Support for this is not consistent (and some places are case sensitive where others are not).

### Reproducible Code Example

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-12681)

```Python
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

data_df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "category": [
            ["exploration", "visualization"],
            ["llm", "visualization"],
            ["exploration"],
        ],
    }
)

st.data_editor(
    data_df,
    column_config={
        "category": st.column_config.MultiselectColumn(
            "App Categories",
            help="The categories of the app",
            options=[
                "exploration",
                "visualization",
                "llm",
            ],
            color=[
                "rgb(99 51 255)",
                "rgba(99 51 255 / 0.5)",
            ],
            format_func=lambda x: x.capitalize(),
        ),
    },
)
```

### Expected Behavior

Everywhere that we can put CSS colors should follow the same rules and accept the most modern format.

### Current Behavior

#### primaryColor doesn't accept the modern format
```
[theme]
primaryColor = "rgb(99 51 255)"
```
raised an error: `Bad message format Failed to parse color: "rgb(99 51 255)"`

```
[theme]
primaryColor = "rgb(99, 51, 255)"
```
works fine.

#### chartCategoricalColors accepts the modern format

```
[theme]
chartCategoricalColors =[
    "rgb(99 51 255)",
    "rgba(99 51 255 / 0.5)",
    "rgb(99, 51, 255)",
    "rgba(99, 51, 255, 0.5)",
]
```
works fine. In fact, invalid colors don't raise a warning at all. However, the modern formats are passed through and used just fine.

#### MultiselectColumn doesn't support the modern format

The previous code raises `Failed to parse color: "rgb(99 51 255)"`

### Is this a regression?

### Debug info

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a `max_size `parameter to `st.file_uploader` to allow developers to restrict the maximum file size before the file is uploaded. This would provide immediate feedback to the user and prevent large files from being uploaded unnecessarily.

### Why?

Currently, Streamlit only allows file size limitation through:

- Post-upload checks (file.size).
- Global configuration via maxUploadSize in config.toml.

This creates a few problems:

- Bandwidth waste: Large files are uploaded even if they will later be rejected.
- Poor UX: Users receive feedback only after the upload has completed.
- Lack of granularity: You can’t set different file size limits for different uploaders in the same app.
- No UI indication: The upload widget does not show any size limitation unless the global config limit is exceeded.

### How?

Add an optional `max_size `parameter (in bytes, KB, or MB) to `st.file_uploader`. For example:

```
st.file_uploader(
"Upload your data",
max_size=5 * 1024 * 1024
)  # 5MB
```

Expected behavior:

- Files larger than the specified limit are not accepted.
- A clear, user-friendly error message is shown before the upload begins (e.g., "File exceeds 5MB limit").
- Consistent feedback across the UI.

This should work independently of the global maxUploadSize setting and would allow per-upload granularity.

### Additional Context

Currently, developers are forced to do this after the file has already been uploaded:

```
uploaded_file = st.file_uploader("Upload a file")

if uploaded_file is not None:
    if uploaded_file.size > 5 * 1024 * 1024:
        st.error("File too large! Maximum allowed is 5MB.")
```

This defeats the purpose in many use cases, especially when working with limited bandwidth, slow connections, or when handling large files that could affect performance or cost.

This feature is common in many web frameworks and frontend components, and would be a great improvement to Streamlit’s already excellent developer experience.
issues.title: Add max_size parameter to each st.file_uploader to restrict file size before upload

### Problem

Currently, Streamlit allows us to define only **one** custom theme in the .streamlit/config.toml file. While this is a great feature, it feels limiting. Much like developers/users who enjoy switching between light and dark modes in their IDEs/browsers, I often want to change the look and feel of my app based on different contexts, events, or even personal mood. 

### Solution

```toml
# .streamlit/config.toml

[theme]
base = "corporate-light" # Default active theme key

# Define the "Corporate Light" theme
[theme.corporate-light]
name = "Corporate Light" # A friendly name, cannot use default theme 'dark' or 'light'
primaryColor = "#1e3a8a"
backgroundColor = "#ffffff"
secondaryBackgroundColor = "#f0f0f0"
textColor = "#31333F"
font = "sans serif"

# Define a "Midnight Dark" theme
[theme.midnight-dark]
name = "Midnight Dark"
primaryColor = "#bfdbfe"
backgroundColor = "#1e293b"
secondaryBackgroundColor = "#334155"
textColor = "#f1f5f9"
font = "sans serif"
```

### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

### Feature Request: Selective Rerun and Execution Control for `st.fragment`

Hi Streamlit team 👋

First of all, great job with the `st.fragment` feature — it’s super useful for improving interactivity and modularizing Streamlit apps.

I’d like to suggest two improvements for `st.fragment` that would make it even more powerful in terms of performance and control.

1. [also covered in #10603] The first is the ability to explicitly trigger the rerun of specific fragments from anywhere in the app, instead of being limited to interactions within that fragment. This would allow for more coordinated updates between fragments without requiring a full app rerun.

2. The second idea is to let developers prevent certain fragments from re-executing during a full rerun, keeping their state and UI output intact unless their input parameters change or they are explicitly refreshed. This would improve performance and user experience by avoiding unnecessary recomputation and visual flickering.

Overall, these additions would give developers finer control over fragment behavior and app performance.

Thanks for considering this! 🙏

### Why?

#### Why this would be useful

These two ideas would allow for finer-grained control over how fragments behave during reruns, enabling developers to:

* Improve performance in apps with multiple heavy components.
* Avoid unnecessary recomputation and UI flicker.
* Trigger coordinated updates between fragments dynamically.

Internally, I imagine Streamlit already tracks the execution scope and state for each fragment, so this might be feasible with some form of dependency or caching mechanism.

Thanks a lot for considering this! 🙏
I’d be happy to help clarify or provide examples if needed.

### How?

#### 1. Selective rerun of specific fragments

Right now, when something inside a fragment is interacted with, Streamlit reruns that fragment only, which is great.
However, it would be even better if we could *trigger reruns of specific fragments programmatically* — for example, from another fragment or from the main app.

Imagine something like:

```python
st.fragment(key="fragment_a")
def my_fragmen_a(param1, param2):
    ...

st.fragment(key="fragment_b")
def my_fragmen_b(param1, param2):
    ...

# Somewhere else:
st.rerun(scope=["fragment_a", "fragment_b"])
```

So if you define a fragment with a key, you could explicitly trigger its rerun (with or without passing new parameters).
This would make it possible to coordinate updates between fragments in a controlled way, without forcing a full rerun of the app.

---

#### 2. Ability to skip rerun for some fragments on full app rerun

Another idea: when the app performs a full rerun, it would be great to have a way to mark certain fragments so they *don’t* re-execute — keeping their current state and UI output as-is.

For example, you might have a heavy fragment (long computation, visualization, etc.) that you don’t want to rerun unless its input parameters have actually changed.

Something like:

```python
@st.fragment(key="heavy_plot", rerun="explicit")
def heavy_plot(data):
    ...
```

If the fragment’s inputs haven’t changed and no internal interaction happened, Streamlit could just reuse the previous rendered output instead of re-running the code.
This would not only improve performance but also help avoid UI flickering (the “greyed out” state that appears during reruns).

### Additional Context

_No response_
issues.title: Fragments are awesome but must to be more: Selective Rerun and Execution Control

### Checklist

### Summary

It would be great, if `AppTest` would check whether an element is disabled before updating its value. Trying to do so should lead to an error or at least a warning.

### Why?

When running AppTests I sometimes stumble upon cases, where the tests work even when they shouldn't ... just for me to find out, that again I changed values of disabled elements within the tests and `AppTest` happily does that.

Having at least a warning would make it easier to find those quirks in the tests.

### How?

Nothing needs to change in the interface.

For convenience and backward compatibility it would be possible to include a flag in `AppTest` to configure the behavior, e.g. `at = AppTest('test_main.py', default_timeout=30, on_update_disabled_element='warning')`
with the possible values:
- `accept`: take the new value without complaint (default, current behavior)
- `warning`: take the new value and issue a warning
- `error`: raise an error when trying to update a disabled element

### Additional Context

Below you can find a short example to illustrate the problem: currently the test succeeds even though changing the value would not be possible in the app itself.

To run the example
- save the code as `test_main.py`
- run `pytest`

```python
import streamlit as st
from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest

st.text_input('Text', value='initial value', disabled=True, key='k_text')


def test_disabled_input():
    at = AppTest('test_main.py', default_timeout=30)
    at.run()

    at.text_input(key='k_text').set_value('new value')
    at.run()

    assert at.text_input(key='k_text').value == 'new value'
```
issues.title: Prevent updates of disabled inputs in `AppTest`

### Summary

Give users the ability to control whether an empty expander should be rendered.  e.g.,
`st.expander(label, expanded=False, *, icon=None, width="stretch", display_empty=True)`

### Why?


I have an app that creates a series of expanders (to control the order in which they are rendered) and then populates them based on user selections.  Some expanders may thus not have any content.  It is desirable for these expanders to not be rendered.

Starting with Streamlit 1.47.0 empty expanders are displayed by default.  This was viewed as a bug fix.  Previously they were not rendered.  From my perspective, the older behavior was desirable. and the bug "fix" actually introduced a bug.  If there are some use cases for which one behavior is desired and other use cases where it is not then it should be user controlled.

### How?

Introduce an optional 'display_empty' parameter to the existing st.expander function.  It should accept a boolean that controls whether the expander is rendered when empty.  It can default to 'True' to be backwards compatible with current behavior.
`st.expander(label, expanded=False, *, icon=None, width="stretch", display_empty=True)`

### Additional Context

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

**The issue:** When you change a widget's value in the initialization of the widget (as opposed to session state update) **and** a key is specified, the widget value does not actually change.

**Motivation:** Per your release notes, I do recognize that this is an intended feature and not a bug. However, in practice, many of our applications heavily rely on some widgets/processes changing the state of other widgets. As a result this would force us to add more callback functionality with session state based updates of the widgets. For additional context of why we desire the previous behavior, consider that we initialize widgets via `st.query_params(...)`. This means that now that's no longer possible without also using callbacks and session state.

**Suggestion:** If this new feature is absolutely necessary, perhaps you can consider adding a kwarg to widgets along the lines of "allow override".

**Recorded Illustrations:**

In the illustrations below, I compare 1.50 to 1.49 using `st.text_area`, but this behavior applies to many other widgets. In the illustrations, what's different about 1.50 is that when the text area widget is asked to use a key (i.e. not `None`), then its value is unaffected by the other widget. This forces a cumbersome workaround of having to use callbacks with session state.

**Using 1.49.1**

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c94c163b-f512-488c-9d61-18eee2ad1138

**Using 1.50.0**

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bd60bda7-3dc9-4c27-bf40-3040f2ef2d31

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
some_text = st.text_input("Input")

key = "mirror_text" if st.checkbox("Use key for `st.text_area`", value=False) else None

mirror_text = st.text_area("Mirror", value=some_text, key=key)

mirror_text
```

### Steps To Reproduce

Run the code attached, and compare the behavior below with the checkbox **checked** vs **unchecked**.
1. Type something in the upper input box and hit Enter (to apply).
2. Observe whether the entered text appears in the text area (and subsequent output).
3. If you're in 1.50.0 **and you checked the the checkbox**, you will find that the output does NOT mirror the input. In 1.49.1, even if you check the checkbox, it will still mirror (desired behavior).

### Expected Behavior

Expected to see the second widget mirror the first, even though a key is specified (i.e. not `None`).

### Current Behavior

When a key is specified (i.e. not `None`) the second widget does NOT mirror the first.

### Is this a regression?

- [x] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.50.0
- Python version: 3.12
- Operating System: Windows/Linux
- Browser: Edge/Chrome


### Additional Information

_No response_
issues.title: widget values not updating if key is specified

I'd like to request the ability to provide our own relative dates. My suggestion is something like this: ```python custom_ranges = [ ("Yesterday & Today", lambda: (datetime.now().date() - timedelta(days=1), datetime.now().date())), ... # (label, method returning start & end) ] ``` I understand that this might be a problem since the frontend is not running python, so it's reasonable to alternatively rely on frontend-based solutions. Perhaps instead of the `lambda`, one could specify some string understood by the widget? 🤔 ### Why? Currently, we rely on the use of expanders/popovers and buttons to deliver the custom dates solution, but that takes up much valuable real estate on the screen. ### How? Please see above. Furthermore, I recommend using `list` not `dict` to ensure order. Yes, you can order in `dict` but probably many users might not handle that well. As for items, of course the label is included - would be nice if it can support all the cool streamlit features such as supporting material icons etc. As for dates, I suggested `lambda` as opposed to fixed dates since it's very likely that the user has a streamlit session open right around midnight (in the timezone of the server) when the day transitions. In the example, I used `datetime` and `timedelta` only for illustration, not for any preference. ### Additional Context _No response_

### Summary

Hello everyone, thank you for everything you have done. I am trying to encapsulate React components as streamlit components using custom components v2, but I have found that nesting between components is not possible. 

### Why?

Most React components require passing children to achieve their functionality, but passing child components seems impossible in streamlit. I have checked the documentation and community of v2 and have not found any solutions.

### How?

Usually we do this in React components：

```
<ConfigProvider>
  <Button>My Button</Button>
</ConfigProvider>
```

In streamlit, it seems like we should do it this way：

```
import custom_components as cc


cc.config_provider(cc.button("My Button"))
```

or

```
import custom_components as cc


with cc.config_provider():
       cc.button("My Button")
```

Taking this as an example, in React components, the ConfigProvider must have child components to demonstrate its function, but currently custom components v2 does not support this feature, so it is impossible to convert the ConfigProvider component into a streamlit component.

### Additional Context

_No response_
issues.title: Implement component nesting using custom components v2

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Instead of requiring an actual python file to be passed into `streamlit run`, it would be nice to use a python package location instead





### Why?

We use pants, and a launch by module feature would make our lives much better.

I would want to do the following in pants, where I do not have access to the final file path of the built module)

```python
pex_binary(
    name="streamlit_dash",
    entry_point="streamlit",
    dependencies=[
        "3rdparty/python#streamlit",
        "//my/dash:module",
    ],
    include_tools=True,
    # If I knew the final resolved path here I could use that, but I don't!
    # But I do know the module!
    args=["run", "my.dash.module"],
)
```


### How?

If a module was passed in, it could be converted to a file with the following:

```python
import importlib

module_file = importlib.import_module(module_name).__file__
```

In fact, I am currently using the following shim to make this work, but it's a little bit hacky:
```python
"""Shim so we can launch streamlit by module instead of by file.

This plays much better with pants pex binaries.
"""

import importlib
import sys

import streamlit.web.cli

if len(sys.argv) < 2:
    raise ValueError("No module specified to run.")
module_name = sys.argv[1]
module_file = importlib.import_module(module_name).__file__
sys.argv = ["streamlit", "run", module_file] + sys.argv[2:]
sys.exit(streamlit.web.cli.main())
```

It could even be behind a flag if that was easier, e.g. `--module=<module>`

### Additional Context

Similar to #662 but with a twist!

All code snippets included in this FR are released to the public domain.
issues.title: Launch by module - redux!

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Currently, Streamlit requires rerunning the entire script to refresh visual elements such as charts or plots.
This feature request suggests adding native support for incremental or real-time updates to chart components, allowing smoother dashboards for live data without script reruns.

### Why?

I often build dashboards with data that changes every few seconds (e.g. IoT sensors, live logs, financial data).
The current rerun mechanism makes the app flicker and consume excessive CPU, as every update forces Streamlit to re-execute all widgets and scripts.
A lighter update mechanism would make Streamlit much more efficient for real-time applications.

### How?

Introduce a new method, for example:

chart = st.line_chart(initial_data)
chart.update(new_data)


or a context manager such as:

with st.chart("my_chart") as chart:
    chart.update(data)


This would allow partial UI updates for selected components instead of full script reruns, leading to faster refresh rates and better performance.

### Additional Context

This feature would be highly valuable for real-time dashboards and data streaming use cases.
Similar functionality exists in libraries like Plotly Dash (dcc.Interval) or Bokeh Server.
Discussion inspiration: Streamlit Community Forum – Real-time dashboard performance
issues.title: Support real-time chart updates without rerunning the entire script

### Summary

If Streamlit shows an exception today, it lets you click a link to open the exception in ChatGPT. Could we automatically run it through an LLM instead and show a summary or some helpful tips inside the app?

### Why?

Makes it easier to understand exceptions shown in the app and saves time copy pasting things back and forth. 

### How?

- Probably we need some way for the dev to input an API key for their LLM of choice, ideally on a global level, so they could set it up for their laptop once and reuse it in every app. 
- Send the exception text and stacktrace to the LLM and ask for short advice. Show that in the app above or below the error. Should probably also show a nice loading animation while we're waiting for the reply. 
- Maybe we'd also want to put that behind a button, so it doesn't trigger a bunch of LLM requests on every error. 
- In Streamlit in Snowflake, maybe we enable this by default?

_No response_

issues.body:
Currently, Streamlit always renders the sidebar and multipage navigation menu before any backend logic runs.
This causes a brief flash (“flicker”) of the sidebar, even when developers try to hide it using CSS, st.set_page_config(initial_sidebar_state="collapsed"), or st.stop() during login checks.

Problem

When implementing authentication or loading processes (e.g., validating user credentials via an API), Streamlit renders the sidebar before the authentication state is known.
This behavior creates two key issues:

Security concern:
Unauthenticated users can briefly see and click sidebar navigation links before st.stop() halts the script, allowing them to access or attempt to load protected pages.
Even if no data is exposed, it creates a visible loophole and inconsistent behavior.

UX inconsistency:
The sidebar “flashes” for a fraction of a second during app load, even when the developer intends to display only a centered login screen or full-screen loading animation.
This leads to a jarring visual experience and makes professional deployments look less polished.

Why this matters

Many enterprise and production Streamlit apps use custom login systems, SSO integrations, or data validation APIs before showing any content.

In these cases, developers need full control over what renders before authentication completes.

There’s currently no reliable way to prevent the sidebar or multipage navigation from being rendered briefly.


Proposed solution

Add a configuration flag such as:
st.set_page_config(show_sidebar_on_load=False)
issues.title: Add an option to fully disable sidebar rendering until authentication or page load is complete

Run the app demo

issues.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

[`brand.yml`](https://posit-dev.github.io/brand-yml/) is an emerging simple YAML specification format designed to codify a company's branding guidelines. While developed by Posit and originally supported by Quarto and Shiny frameworks, the format is open-source and could be integrated with other tools and frameworks. Streamlit's support for `brand.yml` would benefit its users by allowing better interoperability with existing stack whilst providing maintainers with a ready-to-use specification for theming.

### Why?

Streamlit has recently added a number of features to enable wider customisation and theming of applications. Notably, #12572 introduced support for reusable custom themes. However, the library has been relying on `config.toml` as the way to define styling rules, such as colours, fonts, among other things. Adding support for `brand.yml` is not so much about solving a particular problem – in that one *can* already style applications using the TOML file – as it is about *streamlining the way* it's one. Here are a few potential benefits:

1. **Separation of configuration and theming logic**. `config.toml` can be used to configure various aspects of an application, including client, browser and server settings. Most of these are related to runtime settings rather than styling. Defining theme options in a separate `brand.yml` file would help to better structure applications.
2. **Industry standardisation**. Shiny for Python is a popular web app framework in Python. R Shiny is arguably the most popular web app framework in R. Quarto is a polyglot multi-format publishing system. All have some form of support for `brand.yml`. Adding integration with data visualisation libraries in Python is planned too (e.g., posit-dev/brand-yml#69, posit-dev/brand-yml#71). Supporting `brand.yml` in Streamlit would be a huge step in establishing a standardised way to define theming in the community.
3. **Enhanced operability**. Teams using a diverse stack would have easier time maintaining a single YAML file across different applications. In cross-functional teams, the work on `brand.yml` could be delegated to non-developers, such as designers, without exposing unnecessary runtime configuration and settings from `config.toml`.

### How?

In the short run, supporting the format would require adding an internal helper function that maps `brand.yml` specs to the options currently used by Streamlit. Many of these would nicely map to one another, e.g.,

| `brand.yml`                        | `config.toml`            |
|--------------------------|---------------------|
| `color.primary`                  | `primaryColor`         |
| `color.background`           | `backgroundColor` |
| `typography.link.color`     | `linkColor`                |
| `typography.base.family` | `font`                         |
| `typography.base.size`    | `baseFontSize `        |
| `typography.base.weight`| `baseFontWeight `   |

For end-users, one would either allow reusing `base` entry under `[theme]` section or add a new key `brand` in the same section:

```toml
[theme]

base ="https://company.com/brand.yml"
```

or

```toml
[theme]

brand ="https://company.com/brand.yml" # or a local path
```

Alternatively, `brand.yml` could be used automatically if present in the current working directory (which is what Quarto does).

In the long run, I would consider dropping the `theme` section in `config.toml` altogether in favour of a separate `brand.yml` file.

### Additional Context

- [`brand.yml` homepage](https://posit-dev.github.io/brand-yml/)
- There is also the [`defaults` section](https://posit-dev.github.io/brand-yml/brand/defaults.html). It does not have any strict validation rules, so this is where any theme settings Streamlit uses that cannot be mapped to existing brand sections could go.
- [`brand_yml` package](https://posit-dev.github.io/brand-yml/pkg/py/) in Python provides a lightweight wrapper with validation.
issues.title: Add support for `brand.yml` for theming

### Summary

Enhance Streamlit’s Exception Element to include key runtime metadata (for example, the user's Streamlit runtime version) alongside error messages. This would make errors more self-explanatory, help users quickly validate behavior against the correct docs for their version, and reduce unnecessary support cycles.

### Why?

Today, errors often lack the context needed for users to understand _why_ they’re happening. Adding concise metadata would empower users to self-diagnose version mismatches and environment issues more easily, while keeping the experience friendly and low-friction.

### How?

A possible approach is to enrich the Exception Element with a small "Environment" or "Details" section (ideally collapsible) that shows fields like Streamlit version, Python version, and OS.

The main error message would remain front-and-center, but users could expand this panel to see metadata and a short hint such as "You’re running Streamlit X.Y.Z. Check the X.Y.Z docs for feature availability."

Additionally, since our Docs supports versioned URLs, we could potentially deeplink to docs for the specific runtime version. eg: https://docs.streamlit.io/1.39.0/develop/api-reference/layout/st.container#stcontainer

### Additional Context

_No response_

### Summary

There was a recent fix to make the data and time icons visible in dark mode, but the color is hardcoded with the default for dark mode and doesn't pull from theming.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
from datetime import datetime
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

data_df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "appointment": [
            datetime(2024, 2, 5, 12, 30),
            datetime(2023, 11, 10, 18, 0),
            datetime(2024, 3, 11, 20, 10),
            datetime(2023, 9, 12, 3, 0),
        ]
    }
)

st.data_editor(
    data_df,
    column_config={
        "appointment": st.column_config.DatetimeColumn(
            "Appointment",
            min_value=datetime(2023, 6, 1),
            max_value=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
            format="D MMM YYYY, h:mm a",
            step=60,
        ),
    },
    hide_index=True,
)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Use:
  ```
  [theme]
  base="dark"
  textColor="red"
  ```
2. Double click in a cell to edit. (Also try with light base.)

### Expected Behavior

Both the "editting" color and the color icon should match the theme.

### Current Behavior

The "editting" color and icon color are stuck at the default text color for the base.
Light base: Editing text is black with a blue highlight and icon is black.
Dark base: Editing text is black with a blue highlight and icon is white.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.51.1.dev20251130
- Python version: 3.13
- Operating System: Mac
- Browser: Prisma

Add support in Streamlit’s data APIs (e.g. st.dataframe, charts) for consuming objects that implement [Apache Arrow’s PyCapsule](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/CDataInterface/PyCapsuleInterface.html) C data interface (via `__arrow_c_schema__`, `__arrow_c_array__`, `__arrow_c_stream__`, etc.), so that Arrow-compatible tables/streams from any library can be passed in without requiring a hard dependency on PyArrow or extra data copies. This would enable zero-copy interoperability with other Arrow-based ecosystems (including potential device-backed data via the device variants of these methods) and make Streamlit more future-proof as more Python libraries adopt this standardized Arrow PyCapsule protocol.

### Additional Context

- https://github.com/vega/altair/issues/3568#issue-2506363561
- https://github.com/narwhals-dev/narwhals/pull/1181

     # has more control over the conversion, and may have broader compatibility. 
     # This is the case for Polars, which supports Date32 columns in direct conversion 
     # while pyarrow does not yet support this type in from_dataframe 
     for convert_method_name in ("arrow", "to_arrow", "to_arrow_table", "to_pyarrow"): 
         convert_method = getattr(dfi_df, convert_method_name, None) 
         if callable(convert_method): 
```

    return pa.table(dfi_df)

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

**Description:**

As a Streamlit user, I've noticed that default error messages include helpful links like "Ask Google" and "Ask ChatGPT" to assist with debugging. This is a great feature for quick troubleshooting.

I propose adding "Ask Ollama" as an additional option. Ollama is an open-source platform for running LLMs locally (https://ollama.com/), which could provide users with a privacy-focused, offline alternative for querying errors.

**Rationale:**
- Promotes open-source tools in the ecosystem.
- Appeals to users concerned about data privacy or those without reliable internet.
- Keeps the suggestions balanced between cloud (Google, ChatGPT) and local options.

**Potential Implementation:**
- Add a link similar to the existing ones, perhaps pointing to a pre-formatted query for Ollama's interface or documentation on how to use it for code errors.
- Ensure it's optional or configurable if needed.

This could enhance Streamlit's developer experience without significant overhead. Happy to discuss or contribute if feasible!

### Why?

### Why Consider Adding Ollama?
Ollama is an open-source tool for running large language models locally, offering privacy and customization benefits over cloud-based services like ChatGPT. Integrating it as a suggestion could appeal to users preferring offline or self-hosted AI for error analysis. However, implementation might involve UI changes and ensuring compatibility with Streamlit's error rendering system.

### How?

### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

If you use deferred download with `st.download_button`, there should be a way to catch errors that may be raised by the deferred generation function. Currently, if the funciton encounters an error, a warning message is displayed on the frontend and isn't accessible on the backend.

### Why?

When you use deferred download with `st.download_button`, the function which returns the download runs on its own thread so it won't block the script thread. This has two consequences:
1. There is no script context, so you can't use any Streamlit command, like `st.session_state`. (See #13337).
2. You can't handle errors raised by the deferred download function.

You can put try-catch blocks in your download function to avoid an unhandled error, but you can't really _do_ anything about it because you can't display a custom message or log something in Session State. (Maybe you could hack a solution by writing something to a temporary file on the server, but that doesn't seem ideal.)

### How?

A couple different solutions:
* Have the download button return an error if encountered so it can be caught in the main script.
* Give the download thread some (possibly restricted) script context (like #13337).
* Improve multithreading support more generally, and have some hook at the end of a script run to catch a session's child threads, like the download thread.

### Additional Context

_No response_
issues.title: For deferred download with `st.download_button`, pipe errors to the script thread

### Summary

Streamlit should automatically refresh an expired access token (and retry the failed request) when using auth flows that rely on short-lived access tokens plus a refresh token (OAuth 2.0, OIDC). This would prevent apps from breaking mid-session and reduce the need for developers to implement custom retry and refresh logic.

### Why?

Access tokens are commonly short-lived by design. In a typical Streamlit app session, a user may keep a tab open for hours while interacting intermittently. When the token expires, the next API call fails (often with a 401/403), forcing developers to handle a messy set of edge cases:
- Users experience confusing failures, blank charts, or “something went wrong” messages, even though their session is otherwise valid.
- Developers end up re-implementing token refresh in many slightly different ways, often with subtle bugs (race conditions across reruns, double refresh, infinite retry loops).
- Re-auth flows can be disruptive, especially if the only issue is an expired access token and a refresh token is available.
- This is especially common when Streamlit is used as a front-end for calling third-party APIs (Google, Microsoft, GitHub, Salesforce, custom OAuth providers) or internal services behind OIDC.
A built-in refresh mechanism improves reliability, reduces boilerplate, and aligns Streamlit with how most modern client apps handle expiring tokens.

issues.body:
# Feature Request: Allow hashing of plain Python classes by handling standard library functions

## Summary

Streamlit's caching mechanism currently rejects plain Python classes because it cannot hash the `copyreg._reconstructor` function that appears in their default `__reduce__()` output. This can be fixed by adding support for hashing standard library functions by their fully qualified names, allowing common Python classes to work with `st.cache_resource` and `st.cache_data` without requiring the verbose `hash_funcs` workaround.

## Why?

**Current Problem:**

When users try to cache functions with plain Python class instances as arguments, they get a confusing error:

```python
import streamlit as st

class Data:
    def __init__(self, payload: bytes):
        self.payload = payload

@st.cache_resource
def transform(data: Data) -> Data:
    return Data(payload=b'new')

data = Data(payload=b'old')
transform(data)  # ❌ UnhashableParamError: Cannot hash argument 'data'
```

**Error:** `TypeError: cannot pickle 'function' object` → `UnhashableParamError`

This is confusing because:

- The `Data` class IS pickle-serializable (`pickle.dumps(data)` works fine)
- The documentation says "arguments must be hashable" but plain classes fail
- Users must add `hash_funcs` to every decorator, which is verbose

**Root Cause:**

Streamlit uses `__reduce__()` (from the pickle protocol) to generate cache keys. Python's default `__reduce__()` for plain classes returns `copyreg._reconstructor` as the first element. Streamlit can hash builtins but not regular standard library functions, so it tries to call `__reduce__()` on the function itself, which fails.

**Impact:**

This affects all plain Python classes without custom `__reduce__()` methods - a very common use case. Users must use the `hash_funcs` workaround for every cached function:

```python
@st.cache_resource(hash_funcs={Data: lambda d: d.payload})
def transform(data: Data):
    return Data(payload=b'new')
```

## How?

Add handling for standard library functions in `lib/streamlit/runtime/caching/hashing.py`.

## Additional Context

**Related Issues:**

- **#13480** - Original bug report (this enhancement solves it)
- **#10348** - Feature request for custom `__streamlit_hash__()` (complementary - handles advanced cases)
- **#7966** - Broader request to improve custom class hashing
- **#6703** - Request for non-serializable objects (different problem)
- **#1399** (docs repo) - Documentation clarity improvement

---

**Note:** This enhancement provides automatic support for the common case (plain classes). Issue #10348 proposes adding `__streamlit_hash__()` for advanced customization. Together, these would provide both automatic support (this enhancement) and user control (#10348).
issues.title: Allow hashing of plain Python classes by handling standard library functions

Starting with **Streamlit 1.53**, we're introducing experimental support for running Streamlit with [Starlette](https://www.starlette.io/) as the underlying web framework. This is the first step toward our long-term goal of **fully migrating from Tornado to Starlette/ASGI**, and we need your help to identify any issues or gaps before the full transition. ## What's New > **Note:** To use the experimental Starlette features, you need to install the optional dependencies: > > ```bash > pip install streamlit[starlette] > ``` ### 1. Starlette Server Mode (Experimental) You can now run Streamlit using Starlette instead of Tornado by setting a config option: ```toml # .streamlit/config.toml [server] useStarlette = true ``` Or via command line: ```bash streamlit run app.py --server.useStarlette=true ``` ### 2. ASGI App Entry Point (Experimental) For advanced use cases, you can now create an ASGI-compatible Streamlit application using the new `App` class: ```python from streamlit.starlette import App app = App("main.py") ``` Run it with `streamlit run` (preferred): ```bash streamlit run myapp.py ``` Streamlit will automatically detect the `App` instance and run it in Starlette mode. Alternatively, you can use any ASGI server directly: ```bash uvicorn myapp:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8501 ``` The `App` class supports advanced configuration including: - **Custom HTTP routes** — Add REST API endpoints alongside your Streamlit app - **Middleware** — Add security headers, authentication, logging, etc. - **Lifespan hooks** — Run code on startup/shutdown (e.g., pre-warm caches, initialize resources) - **Framework integration** — Mount Streamlit inside FastAPI, Django, or other ASGI frameworks > 📖 For more details on the `App` interface and its full capabilities, see the [specification in PR #13449](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/13449).
Example: Adding custom routes ```python from streamlit.starlette import App from starlette.routing import Route from starlette.responses import JSONResponse async def health_check(request): return JSONResponse({"status": "healthy", "service": "streamlit-app"}) async def get_data(request): return JSONResponse({"items": ["apple", "banana", "cherry"], "count": 3}) app = App( "main.py", routes=[ Route("/api/health", health_check), Route("/api/data", get_data), ], ) ```
Example: Adding custom middleware ```python from streamlit.starlette import App from starlette.middleware import Middleware from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware class SecurityHeadersMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware): async def dispatch(self, request, call_next): response = await call_next(request) response.headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff" response.headers["X-Frame-Options"] = "SAMEORIGIN" return response app = App( "main.py", middleware=[Middleware(SecurityHeadersMiddleware)], ) ```
Example: Mounting FastAPI in Streamlit ```python from fastapi import FastAPI from starlette.routing import Mount from streamlit.starlette import App # Create FastAPI sub-application api = FastAPI() @api.get("/health") async def health(): return {"status": "healthy"} @api.post("/predict") async def predict(data: dict): return {"prediction": data.get("value", 0) * 2} # Mount FastAPI into Streamlit app # - Streamlit UI at / # - FastAPI endpoints at /api/* # - FastAPI docs at /api/docs app = App( "dashboard.py", routes=[Mount("/api", app=api)], ) ```
Example: Mounting Streamlit in FastAPI ```python from fastapi import FastAPI from streamlit.starlette import App # Create the Streamlit sub-application streamlit_app = App("dashboard.py") # Create FastAPI with Streamlit's lifespan to manage the runtime lifecycle api = FastAPI(lifespan=streamlit_app.lifespan()) @api.get("/api/data") async def get_data(): return {"data": [1, 2, 3]} # Mount Streamlit under /dashboard api.mount("/dashboard", streamlit_app) # Run with: uvicorn myapp:api ```
Example: Lifespan hooks for startup/shutdown ```python from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from streamlit.starlette import App @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app): # Startup: runs before accepting connections print("🚀 Starting up...") model = load_ml_model() # Pre-warm caches db = init_db_connection() # Yield state accessible via app.state yield {"model": model, "db": db} # Shutdown: cleanup resources print("👋 Shutting down...") db.close() app = App("main.py", lifespan=lifespan) ```
## Why We're Migrating to Starlette/ASGI The migration to Starlette/ASGI will unlock numerous frequently-requested features: ### Custom HTTP Endpoints - #439 - #9673 - #6195 - #9090 - #11333 - #8713 ### Security Headers & Middleware - #6417 - #9160 - #861 - #8823 ### Framework Integration & ASGI Support - #4311 - #4567 - #927 - #7546 ### Server Configuration & Lifecycle - #7688 - #8991 - #6108 - #9916 - #8545 - #7667 - #11050 - #10543 - #3426 - #8661 ### SEO & Metadata - #5673 - #8999 ### Advanced App Execution - #4162 - #9450 - #12972 - #662 ## We Need Your Feedback Since we plan to eventually make Starlette the default (and only) server backend, we want to catch any compatibility issues early. Please help us by: ### 1. Try it out Enable Starlette mode in your existing apps: ```bash streamlit run your_app.py --server.useStarlette=true ``` ### 2. Report any issues If you encounter problems, please comment below with: - **What happened** — Error messages, unexpected behavior - **Your environment** — OS, Python version, Streamlit version - **How to reproduce** — Minimal code example if possible - **Comparison** — Does the issue occur with the default Tornado server? ### 3. Share your use cases We're especially interested in: - ⚡ Performance comparisons (response times, memory usage, concurrent users) - 🔌 Integration scenarios (FastAPI, Django, other ASGI frameworks) - 🛡️ Security/middleware requirements - 🚀 Deployment configurations (uvicorn, gunicorn, hypercorn, cloud platforms) ## Known Limitations - This is **experimental** — APIs may change before the final release - TBD --- **Thank you for helping us build a better Streamlit!** Your early feedback is invaluable in ensuring a smooth transition for the entire community. 🙏 Please comment below with your experiences, questions, or concerns. ![Views](https://api.views-badge.org/badge/st-issue-13600)

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

A streamlit log handler to allow using Streamlit to show logs.

### Why?

Python's built-in logging framework is extremely versatile. Hooking into that would make debugging easier.

In my own app, I have observations I both want to save to a log system and show to the user. Having a streamlit log handler allows me to do that without duplicating code.

### How?

I have written something that I use in my own project that can be used as a starting place:

```
import logging

import streamlit as st


class StreamlitLogHandler(logging.Handler):
    """
    Log handler to display logs in Streamlit app.

    This handler formats log messages and sends them to the Streamlit app for display.
    If the log record contains an "object" attribute, its value will be displayed in an expander.
    If the log record contains a "link" attribute, the log text will be a link with the content as the target address.

    If streamlit session state contains a "log_container", logs will be displayed there.
    Otherwise, logs will be displayed on the page as they are emitted.
    """

    @staticmethod
    def get_icon(levelno: int) -> str:
        if levelno <= logging.INFO:
            return "ℹ️"
        elif levelno <= logging.WARNING:
            return "⚠️"
        elif levelno <= logging.ERROR:
            return "❌"
        else:
            return "🛑"

    def emit(self, record: logging.LogRecord):
        if "log_container" in st.session_state and isinstance(
            st.session_state["log_container"], st.delta_generator.DeltaGenerator
        ):
            log_container = st.session_state["log_container"]
        else:
            log_container = st
        msg = self.format(record)
        if "link" in record.__dict__:
            msg = f"[{msg}]({record.__dict__['link']})"
        if "object" in record.__dict__:
            with log_container.expander(
                msg, expanded=False, icon=self.get_icon(record.levelno)
            ):
                log_container.write(record.__dict__["object"])
        else:
            if record.levelno <= logging.INFO:
                log_container.info(msg)
            elif record.levelno <= logging.WARNING:
                log_container.warning(msg)
            else:
                log_container.error(msg)

```

The "log_containter" in st.session_state allows you to specify where the logs should be shown. The obvious use case is a collapsed expander that can be opened to see what logs there are. It is not the most transparent way of doing it, and it risks them not being shown (if it is set on on page, and the page is then changed).

You can set the object to show by e.g. `logger.error("Example error log message", extra={"object": object_to_log})`

You can set where you want the text to link to by e.g `logger.error("Example error log message.",extra={"link": "#" + self.name})`. This allows you to link in the same page (used as shown) or another page. You could also make the log message into a markdown text with the link, but you typically don't want that in other log systems, so doing that would make the logging less versatile.

This is just a suggestion, it works for my app, but I am sure many improvements can be done. 

### Additional Context

_No response_

### Summary


The current `st.number_input` converts numbers to float when using the increment/decrement buttons and discards leading zeros. This makes it unsuitable for fields like phone numbers, OTPs, or IDs. A new number input field is needed that allows specifying type (int or float), preserves exact input formatting, and supports min, max, and step attributes.


### Why?


I'm often frustrated when trying to use `st.number_input` for inputs like phone numbers, OTPs, or IDs. Even when using `step=1` to indicate integers, the input still removes leading zeros (e.g., entering `043` becomes `43`) and behaves unexpectedly for exact numeric input. This limits the use of `st.number_input` for non-mathematical numeric fields.



### How?


Introduce a new Streamlit input widget, e.g., `st.digit_input`, or extend `st.number_input` with the following features:

- `type`: "int" or "float", to preserve the desired numeric type
- `min_value` and `max_value` support as currently implemented
- `step`: optional, for increment/decrement buttons
- Preserve exact input as typed, including leading zeros
- Return value type matches `type` argument, without unwanted conversions

### Example usage
```python
import streamlit as st

# Allow exact integer input for phone numbers
phone = st.digit_input("Phone Number", type="int", min_value=0)
st.write(phone)
st.write(type(phone))

### Additional Context


This request comes from issues discussed in the Streamlit community forum regarding using st.number_input for phone numbers, OTPs, and IDs where leading zeros matter. The current behaviour discards leading zeros and returns a float when using step buttons, which is inconvenient for these use cases.
issues.title: Add a number input field that preserves integer formatting and supports min/max without converting to float

### Summary

I am requesting that Streamlit add an `isAuthEnabled` boolean flag to the `/_stcore/host-config` JSON endpoint. This would allow clients and scanners to explicitly verify if a Streamlit instance has authentication configured without needing to execute JavaScript or render the full application.

### Why?

The primary driver for this request is security observability. Because Streamlit is a Single Page Application (SPA), the server returns the same generic HTML skeleton regardless of whether the app is publicly accessible or locked behind a login screen. Standard HTTP scanners cannot differentiate between a secured app and an open one because the UI, including any login forms, is only hydrated after JavaScript execution. This limitation forces teams to use resource-intensive headless browsers like Puppeteer just to perform basic inventory checks. Organizations managing multiple internal tools need a lightweight, programmatic method to instantly detect instances that may have been accidentally deployed without authentication.

### How?

The solution is to modify the host-config endpoint, which is already used to bootstrap frontend configuration, to include the authentication status of the server. This would provide a standard, machine-readable location for the application to declare its security posture.

**Proposed Response:**
```json
{
  "allowedOrigins": [],
  "mapboxToken": "...",
  "isAuthEnabled": true
}
```

### Additional Context

_No response_
issues.title: Expose authentication status in host-config endpoint

### Summary

When running a Streamlit app for the first time in a fresh uv environment, users experience a 5-10 second blank screen before the first element appears. This creates a poor first impression and makes Streamlit appear slow or broken.

`uv` defers Python bytecode compilation (.pyc files) to runtime for faster install times. This means heavy packages like pandas get compiled on first import, causing the delay. Since many Streamlit apps start with `import pandas as pd`, this is a common experience.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st 

st.write("Hello")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

_No response_

### Expected Behavior

### Option 1: Recommend/document UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE

Users (and our own tooling) could install with bytecode pre-compilation:

```
UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 uv pip install streamlit pandas
# or
uv pip install --compile-bytecode streamlit pandas
```

This moves the compilation cost to install time rather than first run.

### Option 2: Surface the delay more clearly

Instead of a blank screen, show a loading indicator or message during initial imports. However, this is tricky since we don't know what packages the user's app imports until it runs.


### Current Behavior

```
uv venv && uv pip install streamlit pandas
streamlit run app.py
# → Browser opens → 5-10 sec blank screen → App finally renders
```

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

- Browser:

import streamlit as st

if (
    "mock_element_id" not in st.session_state
    or st.session_state["mock_element_id"] not in element_to_idx
):

### Summary

Add a `type` parameter to badge markdown syntax (`:color-badge[text]`) to support different visual styles beyond the current filled background. This would enable tertiary (no background) and outline / secondary (border only) badge variants, similar to how `st.button` supports different types.

I guess today the current default is `primary`? 

### Why?

When displaying multiple badges inline (e.g., metadata tags for list items), the current filled-background style can be visually heavy and distracting. Having lighter-weight badge variants would:

- Improve visual hierarchy by allowing less prominent badges alongside primary ones
- Reduce visual clutter in information-dense UIs
- Provide consistency with other Streamlit components that support type variants (buttons, etc.)

**Example use case:** In a list of metrics, each item shows multiple metadata badges (metric type, aggregation unit, estimand). Using all filled badges makes the UI feel cluttered:

```python
# Current - all badges have filled backgrounds, can feel heavy
st.markdown("metric_name :gray-background[:small[2°]] :gray-background[:small[account]] :gray-background[:small[Mean diff]]")
```

### How?

Introduce a `type` modifier to the badge syntax:

```python
st.badge("Active", color="blue", type="tertiary")
```

Also in inline Markdown

```python
# Filled (current default)
st.markdown(":blue-badge[Active]")

# Tertiary - no background, just colored text
st.markdown(":blue-badge-tertiary[Active]")
# or
st.markdown(":blue-badge[Active]{type=tertiary}")

# Outline - transparent background with colored border
st.markdown(":blue-badge-outline[Active]")
# or  
st.markdown(":blue-badge[Active]{type=outline}")
```

**Proposed types:**
| Type | Background | Border | Text |
|------|-----------|--------|------|
| `default` (current) = `primary` | Filled color | None | Contrasting |
| `tertiary` | Transparent | None | Colored |
| `secondary` | Transparent | Colored | Colored |

### Additional Context

This follows the pattern established by `st.button(type="primary|secondary|tertiary")` and would make badges more flexible for different UI contexts.

Visual reference for outline/ghost badge styles:
- [Chakra UI Badge variants](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/components/badge)
- [Ant Design Tag](https://ant.design/components/tag)
issues.title: Add type parameter to badges for different visual styles (tertiary, outline)

### Summary

Add an `anchors=False` parameter to `st.markdown()` to disable automatic anchor links on headers within markdown content. Currently, `st.header()` and `st.subheader()` support `anchor=False`, but there's no way to disable anchors for headers (h1-h6) rendered via `st.markdown()`.

### Why?

When using markdown headers (`###`, `####`, etc.) for styling purposes (e.g., to get larger text) rather than for navigation, the auto-generated anchor links can be confusing for users. The current workarounds are:
- Use raw HTML instead of markdown headers
- Only use `st.header()`/`st.subheader()` which support `anchor=False`, but these don't cover h4-h6

### How?

Introduce a new parameter to `st.markdown()`:

```python
st.markdown("### My heading", anchors=False)
```

This would disable anchor links for all headers in that markdown block.

### Additional Context

This came from an internal discussion. The existing `anchor=False` on `st.header()` and `st.subheader()` is great, but extending this to `st.markdown()` would provide a complete solution for users who want styled text without navigation anchors.
issues.title: Add anchors=False parameter to st.markdown()

### Summary

Our widgets currently mix 16px and 14px font sizes. Some widgets are completely 14px (e.g. `st.pills`) while others are completely 16px (e.g. `st.checkbox`), and others use 16px for their value and 14px for their label (e.g. `st.selectbox). Let's unify to make all of them 14px. 

### Why?

More coherent and modern look. 

### How?

Notes:
- This should also affect some non-widget elements like `st.expander`. 
- The only elements that should stay 16px are normal text (e.g. via `st.markdown`) and status elements (e.g. `st.warning`). 
- We should probably adjust icon sizes as well. We currently use 20px icons (for 16px font size), but should move to 16px icons with 14px font size (same as e.g. the sidebar navigation today). 

Elements affected: 
- st.button, st.download_button, st.link_button
- st.page_link
- st.toggle
- st.checkbox
- st.radio
- st.selectbox (incl. dropdown)
- st.multiselect (incl. dropdown)
- st.color_picker dropdown
- st.number_input
- st.date_input, st.time_input, st.datetime_input (incl. dropdowns)
- st.text_input
- st.text_area
- st.audio_input error text
- st.file_uploader (currently being revamped)
- st.camera_input (incl. error text)
- st.expander, st.status
- st.popover
- st.chat_input

Hi,

I'm following up on the "State and cache visualizer" mentioned in the roadmap. I don't know how high this item is on the roadmap priority list, but I'd like to point out a pain point related to this in the current developer experience. Today, the cache is a bit of a "black box", and in a complex app with dozens of `@st.cache_data` functions, it becomes difficult to identify bottlenecks.

In my case, I want to be able to easily see the following for the entire cache:
- Execution Metrics: Latency (execution time) and last refresh timestamp.
- Efficiency: Hit/Miss ratios per function.
- Resources: Memory footprint of cached objects.

I also wonder if this feature could be delivered incrementally. Even before the full feature is ready, providing a programmatic way to access statistics (e.g., via a `st.cache.get_stats()`) which are already easily available.
issues.title: Cache Observability

### Summary

## Summary
Enable dynamic theme updates at runtime to allow user-specific theming without requiring an application restart. Currently, Streamlit theme settings (e.g., `theme.backgroundColor`, `theme.primaryColor`, etc.) can only be defined via `config.toml` or CLI flags and cannot be modified during execution.

### Why?

## Why
Modern applications commonly support user-personalized themes such as light/dark mode toggles, custom accent colors, and persisted UI preferences. 

In multi-user environments (e.g., SaaS dashboards or internal tools), users expect:
- Theme selection per account
- Persistent UI preferences
- Instant theme switching without downtime

The current limitation forces developers to:
- Use unsupported CSS injection hacks
- Run multiple app instances with different themes
- Or migrate to a full frontend framework

This increases architectural complexity for what should be a UI-level capability.

### How?

## How
Introduce an official runtime API for updating theme settings dynamically, scoped per user session.

Example proposal:

```python
st.set_theme(
    backgroundColor="#f5efe6",
    secondaryBackgroundColor="#e8dfd4",
    primaryColor="#c08a5b",
    textColor="#3a312b"
)

Hi,

I’ve been following the recent updates with great interest, especially @jrieke's  [blog post](https://blog.streamlit.io/one-million-streamlit-developers-3335b0cdc24b) about focusing on dashboards (better dataframes, deeper drill-down and data exploration), and the 🩺 data wrangler planned in the [roadmap](https://roadmap.streamlit.app/). I also noticed @mayagbarnes's  [work on the pivot table prototype](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14254), which looks very promising!

I wanted to share a specific use case from my professional experience, hoping it might help nourish your reflection on how these summary features could evolve.

I work for [Cohorte Constances](https://www.constances.fr/en/home/), the largest epidemiological cohort in France. We manage vast amounts of health data. We are currently in the middle of a major migration from legacy tools to a modern Python stack. In this transition, Streamlit has become our cornerstone for data exploration, monitoring, and sharing research results.

In medical research and epidemiology, our "daily bread" is the construction of summary tables (often called "Table 1" to describe population characteristics). Currently, to achieve a professional-looking summary table in Streamlit, I find myself juggling several tools: the native dataframe component, `streamlit-aggrid`, `tableone`, `great-tables`, and sometimes a lot of custom CSS/HTML. While it works, it feels a bit fragmented.

In the R ecosystem, there is a library called [gtsummary](https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/gtsummary/) that is almost a "gold standard" for researchers. It manages:

- Automatic calculation of statistics (Mean/SD, Median/IQR, N/%) based on variable types.
- Elegant stratification (comparing groups side-by-side).
- Clean, publication-ready layouts (proper indentation, bold labels).

As you work on "pivot tables & summaries" I think looking at the logic of `gtsummary` could be interesting. Imagine a native Streamlit component that combines that kind of statistical power with interactivity.

I don't have a fixed set of specs to propose, but I truly believe that bridging this gap between "raw data" and "statistical summary" would be a game-changer for the scientific community and would attract many researchers to Streamlit.

Thank you for the amazing work you do 😉
