### Summary

Officially support running Streamlit in the browser via Pyodide / WebAssembly (fully client-side, no Python server). Today this is only possible through the community project [stlite](https://github.com/whitphx/stlite), which requires dedicated maintenance and always lags slightly behind Streamlit releases.

### Why?

Running Streamlit fully client-side enables serverless deployment, easy sharing, offline demos, and embedding without hosting a Python backend. The popularity of stlite proves the demand, but as a separate effort it always trails official releases and needs ongoing patching to stay compatible.

### How?

Two possible options:

1. Make the `streamlit` package itself Pyodide-compatible (guard/avoid non-WASM-friendly dependencies and APIs, e.g. threading, sockets, and the tornado/uvicorn server bits).
2. Distribute a second, patched package that is built and published automatically as part of the main Streamlit CI / release process, so it stays in lock-step with every release.

### Additional Context

Community project: https://github.com/whitphx/stlite

### Summary

Introduce an explicit **development mode** vs. **production mode** distinction for Streamlit apps, with each mode optimizing execution and UI for its use case. By default, use development mode when we detect local development, with a configuration option to set it explicitly.

### Why?

Streamlit currently treats local development and deployed apps the same. Local development benefits from richer debugging and warnings, while deployed apps benefit from performance optimizations and a cleaner, end-user-facing UI. A clear mode distinction lets us tune both without compromise.

### How?

**Detection / opt-in:** config option, CLI flag, environment variable, or request origin (e.g. requests from `127.0.0.1` are likely the developer — with a caveat for Docker-based dev). Possibly a dedicated `streamlit debug app.py` command to promote the feature.

**Production mode — optimize execution & clean up UI:**
- Skip code-hashing in `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource` (small speedup when the code isn't changing).
- Disable the file watcher to save resources — but keep it enabled on Streamlit Community Cloud.
- Route deprecation/dev warnings and parameter-hash warnings to stderr instead of printing them in the app UI.
- Optionally hide/simplify the hamburger menu,

**Development mode — a "Debug Toolbar"-style panel** (e.g. a button in the bottom corner, similar to "Manage app"), with focused sub-panels:
- Cache inspector (view & clear cache).
- Metrics panel.
- SQLAlchemy / SQL query inspector.
- Variable, state, and cache inspection/visualization.
- Show deprecation & dev-specific warnings in the browser.
- Theme editing, preheating, and other WYSIWYG dev conveniences.

**Open question:** naming — "Development / Production" vs. "Debug / Release" mode.

### Additional Context

- Related: [Ability to hide the hamburger menu (#395)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/395)
- Prior art: [Django Debug Toolbar](https://django-debug-toolbar.readthedocs.io/) and [streamlit-forum](https://github.com/snehankekre/streamlit-forum).
issues.title: Add dedicated development and production modes to optimize app execution

### Summary

With Flex layout we added `width="stretch"` (and `height="stretch"`) to most elements, making them fill the remaining space. When multiple elements in a container use `"stretch"`, they currently split the available space equally. Add a way to control how much space each stretch element takes **relative to the others** (e.g. make element A take twice the space of element B), similar to `st.columns([2, 1])`.

### Why?

Sometimes you want to distribute the available space unevenly among stretch elements, but today all `"stretch"` elements get equal size, so there's no way to express "A should be twice as wide as B". (Related demand: #11715.)

### How?

Add a relative "weight" to `stretch`. A few API options are under discussion:

- `width="stretch:2"` (string weight — `stretch:1` would be equivalent to `stretch`)
- `width=("stretch", 2)` (tuple — explicitly typeable)
- a new `scale=N` parameter

**Behavior:** weights distribute space proportionally among sibling stretch elements, matching `st.columns`. E.g. if a container is 600px wide, element A has `width="stretch:2"`, and element B has `width="stretch"`, then A is 400px and B is 200px. The same applies to `height`.

### Additional Context

- Related: #11715 (relative amount of available width) and #12900 (multiple `width="stretch"` elements should have same width).
issues.title: Relative stretch widths/heights: control how much space stretch elements take relative to each other

### Summary

```python
st.text_input("Website", prefix="https://")
st.text_input("Email", suffix="@gmail.com")
st.text_input("Weight", suffix="kg")
```

Naming TBD (e.g. `prefix`/`suffix` vs `prepend`/`append`). The added text is display-only and not part of the widget's returned value. Could build on the existing `icon` addon slot.

### Summary

Add a `st.sidebar.bottom` container that pins its elements to the bottom of the sidebar, analogous to how `st.bottom` pins elements to the bottom of the main app section.

### Why?

It's a very common pattern to keep certain sidebar content anchored at the bottom — user/account info, a logout button, app version, links, or a settings/theme toggle — while the rest of the sidebar scrolls above it. Today there's no clean way to do this; users resort to spacers or CSS hacks that break across screen sizes and content lengths.

### How?

Mirror the existing `st.bottom` API, scoped to the sidebar:

```python
with st.sidebar.bottom():
    st.caption("Logged in as jane@example.com")
    st.button("Log out")
```

The container sticks to the bottom of the sidebar, with the normal (scrollable) sidebar content flowing above it.

### Summary

Provide a button group that supports **trigger (click) mode** instead of selection mode — i.e. a horizontal group of buttons that returns the clicked value once (like `st.button`) and clears after the rerun, rather than persisting a selection. This can either be a new `st.button_group` command or an extension of the existing `st.pills` / `st.segmented_control`.

### Why?

It's currently a bit complicated to build things like quick selections / quick replies for chat UIs (a major need for LLM-powered apps), button toolbars, dialog action rows (Confirm / Cancel / Clear), or clickable example grids. Today you have to combine many individual `st.button`s across `st.columns`, which is a lot of boilerplate and looks messy because wrapping depends on each button's label length.

### How?

Two main options:

**Option 1 — Extend `st.pills` / `st.segmented_control` with a trigger mode:**

```python
st.pills(..., selection_mode="single" | "multi" | "trigger")
```

In `trigger` mode the widget doesn't keep state: it returns the clicked value and clears it after the rerun (like a button), returning `None` otherwise. `default` wouldn't be allowed in this mode.

**Option 2 — Add a dedicated `st.button_group` command (preferred):**

```python
st.button_group(
    options,
    *,
    format_func=None,
    key=None,
    on_click=None,
    args=None,
    kwargs=None,
    disabled=False,
    type="default" | "rounded",
    wrap=True,
)
```

Behaves like `st.pills` but tailored for triggers: no top label/help (not needed for quick selections), `on_click` instead of `on_change` (aligns with `st.button`), a `type` option for a rounded pill-like look, and a `wrap` option. Keeping triggers in a separate command avoids overloading the selection API (e.g. `selection_mode="trigger"` reads oddly, `default` becomes incompatible, and typing gets awkward).

### Additional Context

- Related: #8318 (quick replies/suggestions for chat responses) — one of the primary motivating use cases.
- Other use cases: button toolbars, dialog action rows, and clickable example grids.
issues.title: Add a button group widget with trigger (click) mode

### Summary

Add a way to render the rows of a dataset (dataframe or any data structure supported by `st.dataframe`) using **different layouts** — e.g. list, gallery/cards, board (kanban), and timeline — similar to how Notion can display the same database as a table, gallery, list, board, or timeline. Today `st.dataframe` only offers the interactive table layout.

### Why?

The interactive table is great for tabular data, but many datasets are better presented as cards/galleries (e.g. products, images, profiles), lists, kanban boards (grouped by a status column), or timelines (by a date column). Building these today requires a lot of manual layout work with columns/containers/HTML. A first-class element would make rich, non-tabular data presentations a one-liner and reuse the existing dataframe data handling and column config.

### How?

**Preferred — a single `st.data_viewer` command with a `layout` option:**

```python
st.data_viewer(df, layout="gallery" | "list" | "board" | "timeline" | "table")
```

This keeps everything in one element (one command to learn, one place for shared params) without overloading `st.dataframe`, while still exposing all layouts via a single `layout` argument.

Other API ideas that were considered (from internal specs):

**Option A — a `layout` parameter on `st.dataframe`:**

```python
st.dataframe(df, layout="table" | "list" | "gallery" | "board" | "timeline")
```

**Option B — dedicated commands per layout:**

```python
st.data_gallery(df)   # card/gallery view
st.data_list(df)      # list view
st.data_board(df)     # kanban board (grouped by a column)
```

Notes:
- Reuse the same data inputs and `column_config` as `st.dataframe` (e.g. which columns act as the image, title, subtitle, group-by / status, or date field).
- Overlaps with the "image cards" idea and could share infrastructure.

### Summary

Send dataframe (Arrow) data over HTTP rather than through the WebSocket, similar to how we already serve images, video, and audio. HTTP appears to be faster than the WebSocket *and* gets parallelized by the browser, which should speed up BI-style apps with many charts/tables containing thousands of datapoints each.

### Why?

- Browsers make HTTP requests in parallel, so the rest of the app can keep loading *while* the dataframe data downloads (instead of serializing everything through a single WebSocket).
- Anecdotally, the WebSocket seems a bit slower than plain HTTP requests for large payloads.
- If it works well for dataframes, it could be extended to charts (which carry large datasets too).

### How?

An MVP could extend the existing **forward message cache** mechanism to support a *reference message* that carries a URL instead of a hash. If the URL is set, the frontend downloads the message body over HTTP. This would let us put the Arrow data in media file storage and send only a lightweight reference over the WebSocket.

Considerations:
- Likely only beneficial above a certain size threshold, since there's overhead to uploading to storage, exchanging metadata, and cleaning up.
- `st.dataframe` lazy data loading could keep the initial payload small and might pair well with this (e.g. auto-enable for large dataframes).
- **SiS caveat:** new HTTP endpoints have historically been very painful there (file uploader, custom components, download button, forward message cache, static file serving). Prefer reusing existing media-file-storage plumbing rather than introducing a new endpoint, and validate end-to-end upload efficiency in that environment.

### Additional Context

- Could later be extended to charts / other elements that transfer large datasets.
- Related mechanisms: media file storage (used for images/video/audio) and the forward message cache.
issues.title: Send dataframe (Arrow) data via HTTP instead of the WebSocket

### Summary

Add a general-purpose `st.card` layout container — a bordered container with a coherent, built-in structure for common card content: an optional full-width image at the top, a title (and help tooltip), and any elements you add to the body. Like `st.container(border=True)`, but with first-class support for the pieces that are painful today (especially a full-bleed image).

### Why?

Cards are one of the most common UI building blocks (see [Material design cards](https://m3.material.io/components/cards/overview)) and are everywhere in dashboards, galleries, and BI apps. Borders on `st.container`/`st.columns` are already used in a significant number of apps, so demand is clearly high. Today users can get a border via `st.container(border=True)`, but the very common "full-sized image at the top of the card" requires fragile CSS hacks. A dedicated element makes polished cards a one-liner and pairs great with grid/flex layouts and `height="stretch"` for aligned galleries.

### How?

A container command that returns a container you can fill with any elements, plus a few high-value built-in parameters (from the internal spec):

```python
st.card(
    title: str | None = None,
    image: "same types as st.image" | None = None,
    *,
    width: "content" | "stretch" | int = "stretch",
    height: "content" | "stretch" | int = "content",
    help: str | None = None,
)

# Example
with st.card("Card 1", "mountain.jpg"):
    with st.container(direction="horizontal"):
        st.badge("Star", icon=":material/star:")
        st.badge("Home", icon=":material/home:")
    st.write("This is a card with a border. It can also have some text.")
```

Details:
- Returns a container, so users add arbitrary content (text, charts, badges, buttons) to the body.
- `image` is optional and shown full width at the top (no padding, no toolbar), rendered at its natural aspect ratio; `title` is optional (Markdown, ellipsized so side-by-side cards align), with an optional `help` tooltip.
- Both `image` and `title` can be `None` (an empty card ≈ `st.container(border=True)`).
- `width`/`height` mirror `st.container`; `height="stretch"` lets cards in a row/grid align to equal height.

Possible later additions (kept out of scope initially to limit API surface): `subtitle`, `icon`/avatar, `image_height`, background color, and clickable cards.

### Additional Context

- Framed as a general card component (the internal spec called it "Image cards" because the full-sized top image was the main missing capability).
- Related: #12418 (container background / cards), #12301 (container shadow), #3210 and #4175 (older card requests), #12322 (clickable metric actions).
issues.title: Add a `st.card` layout container

### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

`st.cache_data` stores one serialized (pickled) blob per cache key, where the key is derived only from the function + input arguments. If a function returns the *same* value (e.g. the same dataframe) for many different inputs, each of those cache entries stores a full, redundant copy. We could recognize identical serialized return values (e.g. by hashing the serialized value bytes) and store the payload only once, with each cache key referencing it — saving memory (and disk when persisted).

### Why?

- **Memory savings:** Functions that frequently return the same object under different arguments currently blow up memory with duplicate copies. Content-addressed storage would keep a single shared copy.
- Could also help mitigate memory issues when replaying widgets in cached functions (a common source of memory crashes), since the shared thing would be the stored bytes.
- Complements existing cache memory work like #2911 (limit cache size by memory footprint) and #14558 (inspect cache memory usage).

### How?

Introduce a content-addressed layer for cached values:

- On write, hash the serialized **value payload** and store it once in a blob store keyed by that digest; the per-argument cache key stores a lightweight reference (digest + metadata) plus a reference count.
- On read, resolve the reference to the shared blob and deserialize as usual.
- Evict a blob only when no cache key references it anymore.

Key implementation note: today the pickled entry is a `CachedResult` that bundles the value **and** per-call metadata (replayed `messages`, `main_id`/`sidebar_id`, `stored_at`). Because that metadata differs per key, hashing the whole `CachedResult` blob wouldn't dedup much — the design should **separate the value payload (content-addressable, shared) from the per-key metadata** so identical values actually collide.

Notes:
- Copy semantics are preserved: `st.cache_data` still returns independent copies on each read (values are deserialized per call); only the *stored bytes* are shared.
- Likely only worth it above a size threshold, given the hashing/bookkeeping overhead.

### Additional Context

Current behavior (from a code investigation): storage keys are built from input args only (`_make_value_key`), the return value is `pickle.dumps(CachedResult(...))` and written via `storage.set(value_key, bytes)`, and the in-memory layer is a `TTLCache[str, bytes]` with one independent blob per key. There is no hashing of the return-value bytes and no cross-key dedup today (the only "dedup" in the caching code is background-refresh scheduling).

- Related: #2911 (limit cache by memory footprint), #14558 (inspect cache memory usage), #13992 (cache observability).
issues.title: Deduplicate identical `st.cache_data` return values to save memory

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the existing issues for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

Opening this to record a measurement rather than to assert a bug, because it corrects an assumption I had been carrying.

Large pandas/polars/numpy objects are hashed from a sample rather than in full (`_PANDAS_ROWS_LARGE = 50_000`, `_PANDAS_SAMPLE_SIZE = 10_000` in `lib/streamlit/runtime/caching/hashing.py`). I had noted "polars sampling is a pessimization between 50k and 100k rows" as a follow-up while working on #16284. **Measuring it shows that framing is wrong** — sampling is never slower for polars. But the numbers do raise a different, narrower question about the threshold that seemed worth writing down.

### The measurement

Median of 5–7 runs, comparing the full content hash against sample-then-hash, using the same call shape as `hashing.py` (`hash_rows(seed=0).hash(seed=0)`).

Narrow frame (2 columns, ints):

```
     rows   full_ms  sampled_ms      verdict
    50000      0.32        0.31 sampling helps
    60000      0.25        0.24 sampling helps
   100000      0.31        0.21 sampling helps
   200000      0.42        0.24 sampling helps
   500000      1.24        0.29 sampling helps
  1000000      3.24        0.35 sampling helps
```

Wide frame (10 columns, half of them strings) — closer to real-world use:

```
    rows   full_ms  sampled_ms  saved_ms  rows_seen
   50000      0.58        0.57      0.01      20.0%
   60000      0.59        0.41      0.19      16.7%
  100000      1.32        0.83      0.49      10.0%
  300000      3.11        1.23      1.88       3.3%
```

### What this shows

Sampling is equal-or-faster at every size, so there is no performance regression to fix. The scaling is also clearly worth keeping at the large end — 9x at 1M rows.

The narrower observation is at the bottom of the range. At 50k rows, sampling saves **0.01 ms** (inside noise) while hashing only **20%** of the rows. At 60k it saves 0.19 ms for 16.7% coverage. So immediately above the threshold, the collision exposure is taken on for essentially no time saved.

### The question, not a proposal

Is `_PANDAS_ROWS_LARGE = 50_000` the right point for polars, given a full hash of a 50k-row frame costs well under a millisecond?

I am explicitly **not** proposing a change, for two reasons:

1. **It changes cache keys.** Any object in the affected size range would hash differently, invalidating live cache entries on upgrade — a user-visible effect that needs a deliberate decision, not a tuning tweak.
2. **The trade is a judgement about collision risk, not a measurement.** Both maintainers assessed the collision risk on #14622 as negligible, which is a reasonable basis for leaving this exactly as it is. My data can say what sampling costs; it cannot say how much collision exposure is acceptable.

The threshold is also shared with pandas (`_PANDAS_ROWS_LARGE` gates both), so a polars-specific change would mean splitting a currently-shared constant — additional complexity that only pays off if the answer to the above is "yes".

Happy to run more measurements (pandas at the same sizes, or other dtypes) if that would help settle it. Equally happy for this to be closed as working-as-intended — the measurement is the useful part.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: `develop` (measured at `a2414ead3f`)
- polars 1.43.2, Python 3.14.5, macOS 15.5

### Additional Information

Context: #14622 / #16284, where `runner.cacheHashSeed` was added as an escape hatch for sampling collisions. That option relocates collisions; it does not reduce them, which is what made the threshold worth measuring.
issues.title: Measurement: is the 50k sampling threshold right for polars cache hashing?

### Summary

Add a `"progress"` option to the existing `chart_type` parameter of `st.metric`, rendering the metric's `chart_data` as a horizontal progress line/bar (progress toward a goal) instead of a line/bar/area sparkline. This is a very common dashboard/BI card pattern (e.g. "Overall Growth 36%" with a filled progress bar, or "48 ▮▮▯▯ 100").

### Why?

`st.metric` already supports `chart_type="line" | "bar" | "area"` for a small trend sparkline. But a huge number of dashboards visualize a metric as **progress toward a target** (current vs. goal) using a slim horizontal bar under the value. Today you can't get this look natively — you'd combine `st.metric` with `st.progress` or custom HTML, which doesn't align nicely inside the metric card. A `"progress"` chart type would make these polished "KPI progress" cards a one-liner and fits naturally alongside the existing chart types.

### How?

Extend the existing parameter:

```python
st.metric(
    "New Likes",
    48,
    chart_data=[48, 100],        # or a trend that resolves to current/goal
    chart_type="progress",
)
```

Rough behavior:
- Render a horizontal progress bar/line inside the metric card, filled according to the value relative to a goal/max.
- Reuse the metric's color semantics (e.g. delta/positive-negative coloring), matching the reference dashboards.

Open question — how the target/max is determined:
- Infer from `chart_data` (e.g. current = value, max = `max(chart_data)` or last element), or
- Add a small dedicated parameter (e.g. `chart_data` as `(current, goal)`, or a new `target`/`max_value` arg).

**Reference visuals:** BI dashboard KPI cards that place a slim horizontal progress bar under the metric value — e.g. cards like "Userbase Growth 36%", "Traffic Values 54%", "New Likes 48 / 100", and "Sessions 290.9k / 2M", each showing a filled progress bar indicating progress toward a goal. ### Summary

### Observed WebSocket session payload


### Steps To Reproduce

Information Disclosure via WebSocket Messages

The DAST scanner observes the initial WebSocket/session message and identifies OS/software version information.

The finding is generated from Streamlit framework-generated WebSocket/session data rather than application-generated content.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

- Streamlit version: `1.60.0`
- Python version: 3.12.13
- Operating system: `linux`
- Application/script information: `app`

### Additional Information

Is there currently a supported configuration to suppress OS and software/version information from Streamlit's client-facing session messages?

### Summary

Add a `dataframeHeaderTextColor` theme option to control the foreground (text) color of `st.dataframe` / `st.data_editor` column headers. Today `dataframeHeaderBackgroundColor` exists, but the header text color can't be customized — it's always derived from the body `textColor` (as `fadedText60`), so a custom/tinted/dark header background often results in weak or unreadable header text.

### Why?

Users can already set a custom header background via `dataframeHeaderBackgroundColor`, but there's no matching control for the header text. With a dark or strongly tinted header background, the faded, body-derived header text has poor contrast and can be hard to read. A dedicated `dataframeHeaderTextColor` lets the header background and foreground be styled together for a readable, on-brand look.

### How?

Add a theme config option, e.g.:

```toml
[theme]
dataframeHeaderBackgroundColor = "#1f2937"
dataframeHeaderTextColor = "#ffffff"
```

Implementation notes:
- Wire it through the dataframe's custom theme so it overrides the header text color instead of the hardcoded default.
- In the frontend this currently maps to the glide-data-grid `textHeader` (and likely `textGroupHeader`), which today is set to `theme.colors.fadedText60`:

### Summary

Add a `type` parameter to `st.radio` with a `"cards"` variant that renders each option as a bordered, selectable card (with the selected card highlighted) instead of the default radio-button list. Same widget behavior — only the visual style changes. See [Tremor's Radio Card Group](https://www.tremor.so/docs/inputs/radio-card-group) for the look.

### Why?

Card-style single-select is a very common, more prominent and touch-friendly pattern for choosing between a few richer options (e.g. plans, payment methods, layouts, modes). Today users approximate it with columns + bordered containers + buttons/`st.radio` and a lot of manual state/CSS work. A built-in `"cards"` variant makes this polished pattern a one-liner.

### How?

Add a `type` parameter (default preserves today's look):

```python
choice = st.radio(
    "Choose a plan",
    ["Starter", "Pro", "Enterprise"],
    captions=[
        "For individuals getting started",
        "For growing teams",
        "Advanced controls & support",
    ],
    type="cards",
)
```

- `type="default"` — current radio-button list.
- `type="cards"` — render each option as a bordered card; the selected option is visually highlighted.
- Keep existing params working (`captions`, `horizontal`, `format_func`, `index=None`, etc.). Captions map naturally to a description line inside each card.

**Alternative solution — a `border: bool` parameter:** Instead of a `type` enum, just add `st.radio(..., border=True)` that wraps each option in a bordered card. This mirrors the `border` parameter on `st.container` and keeps the API minimal. Downside: it's less extensible than a `type` enum if we later want more visual variants (e.g. `"pills"`), and it's a boolean rather than a named style.

### Additional Context

- Reference designs:
  - [Tremor — Radio Card Group](https://www.tremor.so/docs/inputs/radio-card-group)
  - [Tailwind Plus — Radio Groups (card designs)](https://tailwindcss.com/plus/ui-blocks/application-ui/forms/radio-groups)
  - [streamlit-extras — Card Selector](https://extras.streamlit.app/?extra=%F0%9F%83%8F+Card+Selector) (existing community implementation)
- Related: #2325 (`st.radio` with sections), #7184 (stretch horizontal radio), #11959 (consistent API for selectbox/pills/segmented_control/radio).

### Summary

After Altair/Vega-Lite charts started using the native Streamlit toolbar, clicking the download icon next to Fullscreen saves a PNG only. Please keep that native download icon, and on hover show a small toolbar-styled dropdown so the user can choose PNG or SVG.

### Why?

I'm always frustrated when I hover an Altair/Vega-Lite chart, see the native download icon beside Fullscreen, click it, and can only get PNG.

For reports and papers I often need SVG (vector, scalable) as well as PNG. The old Vega-Embed ⋯ menu offered "Save as PNG" / "Save as SVG". After https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/15806, that menu is gone, SVG export is gone, and `usermeta.embedOptions` can no longer restore export actions.

Workarounds (custom HTML components, extra `st.download_button`s, or DOM hacks) either leave the native toolbar unused or drift out of style as Streamlit's toolbar design changes. There is no public API to attach a format menu to the existing toolbar download button.

Related but different: #8177 is about PNG resolution, not choosing a format.

### How?

Keep the existing native download icon on Altair/Vega-Lite (and other Vega) charts, in the same toolbar row as Fullscreen.

When the pointer hovers that download icon, show a compact dropdown that matches the toolbar (same icon size, radius, colors, light/dark theme). Suggested items:

- Download PNG
- Download SVG

Clicking an item exports from the current Vega view (`toImageURL("png")` / `toImageURL("svg")`) and starts a browser download.

A click with no menu selection can keep today's PNG-only behavior as the default.

I do not need a new `st` command. Optional later: `st.altair_chart(..., download_formats=("png", "svg"))` to choose which items appear. A Python API is nice-to-have; the hover menu on the native icon is the main request.

Please do not bring back the old Vega-Embed ⋯ menu (View Source / Open in Vega Editor). This should stay a Streamlit toolbar control.

### Additional Context

- Native toolbar change that removed SVG: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/15806
- Older embedOptions / actions discussion: https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/does-altairs-set-embed-options-work-with-streamlit/1675
- PNG quality (related, not this request): https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8177

I am building a Streamlit questionnaire analysis app that shows many static Altair charts. Users expect the hover toolbar download icon (same family as Fullscreen) to let them pick PNG vs SVG, without a separate download widget beside every chart.

### Summary

Refresh Streamlit's built-in default light and dark themes to feel more modern and polished out of the box — updated colors, typography, spacing, radii, and component styling — so that apps look great by default without custom theming.

### Why?

The default look is what every new app and most demos ship with, so it strongly shapes the perception of Streamlit. The current defaults feel somewhat dated compared to modern design systems (e.g. shadcn, Tailwind, Tremor, Material 3). A refreshed, cohesive default theme would make apps look more professional immediately, improve the first impression for new users, and reduce how often people reach for custom CSS/themes just to look current.

### How?

- **Color palette:** refined neutrals/grays, a more modern primary color, and better semantic colors (success/warning/error/info) with good contrast in both modes.
- **Dark mode:** ensure it's a first-class, well-balanced theme (not just an inversion) — proper surface elevations, borders, and contrast.
- **Typography:** modern default font, refined sizes/weights/line-heights and hierarchy.
- **Spacing & shape:** consistent spacing scale and slightly softer, contemporary border radii and borders.
- **Components:** cohesive styling across widgets, containers, dataframes, charts, etc.

Considerations:
- Accessibility: maintain/improve WCAG contrast in both themes.
- Backwards compatibility: this changes the look of existing apps, so consider how to roll it out (e.g. a new theme version/opt-in, migration notes) to avoid surprising users.

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Extend the existing `validate` parameter of `st.text_input` to also accept a **callable** for server-side validation, executed on the backend when the value is submitted. When validation fails, the input shows an error state with a message and the value is **not** committed (no rerun). Client-side regex validation (`str` / `(regex, message)` tuple) is already implemented and shipped; this issue tracks the remaining **server-side** part of the approved [product spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2025-12-03-text-input-validation/product-spec.md).

### Why?

Client-side regex validation gives instant feedback but can be bypassed and can't express checks that need backend resources (e.g. database lookups) or must be secure. Server-side callable validation covers those cases — username availability, complex business logic, and security-sensitive validation — without the developer having to manually track/display errors or trigger extra reruns.

### How?

Widen the `validate` type to also accept a callable:

```python
st.text_input(
    ...,
    validate: str | tuple[str, str] | Callable[[str], bool | str] | None = None,
    #                                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ NEW (callable)
)
```

The callable is executed on the backend on submit (Enter/blur/form submit) via a deferred-execution pattern (like `st.download_button` with callable data), without a full rerun. It returns `True` (valid), `False` (generic error), or a `str` (custom error message):

```python
def check_username(value: str) -> bool | str:
    if len(value) < 3:
        return "Username must be at least 3 characters."
    if db.username_exists(value):
        return "Username already taken."
    return True

st.text_input("Username", validate=check_username)
```

Key behaviors (from the spec):
- Runs on commit (blur/Enter/form submit), not on initial render; error state clears as the user types.
- Empty string / `None` bypasses validation (requiredness stays a separate future `required` parameter).
- On success: the deferred commit goes through and triggers the normal rerun / `on_change`. On failure: error state, no rerun.
- While validating: loading spinner, submit disabled, 10s timeout, in-progress validation cancelled if the user edits the value.
- Non-`bool`/`str` return or a raised exception → value rejected with a generic error; exception + traceback logged to the backend console (not sent to the frontend).
- Forms: validation runs on form submit (client-side regex first, then callables); all fields must pass before the single submit rerun.

### Additional Context

- Approved product spec: [`specs/2025-12-03-text-input-validation/product-spec.md`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2025-12-03-text-input-validation/product-spec.md) (client-side portion already shipped; this issue covers the server-side callable).
- Future extensions noted in the spec: server-side callable validation for `st.text_area`, `st.column_config.TextColumn`, `st.number_input`, `st.date_input`, `st.selectbox`, and `st.chat_input`.
issues.title: Add server-side (callable) input validation to `st.text_input`

### Summary

Add a `resizable: bool = False` parameter to `st.columns` that lets users resize columns by dragging the border between them. When enabled, a border indicator appears on hover between adjacent columns, and dragging adjusts their widths interactively. Resizing is purely client-side and does not trigger a rerun. Specced in [PR #14687](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14687).

### Why?

Column widths in `st.columns` are static today — once set via `spec`, they can't be adjusted without changing code and rerunning. Interactive resizing helps with dashboard customization, data exploration (temporarily expand a column to see more), fine-tuning responsive layouts, and adjusting proportions live during demos/presentations. Current workarounds (layout presets via `st.selectbox`, CSS hacks in custom components, or just accepting fixed layouts) are clunky or fragile.

Related: #5003 (deactivate responsiveness of `st.columns`), #6592 (configurable column responsiveness threshold).

### How?

```python
st.columns(
    spec,
    *,
    gap="small",
    vertical_alignment="top",
    border=False,
    width="stretch",
    resizable=False,  # NEW
)
```

- `resizable=False` (default): current fixed-width behavior, no handles.
- `resizable=True`: drag the border between adjacent columns to resize.

Behavior (from the spec):
- **Hover indicator** + `col-resize` cursor over the resize area; border fades in/out (150ms).
- **Drag** resizes only the two adjacent columns; total row width is preserved (neighbor shrinks as one grows); other columns unchanged.
- **Double-click** the handle resets the adjacent pair to their original `spec` proportions.
- **Minimum width** of 64px prevents collapse; throttled updates for performance.
- **Keyboard**: Arrow Left/Right resize in 10px increments when focused.
- **Accessibility**: handles use `role="separator"`, `aria-orientation="vertical"`, `aria-valuenow/min/max`, and visible focus indicators (WCAG 2.1).
- **Touch**: drag works via touch; indicator shows on touch start.
- **Narrow viewports**: when columns stack (below `theme.breakpoints.columns`, 640px), handles are hidden and reappear when it widens.
- **State**: resized widths persist within the session (React state) and reset on refresh, a `spec`/column-count change, or stack/unstack.

### Alternatives considered (from the spec)

- `resizable: bool` (preferred) vs `resize_mode: Literal["off", "drag"]` — boolean chosen to match the existing `border=True` precedent and the binary nature of the feature; can migrate to an enum later if multiple resize modes are demanded.
- Naming: `resizable` over `adjustable` (too generic) / `flexible` (clashes with flexbox).

### Out of scope (future work)

Persist widths across sessions, snap-to-grid, per-column `min_width`/`max_width`, `on_resize` callback, and named/saveable layout presets.

### Additional Context

- Spec: [PR #14687 — \`[spec] Allow interactive resizing of st.columns\`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14687) (`specs/2026-04-08-resizable-columns/product-spec.md`).
issues.title: Allow interactive resizing of `st.columns` via drag-and-drop

### Checklist

- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

In `uploadFileUploaderFile`, the frontend constructs a `FormData` object for file uploads using the file's own name (`name`) as the multipart form-data field name: `form.append(name, file, fileName)`. Because the backend does not rely on this dynamic field name and files are uploaded individually, using the user-controlled filename introduces potential security risks, such as bypassing security filters, WAFs, or length restrictions designed for form field names.


```typescript
const form = new FormData()
const { name, webkitRelativePath } = file
// For directory uploads, use the relative path as fileName to preserve directory structure
const fileName = webkitRelativePath || name
form.append(name, file, fileName)

```

### Proposed Solution

Replace the dynamic `name` variable with a static string (such as `"file"`), since files are handled individually and the backend does not require the field name to match the filename.

```typescript
const form = new FormData()
const { name, webkitRelativePath } = file
// For directory uploads, use the relative path as fileName to preserve directory structure
const fileName = webkitRelativePath || name
form.append("file", file, fileName)

```


### Security Impact

* **User-Controlled Field Names:** Attackers can manipulate file names (including special characters, injection sequences, or excessive lengths) which are then directly injected into the multipart form-data structure as the field name.
* **Validation & WAF Bypasses:** Backend proxies, Web Application Firewalls (WAFs), or API gateways often enforce strict validation rules (character sets, maximum length) on form field names. Allowing client-side filenames to define these keys can lead to unexpected parsing behavior or security filter evasion.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

uploaded_file = st.file_uploader("Choose a file")
if uploaded_file is not None:
    st.write(f"Uploaded filename: {uploaded_file.name}")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the provided Python script using Streamlit.
2. Open your browser's Developer Tools and navigate to the **Network** tab.
3. Upload a file via the file uploader (e.g., a file named `malicious_name_test.txt`).
4. Inspect the multipart `form-data` payload sent in the upload request.
5. Observe that the form field `name` attribute equals the file's name (`malicious_name_test.txt`) instead of a static, controlled identifier.

### Expected Behavior

The multipart form-data request should use a static, predefined field name (such as `name="file"`) for the upload payload, ensuring that the form field name is fully controlled and sanitized, while the actual file name/path remains properly preserved only in the filename parameter.

### Current Behavior

When a file is uploaded through `st.file_uploader`, the frontend dynamically sets the multipart form-data field name to match the uploaded file's name (`form.append(name, file, fileName)`). As a result, user-controlled strings, special characters, and arbitrary lengths are directly injected into the request's form field name.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.58.0
- Python version: 3.11
- Operating System: Windows
- Browser: Chrome


### Additional Information

_No response_

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a dedicated `st.column_config.DurationColumn` as the first-class column type for `datetime.timedelta` / `pandas.Timedelta` / Arrow duration values. It should own duration-specific display formats, `min`/`max`/`step` as timedeltas, and a real duration editor. `TimeColumn` should stay clock-of-day only; `NumberColumn` can remain the escape hatch for “treat this duration as seconds.”

### Why?

Timedelta is elapsed time (negatives, multi-day, 336 hours). That is a different type from:

- **`TimeColumn`**: clock-of-day. HTML `<input type="time">`, `min`/`max` as `datetime.time`, wraps at 24h, string sort. Read-only rendering only looks right for the narrow case of a positive duration under 24 hours (`1s` → `00:00:01`). Everything else is a silent lie (`14 days` wraps or fakes `336:00:00`; negatives have no representation). That is the same class of bug as #9751 (`1s` shown as `00:16:40`). If `TimeColumn` cannot represent a value, it should error rather than show a wrong clock time.
- **`NumberColumn`**: numeric sort and printf formats. Good enough as a v1 for display + sort (#8949), including `format="clock"` for an elapsed-time clock. It is a leaky API for durations: `min`/`max`/`step` are raw seconds, and the editor is a number spinner on `7200`.

A dedicated type is what pays off once we want a real duration API: discoverable config, a format namespace that is not a number format, timedelta-typed bounds, and an editor that is not “type 7200 to mean 2 hours.”

### How?

```python
st.dataframe(
    df,
    column_config={
        "latency": st.column_config.DurationColumn(
            format="duration",  # humanize, default
            min_value=datetime.timedelta(0),
            max_value=datetime.timedelta(days=14),
            step=datetime.timedelta(seconds=1),
        ),
        "runtime": st.column_config.DurationColumn(format="clock"),
    },
)
```

**Default mapping:** Arrow duration / pandas timedelta → `DurationColumn` (read-only until editing ships). Keep `NumberColumn` as the opt-in for numeric / printf formats on seconds.

**Do not reuse `TimeColumn`.** Do not send nanosecond ticks to JS (overflows `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` after ~104 days). Wire format should stay **seconds as a float**; Python applies `pd.Timedelta(seconds=value)` so pandas writes the column’s native unit (`us` on pandas 3, `ns` on pandas 2). Strings can stay as a fallback (`pd.Timedelta("2 hours")`).

**Editing, in order of cost / quality:**

1. **Text parse (best first editor).** Overlay is a text field. Accept the same strings pandas already understands: `"2 hours"`, `"1 day 03:00:00"`, `"00:00:01"`, `"P2DT3H"`, `"-3 days"`. Display can stay humanized or clock; the committed value is still seconds (or a normalized string). Handles negatives and multi-day.
2. **Custom elapsed-time overlay (best UX).** Glide custom cell: optional days + `HH:mm:ss`, hours not wrapped at 24, optional sign. `min`/`max`/`step` are timedeltas. This is the main reason for `DurationColumn` to exist rather than piggyback on `NumberColumn`.
3. **Number + unit.** Spinner plus s/min/h/d. Fine as a power-user option, poor as the default for mixed-scale columns.
4. **`NumberColumn(disabled=False)`.** Already works as an escape hatch (edits raw seconds). Not product-quality as the default editor.

Suggested `format` values (duration namespace, not number formats): `"duration"` (humanize, default), `"clock"` (elapsed clock, hours not wrapped at 24), `"localized"` (Intl.DurationFormat), maybe ISO `PT2H` later.

### Additional Context

Related:

- #8949 — timedelta sort used the humanized string (`14 days`, `2 hours`, `a day`) instead of the underlying value. Fixed by mapping duration → `NumberColumn` with values stored as seconds.
- #9751 — `TimeColumn` on `pd.Timedelta` showed a wrong clock time. `TimeColumn` should keep erroring on duration; the clock display belongs on `DurationColumn` / `NumberColumn(format="clock")`.

Display + numeric sort do not require this type. Add `DurationColumn` when we want first-class editing or a cleaner public API.
issues.title: Add `st.column_config.DurationColumn` for timedelta / duration values

### Summary

Reduce how often developers hit `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` (duplicate widget/element ID) errors by making element ID generation smarter about the surrounding container context — so that identical widgets placed in different containers (chat messages, fragments, columns, etc.) don't collide without the developer having to manually craft unique `key`s everywhere.

### Why?

It's increasingly common to have repeating identical widgets across different chat messages, fragment calls, or columns. Today the developer must manage and track a unique `key` for each, which adds a lot of boilerplate and complexity. This is especially painful in chat/LLM apps (in-chat interactive widgets, code-eval "run" buttons, generated suggestion buttons) — and for LLM-generated code it can be nearly impossible to solve, since the model may emit duplicate widgets across messages. `st.form` already avoids this within forms (the `form_id` is part of the ID), which shows the approach can work more broadly.

This is a high-impact papercut: `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` is the **No. 3 most thrown uncaught exception type**, occurring in ~**0.5% of all apps**.

A related pain point: some elements raise `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` and tell you to add a `key`, but **don't actually support a `key` argument**, leaving no clean fix. Examples:
- #11424 — showing the same `st.plotly_chart` multiple times raises `StreamlitDuplicateElementId`.
- #11360 — multiple `st.audio` calls with the same parameters and `autoplay=True` raise a duplicate error that prompts you to add a key, but `st.audio` has no `key`.

### How?

Incorporate more of the container context into an element's ID computation, focusing on **stable, explicit signals** (not user-facing text). Ideas:

- **Wrapping container keys:** automatically include the `key` of wrapping containers / `st.fragment` / `st.form` (those that support keys) in the child element's ID computation. Only for containers that have an explicit key set.
  - If we do this, it strengthens the case for **adding `key` to more containers and elements** — see #9580 and the concrete cases #11424 (`st.plotly_chart`) and #11360 (`st.audio`), plus #6152.
- **Re-evaluate key namespaces and parent-key reuse:** regular element keys, form IDs, and fragment definition keys are currently tracked in separate registries. `st.form` already contributes its `form_id` to the auto-generated IDs of unkeyed children; fragment keys identify fragment definitions but are not currently part of regular child element ID computation. Consider both:
  - Reusing explicit form / fragment / keyed-container keys as stable parent context for **unkeyed** descendants.
  - Whether form and fragment keys should participate in the same duplicate-key checks as regular element keys, or remain separate namespaces that only contribute parent context.

  Treat registry unification as a compatibility decision: the same string can currently be reused between some form / fragment and regular-element keys, and one keyed fragment definition can intentionally run from multiple call sites. Preserve the rule that an explicit child `key` is authoritative and independent of its container.
- **Column index in `st.columns`:** include the column number in the ID computation so the same widget in different columns of the same `st.columns` call doesn't collide.
- **Parent container types:** include the parent container type(s) as part of the ID computation.

**Important caution — be conservative about what goes into ID generation.** Adding container context to the ID changes element identity, which has a subtle downside: a widget that **dynamically moves between containers** (e.g. its wrapping container changes across reruns) would get a new ID and thus lose its identity and state. This is the main risk to weigh (more so than existing widget state resetting on upgrade), and it can be fixed by explicitly setting a `key` on that element so its identity no longer depends on the container context. In particular:
- **Do not** include user-facing **labels/titles** of wrapping containers (e.g. expander label, dialog title, popover label, tab name) in the ID — these change often and would be fragile/surprising. Prefer **explicitly set keys** for disambiguation instead.
- Auto-added context must apply **only to widgets without an explicit `key`**. When a user sets an explicit `key="x"`, the ID must **not** include the added container context — an explicit key should always behave predictably and stay stable regardless of the surrounding containers. Think through backwards compatibility / migration carefully.

### Additional Context

- Add `key` to more elements/containers: #9580, and concrete duplicate-ID cases where no `key` is available today: #11424 (`st.plotly_chart`), #11360 (`st.audio`).
- Related: #6152 (composable/reusable component API for larger apps).
- `st.form` already includes `form_id` in widget ID generation — a useful precedent.
- There is an older internal product spec exploring options (implicit container key-prefix, adding `key`/`key_prefix` to containers, best-practice docs, or fixing duplicate IDs via enumeration). This issue intentionally leans toward the conservative, explicit-key-based approaches from that discussion.
issues.title: Minimize `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` errors

### Summary

Refresh the visual design and interaction model of `st.chat_message` so chat/agentic apps look modern out of the box — closer to the chat UIs people expect from tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and other assistants. This includes rethinking avatars, message alignment, per-message actions, and how the message background is themed.

### Why?

`st.chat_message` is central to Streamlit's most compelling demos (LLM/agentic apps), but its default look feels dated compared to modern chat UIs. Users routinely reach for CSS hacks or custom components to get a contemporary look (hidden avatars, right-aligned user bubbles, hover actions). Making the default modern — and the common tweaks first-class — would make agentic apps look polished with no effort and reduce reliance on fragile workarounds.

### How?

Modernize the design and add a few high-value options, for example:

- **Avatars:** make the design look clean when avatars are hidden, and consider hiding them by default (or an easy option to hide them). Today an avatar is always shown.
- **User vs. assistant alignment:** support right-aligned user messages (bubble style) and left-aligned assistant messages, matching common chat UIs.
- **Per-message actions:** built-in, hover-revealed actions on a message (e.g. copy, thumbs up/down, regenerate, custom actions) that can trigger callbacks/reruns.
- **General styling refresh:** spacing, bubble/background treatment, and typography that feel modern and cohesive with the rest of the app theme.

**Background & nested-element theming:** Apply the message background via **theming** and update nested elements so they render correctly against it — like the **sidebar** does. Using the **secondary background color** is a promising approach (nested elements already look right in the sidebar), and it should also fix cases like charts not looking good against the current gray background. This is closely related to the background handling in the [`st.container` background/shadow spec (#14683)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14683).

Keep everything backwards compatible (opt-in where it changes existing looks) and themeable.

- [Figma Mockups](https://www.figma.com/design/fzBM3vuV1Dh0lznSzKxOh4/Streamlit-Open-Source-design-system?node-id=3973-16463&t=waRdSwMGoWbMj4A1-4)

### Additional Context

Related issues to fold into this modernization:
- #10740 — configurable toolbar / clickable actions on `st.chat_message`.
- #6921 — "Copy to Clipboard" button in `st.chat_message`.
- #11380 — color and background color support for `st.chat_message` avatars.
issues.title: Modernize `st.chat_message` design to match modern agentic chat UIs

### Summary

Deprecate the `args` and `kwargs` parameters that widgets currently expose for passing arguments to `on_change` / `on_click` callbacks, and recommend `functools.partial` instead. As part of this, support automatically receiving relevant state (e.g. the widget's new value) in the callback, as requested in #5305.

### Why?

- **Redundant API surface:** `args`/`kwargs` exist on essentially every widget purely to forward arguments to callbacks. Python already has a standard, well-understood tool for this — `functools.partial` — so `args`/`kwargs` are extra parameters to learn, document, and maintain on every widget for something the language handles natively.
- **Consistency & simplicity:** removing them shrinks the signature of every widget and aligns with "prefer Pythonic idioms" and "extend/compose over inventing".
- **Better ergonomics for callbacks:** today callbacks often have to read `st.session_state` to find out what value changed, which makes generic reusable handlers awkward. Passing the value (and possibly key) to the callback automatically (#5305) removes that friction.

### How?

- **Recommend `functools.partial`** as the replacement for `args`/`kwargs`:

```python
from functools import partial

def update(param_name, *, value):
    ...

st.selectbox("Pick", options, on_change=partial(update, "selection_1"))
```

- **Deprecate `args`/`kwargs`** on widgets with a long, clearly-communicated deprecation window and docs/migration guidance (they keep working during the deprecation period). See API principle "Graceful Evolution" (3+ months notice, clear migration path).
- **Auto-pass state to callbacks** (#5305): make the widget's new value available to the callback automatically (e.g. as a keyword argument), so reusable/generic handlers don't need to reach into `st.session_state`. The exact mechanism needs design (opt-in signature detection vs. a fixed kwarg) to stay backwards compatible.

### Additional Context

- Incorporates #5305 (pass state as a parameter to the `on_change` callback).
- This is a cross-cutting change affecting all widgets with callbacks (`on_change`/`on_click`), so it warrants a spec and careful, gradual deprecation.
issues.title: Deprecate widget callback `args`/`kwargs` in favor of `functools.partial`

### Summary

Add a link/bookmark element that renders a URL as a rich preview card — with properties like an icon/favicon, title, description, and optionally a preview image — similar to how a bookmark looks in Notion or a link result in Google search. It could optionally **auto-fetch** these properties (e.g. from the page's Open Graph / metadata) when they aren't provided explicitly, and it should **adapt its layout** based on which properties are present.

### Why?

Links are everywhere in apps (sources, references, related resources, docs), but a bare Markdown link is visually flat. A rich, consistent link/bookmark card makes references look polished and scannable — great for dashboards, research/agent apps that cite sources, resource lists, and "read more" sections. Today users hand-build these with columns + images + markdown or custom components, which is fiddly and inconsistent.

### How?

A new element, e.g.:

```python
st.link_preview(
    "https://streamlit.io",
    title="Streamlit • A faster way to build and share data apps",
    description="Streamlit is an open-source Python framework for data scientists and AI/ML engineers to deliver interactive data apps – in only a few lines of code.",
    icon="https://streamlit.io/favicon.png",   # icon/favicon
    image="https://.../preview.png",           # optional large preview image
)

# Minimal — auto-fetch metadata from the URL:
st.link_preview("https://streamlit.io")
```

Behavior:
- **Dynamic layout:** adapt the card to whichever properties are provided — e.g. compact (favicon + title + description) vs. a larger card with a preview image (like the two reference looks below).
- **Auto-fetch (optional):** when title/description/icon/image aren't given, fetch them from the target URL's metadata (Open Graph / `<meta>` / favicon). Should be opt-in-friendly and degrade gracefully if fetching fails or is blocked (fall back to just the URL/title). Consider caching and the SiS/Community-Cloud implications of server-side fetching (and whether fetching happens backend- or frontend-side).
- Whole card is a link to the URL; supports opening in a new tab.

**Alternative / complementary: a Markdown directive.** This could also be exposed as a Markdown directive so bookmarks can be embedded inline in any markdown text (e.g. `st.markdown`), for example:

```
:bookmark[https://python-markdown.github.io/extensions/toc/]{title="Foo" icon=":material/info:"}
```

The directive attributes (`title`, `description`, `icon`, `image`, …) map to the same properties as the element, and unspecified ones can be auto-fetched. A directive plays nicely with LLM-generated content and lets bookmarks appear inline within larger blocks of text.

**Simpler inline "mentions".** The same directive family could also cover a lighter-weight inline link — not a full card, but a link that doesn't use the default link color and instead has a more button-like hover effect, with a configurable icon and title. For example:

```
:mention[URL]{text="My link"}
:mention[URL]{text="My link" icon="🍀"}
:mention[URL]{text="My link" icon="github"}
:mention[URL]{icon="streamlit"}
```

This gives a compact, chip/mention-style link (great inline in text or chat) that sits between a plain Markdown link and the full bookmark card.

Reference looks (a compact link result vs. a larger card with a preview image):

- Compact: favicon + site + bold title (link color) + description snippet.
- Rich: title + description on the left, with a preview image on the right and favicon + URL at the bottom.

### Additional Context

- Inspired by link/bookmark cards in Notion and rich link results in Google search.
- Complements a possible OEmbed feature (embedding Streamlit content elsewhere); this is the inverse — richly embedding external links inside a Streamlit app.
- Related: #11990 (file chip element, e.g. for `st.chat_message`) — a similar compact, reference-style element that could share design/infrastructure.
issues.title: Add a link/bookmark element that renders a rich link preview card

### Summary

Add a way to include inline text in Markdown that shows a tooltip when hovered — like abbreviations/glossary terms with an explanation on hover. This could be exposed as a new Markdown directive, and #12474 (show footnotes as tooltips) could be generalized to cover this.

### Why?

It's common to want to annotate a word or phrase with extra context that appears on hover — glossary terms, acronym expansions, definitions, or short explanations — without cluttering the main text. Today there's no native way to do this in Streamlit Markdown; users resort to raw HTML (`<abbr>`/`title`) which is limited and not always allowed. A first-class inline tooltip makes docs, dashboards, and explanatory text much richer.

### How?

Add a Markdown directive for inline tooltips, where the bracketed text is displayed and the `text` attribute is shown on hover:

```
The :tooltip[HTML]{text="Hyper Text Markup Language"} specification...

:tooltip[Streamlit]{text="Open-source app framework for Machine Learning and Data Science teams."}
```

Notes:
- The visible text (`[...]`) renders inline; hovering shows the tooltip `text`.
- Works wherever Streamlit Markdown is rendered (`st.markdown`, `st.write`, captions, etc.).
- Consider whether the tooltip `text` itself supports Markdown.
- **Alternative / complementary:** generalize #12474 (footnotes → tooltips). Markdown footnotes could render as hover tooltips, giving a standard-Markdown path to the same result; the `:tooltip[...]` directive is the more explicit, inline alternative.

### Additional Context

- Related: #12474 (show markdown footnotes as tooltips) — this issue proposes a more generic, directive-based approach to inline hover text.
issues.title: Support inline tooltips in Markdown (hover text), e.g. via a `:tooltip[...]` directive

### Summary

Add a built-in developer "debug pane" — a panel (e.g. a collapsible sidebar/overlay) that surfaces debug information and dev tools without cluttering the main app. It would visualize `st.session_state` and cache contents, show memory usage and profiling/performance info, and provide a place to dump debug output (`st.help`, variables, etc.). By default it would be visible only to the app developer (not viewers), so developers don't have to comment debug code in and out.

### Why?

Debugging Streamlit apps today means peppering the main UI with `st.write(st.session_state)`, `st.help(...)`, timing prints, etc., then remembering to remove them. There's no first-class way to inspect what's actually going on — state, cache, memory, timings — in a dedicated, developer-only surface. A debug pane (à la [Django Debug Toolbar](https://github.com/jazzband/django-debug-toolbar)) would make development and troubleshooting dramatically easier and keep debug output out of the real app for end users.

### How?

A developer-only container/panel that is disabled by default for viewers other than the app developer. Over time it could host focused tools, for example:

- **State inspector:** visualize `st.session_state` contents.
- **Cache inspector:** visualize `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource` contents (and allow clearing).
- **Memory profiling:** memory usage, and how it changes run-over-run.
- **Execution/performance profiling:** time between/within widget calls and functions; distribution of run times run-over-run (e.g. via a profiler like yappi + a viewer like snakeviz).
- **Debug output container:** a scratch area to write `st.help`, dump variables, etc., that doesn't appear in the main window.
- **Variable inspector:** e.g. a selectbox + `st.help`.
- **Element/DOM inspector:** which widgets were rendered, and their inputs/values; last forward/back message (or equivalent).
- **Console logs** and **error context**.
- Possibly a **Python console** at the end of the app to run quick calculations/inspections (like a Jupyter interactive debugger).

Considerations:
- Developer-only visibility by default (not shown to app viewers); tie into a development vs. production mode.
- Start minimal (state + cache inspection) and grow over time.

### Additional Context

- Prior art: [Django Debug Toolbar](https://github.com/jazzband/django-debug-toolbar), [streamlit-forum](https://github.com/snehankekre/streamlit-forum).
- Closely related: #16306 (dedicated development and production modes) — this debug pane is a natural home for the "development mode" dev tools described there.
issues.title: Add a developer debug pane for inspecting state, cache, memory, and profiling

### Summary

Support `refresh_mode="background"` when `st.cache_data` or `st.cache_resource` decorates an async function.

PR #16168 adds foreground caching for async functions but intentionally rejects this combination:

```python
@st.cache_data(ttl="10m", refresh_mode="background")
async def fetch_data():
    return await load_data()
```

Background refresh is useful for async data fetching because apps can continue serving a cached value while a potentially slow network request refreshes it.

### Why?

Async functions commonly perform latency-sensitive API, database, and cloud requests. Serving stale data while refreshing asynchronously would prevent these operations from blocking an app rerun after the TTL expires.

The existing background-refresh worker invokes cached functions synchronously. Supporting coroutine functions requires explicit behavior for:

- executing the refresh coroutine;
- event-loop ownership;
- cancellation and errors;
- same-key refresh deduplication;
- cache clearing while a refresh is running;
- discarding late results after cache or session invalidation.

### How?

This issue is intended to collect interest and concrete use cases before choosing an execution and lifecycle design. A future implementation could share internal execution primitives with Streamlit background tasks while keeping cache-refresh behavior separate from the public background-task API.

For foreground cached calls, the caller should continue to drive the coroutine. Streamlit-owned task infrastructure could drive refresh coroutines independently in background mode.

Until this is supported, async cached functions should use `refresh_mode="foreground"`.

### Additional context

- Async cache support: #8308
- Foreground async cache implementation: #16168
issues.title: Support background refresh for async cached functions

### Checklist

- [x] I searched the existing issues for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary.

### Summary

Explore supporting reusable event-loop-bound resources, such as async database connections and HTTP or LLM clients, with `st.cache_resource`.

Async cache support in #16168 awaits a coroutine function and caches its completed return value. This works for loop-independent values such as dataframes, API responses, and configuration.

It does not make a cached resource's event loop persistent. A client created on one short-lived loop—for example, through `asyncio.run()`—may fail when reused from another loop on a later rerun:

```python
@st.cache_resource
async def get_client():
    return SomeAsyncClient()
```

Async `validate` and `on_release` callbacks are also unsupported today. Supporting them is part of the same lifecycle problem tracked by this issue: Streamlit must await validation before deciding whether to serve a cache entry and run cleanup on the resource's owning event loop during eviction, clearing, background replacement, or session shutdown.

### Why isn't this currently supported?

Supporting these resources requires more than awaiting the cached function. Streamlit would need defined behavior for:

- persistent event-loop ownership;
- ensuring resource operations execute on the owning loop;
- global versus session-scoped resources;
- async `validate` and `on_release` callback execution;
- cleanup when a cache, session, or server shuts down;
- thread safety and concurrent access;
- reconnects and reruns.

The common case—caching an inert value produced asynchronously—does not require this lifecycle machinery and is covered separately by #16168.

Users can currently avoid the problem by:

- creating, using, and closing the client within one coroutine invocation;
- caching the inert result rather than the client;
- using a synchronous client when one is available; or
- managing a dedicated long-lived event loop themselves.

Given these workarounds and currently limited evidence of demand, this is not planned as part of the initial async cache support.

### Feedback wanted

Please react with a thumbs-up and describe your use case if the workarounds are insufficient. In particular, it would help to know:

- which client or resource you need to cache;
- whether it should be shared globally or only within one session;
- why creating it per operation is impractical; and
- how you currently manage async execution in your Streamlit app.

### Relationship to rerun-resilient streaming

Rerun-resilient streaming is planned separately in #14524. That work addresses streams being interrupted by reruns and may resolve the specific `st.write_stream` workflow in #12076. This feature request covers the broader lifecycle problem of reusing cached event-loop-bound resources across reruns and APIs.

### Additional context

- General async cache request: #8308
- Example `Event loop is closed` failure: #12076
- Initial async cache implementation: #16168
issues.title: Support caching event-loop-bound async resources across reruns

issues.body:
### Summary

When independent top-level async cached functions emit `st.*` messages concurrently, users may need their relative UI placement to stay stable and the layout to be identical on cache misses and hits.

That guarantee is not currently supported. Concurrent calls can mechanically render, but coroutine scheduling controls how their messages interleave. Each cached call owns a separate replay list, and those lists cannot reconstruct the cross-call interleaving observed during the original computations.

This does **not** mean that `asyncio.gather()`, async caching, or normal `st.*` calls from one cached function are unsupported. A single cached call continues to capture and replay its messages in order. The unsupported case is deterministic relative placement across independent concurrent cached calls.

This issue is a decision record and a place to collect demand. We are unlikely to implement a new mechanism unless real use cases show that the alternatives below are insufficient.

### Pattern without an ordering guarantee

The async cache decorators in #16168 make this pattern executable:

```python
import asyncio

import streamlit as st


@st.cache_data
async def load_customers() -> int:
    st.write("Loading customers")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    st.write("Customers loaded")
    return 120


@st.cache_data
async def load_revenue() -> str:
    st.write("Loading revenue")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    st.write("Revenue loaded")
    return "$1.2M"


async def main() -> None:
    await asyncio.gather(load_customers(), load_revenue())


asyncio.run(main())
```

The output order and the miss-versus-hit interleaving are not guaranteed. This is specifically a UI-placement limitation, not a limitation on using `asyncio.gather()`.

### Recommended: join before rendering

Return data from the cached functions, await them concurrently, and render sequentially in source order:

```python
import asyncio

import streamlit as st


@st.cache_data
async def load_customers() -> int:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    return 120


@st.cache_data
async def load_revenue() -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return "$1.2M"


async def load_all() -> tuple[int, str]:
    customers, revenue = await asyncio.gather(load_customers(), load_revenue())
    return customers, revenue


customers, revenue = asyncio.run(load_all())
st.metric("Customers", customers)
st.metric("Revenue", revenue)
```

This provides deterministic source-order layout, at the cost of waiting for all results before rendering them.

### Recommended: reserve stable progressive sections

`@st.fragment(parallel=True)` is already available on `develop` (implemented in #15173). Each fragment reserves its own container at its call site, so sections can complete progressively without moving relative to one another. Until native async cache decorators from #16168 are available, a synchronous cached wrapper can drive each async fetch:

```python
import asyncio

import streamlit as st


async def fetch_customers() -> int:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    return 120


async def fetch_revenue() -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return "$1.2M"


@st.cache_data
def load_customers() -> int:
    return asyncio.run(fetch_customers())


@st.cache_data
def load_revenue() -> str:
    return asyncio.run(fetch_revenue())


@st.fragment(parallel=True)
def customers_section() -> None:
    st.metric("Customers", load_customers())


@st.fragment(parallel=True)
def revenue_section() -> None:
    st.metric("Revenue", load_revenue())


customers_section()
revenue_section()
```

This is the best currently available alternative when progressive rendering and stable source-order placement are both required. After #16168 lands, each fragment can instead call an async cached function through `asyncio.run()`.

Async fragment bodies are not currently justified as a distinct capability for this problem: they would mostly be syntax sugar over driving async work inside a fragment unless users identify a missing lifecycle or compatibility need.

### Feedback wanted

Please comment with concrete cases where join-before-render and independent parallel fragments do not fit, especially if you need:

- progressive results rather than waiting for the full join;
- one shared event loop or loop-bound clients;
- source-order placement versus completion-order placement; or
- behavior that independent parallel fragments cannot provide.

Please also describe why the alternatives fail and what miss/hit layout users should observe.

### Related

- #16168 — async-aware `st.cache_data` and `st.cache_resource`
- #8308 — async cache decorator feature request
- #14277 — merged parallel fragments product spec
- #15173 — parallel fragments implementation
issues.title: Support stable UI placement for concurrent async tasks

issues.body:
## Summary

PR [#16168](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16168) adds async-aware `st.cache_data` and `st.cache_resource`. An async cached function remains awaitable, but the decorated object is a `CachedFunc` whose `__call__` is synchronous and returns an awaitable. As a result:

```python
import inspect

import streamlit as st


@st.cache_data
async def cached_lookup(query: str) -> str:
    return await search_service(query)


assert not inspect.iscoroutinefunction(cached_lookup)
result = cached_lookup("streamlit")
assert inspect.isawaitable(result)
value = await result
```

This issue is a searchable decision record and a place to collect demand for preserving coroutine-function detection through the cache decorators. It is not committed follow-up work and does not block #16168.

## Affected integrations

Some frameworks inspect a callback before invoking it to decide whether to use their sync or async execution path:

- LangChain `RunnableLambda`
- LlamaIndex `FunctionTool`
- MCP callback/tool registration, including decorator-based tool APIs
- Similar callback systems such as Gradio

When the decorated `CachedFunc` is classified as synchronous, a framework may invoke it on its sync path and treat the returned coroutine as the sync result instead of awaiting it.

## Supported compatibility pattern

Keep the cached implementation separate and pass a true `async def` adapter to APIs that inspect callbacks. This reusable adapter preserves coroutine-function detection while still calling through the cache:

```python
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from typing import ParamSpec, TypeVar

P = ParamSpec("P")
R = TypeVar("R")


def as_async_callback(
    cached_func: Callable[P, Awaitable[R]],
) -> Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]:
    async def callback(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        return await cached_func(*args, **kwargs)

    return callback


retrieve_callback = as_async_callback(cached_lookup)

runnable = RunnableLambda(retrieve_callback)
tool = FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn=retrieve_callback)
```

For decorator-based MCP registration, keep the cached function separate from the registered tool:

```python
@st.cache_data
async def cached_customer(customer_id: int) -> dict:
    return await database.fetch(customer_id)


@mcp.tool()
async def lookup_customer(customer_id: int) -> dict:
    return await cached_customer(customer_id)
```

Do not use `inspect.unwrap(cached_lookup)` as the callback. It returns the original function and therefore bypasses Streamlit caching.

## Demand collection

Please comment if the async-adapter pattern cannot satisfy your use case. Include:

- the framework and version;
- how the callback is registered and invoked; and
- why a separate `async def` adapter is insufficient.

That evidence can inform whether Streamlit should preserve coroutine-function detection directly in a future change.

## Related

- [#16168](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16168) — async-aware cache decorators
- [#8308](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8308) — general async cached-function support
issues.title: Preserve coroutine-function detection for async cached functions

### Summary

I would like to propose a new st.sandbox() function that can be used to execute AI-generated Streamlit code for visualization purposes without introducing security risks. This could give users the possibility to create their own dashboards using a chat function.

### Why?

I tried to add different visualizations in a Chatbot within Streamlit. As my Chatbot gives the user the opportunity to chat with our database, I would like to visualize the result received from my agent. I added some functions that offer different visualizations like plotly diagrams and maps, but this procedure is static and not flexible.
I also tried to create html code and embed it with st.html(), but the result was not consistent with the theming and looked awful. I checked also other existing python packages for this purpose but I had the impression they are not reliable. Maybe the limitation on streamlit functions (and limited additional packages) might be easier also from security perspective.

### How?

Something like the following code would maybe be nice:

```
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"],
    "sales": [120, 150, 180]
    })

llm_code = """
import plotly.express as px
fig = px.bar(df, x="month", y="sales")
st.plotly_chart(fig)
"""

result = st.sandbox(
    dataframe=df,
    code=llm_code,
    allowed_packages=[
        "streamlit",
        "pandas",
        "plotly"
    ])

if result.status == "success":
    st.success("Code executed successfully")

elif result.status == "error":
    st.warning(result.error_message)

elif result.status == "security_violation":
    st.error(result.error_message)
```

### Checklist
