### Summary

`use_container_width` was deprecated with a stated removal date of **2025-12-31**. That date is well past (today is 2026-09-08), but the parameter is still accepted on current Streamlit and still logs a warning that claims it will be removed after 2025-12-31.

Please either actually remove `use_container_width` now that the advertised cutoff has passed, or keep the compatibility shim and update the warning copy so it does not cite a date in the past.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import streamlit as st

st.button("Hello", use_container_width=True)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the snippet above on a recent Streamlit version (the warning is still present on `develop`).
2. Observe the terminal / app logs.

### Expected Behavior

After 2025-12-31, either:

- `use_container_width` is rejected / removed, as the deprecation message promised, **or**
- the warning no longer claims a 2025-12-31 removal date (for example, “will be removed in a future release”).

### Current Behavior

The call still works and prints:

```
Please replace `use_container_width` with `width`.

`use_container_width` will be removed after 2025-12-31.

For `use_container_width=True`, use `width='stretch'`. For `use_container_width=False`, use `width='content'`.
```

The date is a hardcoded string in `make_deprecated_name_warning(...)` (for example in `st.image` and the same pattern on other elements). It is not gated on the calendar date, and there is no follow-up removal.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: current `develop` (also observed in Community Cloud apps on 2026-09-08)
- Python version: n/a (API deprecation warning)
- Operating System: n/a
- Browser: n/a

### Additional Information

- Deprecation was introduced with Advanced Layouts, e.g. [PR #11719](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/11719) (“We will remove `use_container_width` after 12-31-2025”).
- I could not find an open GitHub issue or STREAMLIT Jira ticket tracking the actual removal after that date.
- Nearby precedent: [PR #15786](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/15786) already removed the older `use_column_width` parameter from `st.image`.
- Related but different: [#12519](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12519) quoted the same warning in the context of `st.image` + `width="stretch"` (closed as a separate bug).

This is not a Community Cloud platform issue; it is OSS Streamlit still advertising an expired deprecation date.
issues.title: `use_container_width` deprecation date (2025-12-31) has passed; parameter is still accepted

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add first-class authored descriptions at the page and app level: `page_description` on `st.set_page_config`, optionally `description` on `st.Page`, and a static title + description on `st.App`. Today a page can declare a title and icon, and an app has no catalog-level identity at all — so SEO, assistive tech, navigation, and non-browser clients all have to infer meaning from body copy.

### Why?

A Streamlit page already has `page_title` / `title` and `page_icon` / `icon`. There is no matching place to say what the page or the app *is*. Authors stuff that into `st.caption`, `st.markdown`, or `menu_items["About"]`, none of which is structured metadata.

That gap shows up in several places that all want the same authored sentence:

- **SEO and link previews.** Search and social crawlers need a description (and today only Community Cloud injects sharing tags). Related: #16634, #6567, #2469, #9058.
- **Accessibility.** A document-level description is the page analogue of alt text (#8563 covers elements; this is the page/app layer).
- **Multipage navigation.** `st.Page` can name a page but cannot explain it, so a nav list or catalog cannot tell "Regional revenue" from "Reports" without running the page.
- **Non-browser clients.** An agent snapshot currently serializes `url_path`, `title`, and `icon` only. A static app descriptor should be able to return title + description *without executing app code* — which is why the app-level fields belong on `st.App`, not only inside the script.

### How?

**Page description on `st.set_page_config`**, matching `page_title` / `page_icon`:

```python
st.set_page_config(
    page_title="Regional revenue",
    page_icon=":material/payments:",
    page_description=(
        "Net revenue by billing region. Excludes refunds. Periods are UTC."
    ),
)
```

**Optional `description` on `st.Page`**, so the page list carries copy without running each page (consistent with `title` / `icon`, not `page_*`):

```python
st.Page(
    "revenue.py",
    title="Regional revenue",
    icon=":material/payments:",
    description="Net revenue by billing region. Excludes refunds.",
)
```

**Static title and description on `st.App`**, available without executing the script:

```python
app = st.App(
    "main.py",
    title="Finance apps",
    description=(
        "Internal finance dashboards. Net revenue excludes refunds and is in EUR."
    ),
)
```

Suggested behavior:

- `st.Page.description` is the default for that page; `st.set_page_config(page_description=...)` overrides it for the current run (same additive pattern as today's page title).
- Single-page apps that never call `st.Page` still get a description via `set_page_config`.
- `st.App` title/description are app-level and static. They do not replace per-page title/description. For `streamlit run` apps without `st.App`, the default page's title/description (or a future config option) can stand in.
- Consumers of the same strings: HTML `<meta name="description">` / Open Graph, assistive tech, navigation (if we choose to surface it), and structured snapshots / a static app descriptor.

**Naming.** `page_description` on `set_page_config` matches `page_title`. On `st.Page` and `st.App`, `description` / `title` match the existing `title` parameter (the [agent-app interface spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/docs/agent-app-interface/specs/2026-08-28-agent-app-interface/product-spec.md) also floated `app_title` / `app_description` on `st.App` if we want the prefix explicit).

**Not in this request:** element-level alternative text for images, charts, and tables (#8563) and `help` on media (#3133). Arbitrary extra `<meta>` tags (GSC verification, etc.) stay with #16634.

### Additional Context

- Suggested as a standalone follow-up in the [agent-app interface spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/docs/agent-app-interface/specs/2026-08-28-agent-app-interface/product-spec.md) ([#16843](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16843), follow-up #3): apps should explain themselves in authored metadata, not only in body widgets. Worth doing on accessibility and SEO merits even without the agent interface.
- Related:
  - #16634 — inject `<meta>` tags; a first-class `page_description` is the content those tags would publish, not a general meta-tag API
  - #6567 — social sharing meta tags outside Community Cloud
  - #2469 (closed) — `st.set_page_config(description=...)`
  - #9058 — title/favicon in the initial HTML (same "available before JS" problem)
  - #8563 — element-level alt text
  - #5673 (closed) — config-file website metadata
issues.title: Add page and app descriptions (`page_description`, `st.Page`, `st.App`)

### Summary

Add opt-in support for Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) to the native authentication flow, so the _streamlit_user cookie set by st.login() becomes useless when copied off the device it was issued on.

Currently only Chrome takes advantage of this but I am happy to implement it and open a pull request
W3C draft: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-dbsc/

### Why?

Since 1.42, st.login() stores the user's identity in a signed cookie with a 30-day lifetime. The cookie is HttpOnly and Secure, which is right, but there is no server-side session state: a cookie copied from a browser profile by malware or a colleague with the laptop works on any other machine until it expires, and st.logout() only clears the local copy. The app-level mitigations available today are shortening the session age in application code and re-checking an allowlist on every rerun. Neither stops a stolen cookie from being used within its window.

DBSC is the web platform's answer to exactly this. The browser generates a key pair in the device's secure hardware at login, and the server issues a short-lived cookie that the browser can only renew by signing a challenge with that key. A copied cookie expires within minutes and cannot be refreshed elsewhere. Chrome shipped it as generally available on Windows in Chrome 146 and is rolling it out on macOS in Chrome 147, and it is a W3C WebAppSec draft. Browsers without support ignore the header and keep working as today, so it degrades cleanly.

Streamlit apps are frequently internal dashboards with real data behind Google or Entra logins, which is the population this protects.

### How?

The change is contained in the Starlette auth layer and needs no frontend work. Sketch:

1. **Registration header.** In the OAuth callback, alongside the existing cookies, send `Secure-Session-Registration` pointing at a new route, with the supported algorithms (ES256, RS256).
2. **Two new routes** next to `/auth/login`, `/auth/logout` and `/auth/callback`:
   - `/auth/dbsc/register`: verifies the browser's signed registration JWT, records the device public key, returns the session config, and sets a short-lived `__Host-` bound cookie.
   - `/auth/dbsc/refresh`: on a missing or expired bound cookie the browser calls this with a signed challenge; the server verifies it against the registered key and reissues the bound cookie.
3. **Stateless key storage.** Streamlit has no server-side session store and runs as one process, so rather than adding one, the device key's thumbprint is written into the existing signed `_streamlit_user` cookie at registration. Refresh verifies the challenge signature against the thumbprint carried in the cookie. Restarts and multiple replicas are then unaffected, matching how the current cookie works.
4. **Websocket check.** The `/_stcore/stream` endpoint, which already decodes the identity cookie on connect, refuses a connection whose identity cookie is bound but whose bound cookie is absent.
5. **Configuration.** A new `[auth]` option, off by default, for example `device_bound_sessions = true`. Requires HTTPS, since `__Host-` cookies are refused otherwise, which is already true of production `st.login()` deployments.

Signature verification can use authlib's JOSE support, which is already a dependency of the auth feature.

One point to verify during implementation: Chrome defers ordinary requests while it refreshes an expired bound cookie, and the behaviour for a WebSocket upgrade is not spelled out in the spec. The frontend fetches `/_stcore/host-config` and `/_stcore/health` over HTTP before opening the stream, which should trigger the refresh first, but this needs a real-browser test.


### Additional Context

- Chrome for Developers, DBSC overview and server integration: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/device-bound-session-credentials
- Chrome 147 macOS rollout: https://scotthelme.co.uk/device-bound-session-credentials-lands-in-chrome-on-macos/
issues.title: Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) for st.login() sessions

### Summary

Add a first-party, Playwright-based **end-to-end (browser) testing API** for Streamlit apps — `streamlit.testing.e2e` — as an optional `streamlit[testing]` extra, complementing the existing browserless unit-testing API (`AppTest`). It would provide a Streamlit-aware semantic facade for finding and operating elements in a real browser, rerun/navigation-aware synchronization, useful failure artifacts, and an escape hatch to native Playwright `Page`/`Locator`. Design thoughts are in the [app testing toolkit spec (PR #16041)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16041).

### Why?

Today users face an unhelpful choice: `AppTest` is fast and Python-native but runs no real frontend (so it can disagree with a real app, and can't cover rendering, custom components, accessibility, media, charts, or real user journeys), while browser testing can validate the real product but Streamlit provides **no supported way** to start the app, wait for reruns, select elements, collect logs, or test a deployed/embedded app — users must assemble and maintain all that infrastructure. Streamlit's own mature `e2e_playwright/` suite solves these hard problems (process lifecycle, ephemeral ports, app-idle detection, traces, iframes, uploads, dataframes/charts, etc.) but is coupled to the repo layout and private DOM test IDs, so it isn't a releasable public API.

This is especially costly for **AI coding agents**, which need a deterministic run command, semantic element identity, a compact description of the current UI, and actionable failure artifacts to validate their work — indexes, private CSS/test IDs, sleeps, and screenshots alone make brittle tests.

### How?

Ship a two-layer testing story with clear boundaries (don't build a third UI-testing engine, and don't turn AppTest into a browser emulator):

- **AppTest (browserless)** stays the fast option for logic/state/basic widget workflows — with improved runtime fidelity and typed + universal semantic queries (`get_by_key`/`get_by_label`/`get_by_text`) and a compact `snapshot()`.
- **`streamlit.testing.e2e` (browser)** — the new Playwright-based API, installed via `pip install "streamlit[testing]"`.

Proposed shape (from the spec):

```python
from playwright.sync_api import expect
from streamlit.testing.e2e import StreamlitPage, app_fixture

app = app_fixture("app.py")

def test_sign_in(app: StreamlitPage):
    app.get_element_by_label("Username", type="text_input").set_value("ada")
    app.get_element_by_label("Password", type="text_input").set_value("correct horse battery staple")
    app.get_element_by_label("Sign in", type="button").click()

    welcome = app.get_element_by_text("Welcome, ada", type="heading")
    expect(welcome.locator).to_be_visible()
```

Key capabilities:
- **App lifecycle fixture:** `app_fixture()` starts one app server per test module on an ephemeral localhost port, gives an isolated browser page per test, and waits until the initial run is idle. Also target direct/external URLs (deployed/embedded apps).
- **Semantic selection:** strict, retrying finders that understand Streamlit elements and layout containers — `get_element_by_key` / `get_element_by_label` / `get_element_by_text`, plus `get_element(type=...)` / `get_elements(type=...)`; a returned element that is a container (sidebar, form, expander, popover, dialog, tab, column, container) can scope further queries. An optional `type` discriminator maps to a generated public `ElementType` taxonomy for IDE completion.
- **Rerun/navigation-aware synchronization** so tests don't rely on sleeps.
- **Actionable failure artifacts** (text/logs/traces/screenshots) and a **semantic snapshot** (`semantic_snapshot()`) as a token-efficient interface for humans and agents.
- **Escape hatch** to native Playwright `Page`/`Locator` for anything the facade doesn't cover.
- A shared **testability vocabulary** across both layers (public element types, labels, keys, containers), explicitly optimized for AI agents.

### Additional Context

- Spec: [PR #16041 — \`[spec] Streamlit app testing toolkit\`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16041) (`specs/2026-07-16-streamlit-app-testing-toolkit/product-spec.md`).
- Related: open `feature:app-testing` issues, e.g. #9786, #13163, #9128.
issues.title: Add a first-party Playwright-based e2e testing API (`streamlit.testing.e2e`) alongside AppTest

### Summary

Deprecate the [`persist` parameter of `st.cache_data`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/caching-and-state/st.cache_data) (`persist="disk"`). It doesn't fit well with the rest of the API and is incompatible with more recent features. A better, more flexible alternative is to make the **cache storage backend configurable** (e.g. via `st.App`), so users can plug in a storage that persists to disk — or Redis/S3 — consistently across the whole app.

### Why?

`persist="disk"` is a narrow, awkward escape hatch:
- It only supports a single hardcoded mode (`"disk"`) with a non-configurable location (#3018).
- It doesn't compose cleanly with other cache features — e.g. it ignores `ttl` (#4859).
- It's a per-function flag for what is really a deployment/storage concern, so it's easy to misuse and inconsistent across an app.
- It doesn't scale to multi-instance deployments (each replica has its own local disk), where users actually want a shared/central store.

A configurable storage backend addresses all of this in one coherent mechanism, and persistence becomes just one storage implementation rather than a special-cased parameter.

### How?

- **Introduce a configurable cache storage API** (per the [custom storage API spec, PR #14902](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14902)) — e.g. a `cache_storage_manager` parameter on `st.App` — that lets users supply a custom backend (disk, Redis, S3, …) applied consistently to `st.cache_data`.
  - A built-in/example disk-persisting storage would cover today's `persist="disk"` use case (with configurable location, and without the `ttl` incompatibility).
- **Deprecate `persist`** on `st.cache_data` with a long, clearly-communicated window and a documented migration path (it keeps working during deprecation). Follow "Graceful Evolution" — 3+ months notice, clear migration guidance.

### Additional Context

- Docs: [`st.cache_data`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/caching-and-state/st.cache_data).
- Replacement direction: [PR #14902 — custom storage API for `st.App`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14902) (also motivated by #5849 "bring your own Redis cache").

### Summary

When using `refresh_mode="background"` on `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource`, the stale grace window is fixed at 1×TTL (hard expiry at 2×TTL). This means an app idle overnight (longer than 2×TTL) has its cache evicted and the first morning user blocks on a cold miss.

A `max_stale` parameter would let users configure the stale grace window independently from TTL:

```python
@st.cache_data(ttl="2m", max_stale="12h", refresh_mode="background")
def load_data():
    return expensive_query()
```

This separates two concerns: **how often to refresh** (`ttl="2m"`) from **how long stale data is acceptable** (`max_stale="12h"`). Users who want frequent freshness checks but never want to block get exactly that.

### Why?

From [#11050](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11050) (comment by @itsToggle):

> Is there any way that we can influence the "2 × ttl" background cache timeout? In my use case I want a short ttl so the values are updated often, but I never want my users to have to wait for a response. I would like to set the ttl to something like 2 minutes, but the oldest background cache that's allowed to be served can be much older than four minutes.

This is also the more practical solution for the "first user of the day" problem compared to cron scheduling, since it does not require an always-on server and works on scale-to-zero deployments.

### How?

The [background refresh spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-04-08-cache-background-refresh/product-spec.md) already calls this out as future work:

> **`max_stale` parameter**: Explicitly configure the stale grace window (default: equal to `ttl`), e.g. `ttl="1h", max_stale="12h"` to serve stale data across an overnight idle gap without blocking the first morning user

### Additional Context

- Related (closed): [#5871](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5871), [#11050](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11050)
issues.title: Add `max_stale` parameter to `refresh_mode="background"` for configurable stale grace window

issues.body: ### Checklist - [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues. - [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue. - [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue. ### Summary A keyed `st.dataframe` or `st.data_editor` excludes its data from the element identity: `key_as_main_identity={"selection_mode", "is_selection_activated"}` at [arrow.py lines 1280-1284](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/2bd9d77e68e1ef6beaee2bcf98da2c0707bacc63/lib/streamlit/elements/arrow.py#L1280-L1284). The element id therefore survives a data refresh, and the browser resends grid state that was computed against the previous frame. `event.selection.rows` and `edited_rows` are positional, so after a rerun that reorders or inserts rows those positions address different records, and the app receives a selection or an edit for a row the user never touched. There is no error and no warning. The comment directly above that call site acknowledges that selections "can become orphaned when the data changes" and that resetting them "might be a nice enhancement"; the effect on an app that acts on the selection is a wrong-row write, not a cosmetic orphan. ### Reproducible Code Example ```Python import pandas as pd import streamlit as st st.session_state.setdefault("gen", 0) st.session_state.setdefault("closed", []) # Simulates a queue whose contents change between reruns (a new ticket arrived). rows = ["TICK-101", "TICK-102", "TICK-103", "TICK-104"] if st.session_state["gen"]: rows = ["TICK-100", *rows] df = pd.DataFrame({"ticket": rows}) event = st.dataframe(df, key="queue", on_select="rerun", selection_mode="single-row") if st.button("Simulate new ticket arriving", key="refresh"): st.session_state["gen"] += 1 st.rerun() if st.button("Close selected", key="close") and event.selection.rows: position = event.selection.rows[0] st.session_state["closed"].append(df.iloc[position]["ticket"]) st.write("Selected positions:", event.selection.rows) st.write("Closed:", st.session_state["closed"]) ``` ### Steps To Reproduce 1. `streamlit run` (or `uv run streamlit run`) the snippet. 2. Click the row showing `TICK-102` (position 1). The app shows `Selected positions: [1]`. 3. Click "Simulate new ticket arriving". `TICK-102` gets bumped down to position 2, but the highlighted row and `event.selection.rows` are still `[1]`, which is now `TICK-101`. 4. Click "Close selected". You get `Closed: ['TICK-101']` even though you had initially selected `TICK-102`. The same holds for `st.data_editor` with the default `num_rows="fixed"`: a pending `edited_rows` entry is re-applied at the same position after the frame changes. The identity part can be shown without a browser, using `AppTest`: ```python from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest def script(): import pandas as pd import streamlit as st st.session_state.setdefault("gen", 0) if st.button("refresh", key="refresh"): st.session_state["gen"] += 1 rows = ["TICK-101", "TICK-102", "TICK-103", "TICK-104"] if st.session_state["gen"]: rows = ["TICK-100", *rows] df = pd.DataFrame({"ticket": rows}) st.dataframe(df, key="queue", on_select="rerun", selection_mode="single-row") st.dataframe(df, on_select="rerun", selection_mode="single-row") at = AppTest.from_function(script).run() keyed, unkeyed = at.dataframe[0].proto.id, at.dataframe[1].proto.id at.button(key="refresh").click().run() print(keyed == at.dataframe[0].proto.id) # True -> keyed id survives the data change print(unkeyed == at.dataframe[1].proto.id) # False -> unkeyed id does not ``` ### Expected Behavior When the data behind a keyed grid changes, stale selection and edit state should be reset (or the state should be keyed by row identity rather than position), so an app never receives positions computed against a frame it is no longer showing. At minimum the docs for `key=` on `st.dataframe` / `st.data_editor` should say that selection and edit state is positional and survives data changes. ### Current Behavior Positional selection and edit state is preserved across data changes for keyed grids. Dropping `key=` makes the id data-dependent and the stale state orphans to empty, which is safe but discards every pending selection or edit on any data change, and contradicts the general advice to always give widgets a key. ### Is this a regression? - [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version. Not a recent regression, at least. The row retarget in steps 1-4 was observed in Chromium on 1.60.0. The `AppTest` demonstration above prints `True` / `False` on both 1.63.0 and 1.64.0 (the latest release at the time of writing), and the identity code is unchanged at the current tip of `develop`. On 1.60.0 and later the `st.data_editor` case is wider than on 1.59.x: a keyed editor with `num_rows="fixed"` re-applies a pending edit at the same position after a reorder, where 1.59.x discarded it. ### Debug info - Streamlit version: 1.63.0 and 1.64.0, both reproduced - Python version: 3.14.6 - Operating System: Linux Mint 22.3 Zena 64-bit - Browser: Version 152.0.7977.82 (Official Build) for Linux Mint (x86_64) ### Additional Information Related: `_apply_dataframe_edits` ([data_editor.py#L560-L564](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/2bd9d77e68e1ef6beaee2bcf98da2c0707bacc63/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/data_editor.py#L560-L564)) receives no `disabled` argument, so `disabled=["_index"]` is enforced only in the browser; a client-sent index edit is applied server-side. Apps that act on grid state currently have to pin the frame they rendered in `st.session_state`, resolve positions against that frame, and reject anything they did not serve.
issues.title: Keyed `st.dataframe` / `st.data_editor` keep positional selection and edit state across a data change, so actions land on the wrong row

### Checklist

### Summary

Add an opt-in `copy="cow"` mode to `st.cache_data` that uses copy-on-write semantics for cached return values. This avoids unnecessary full-object deserialization on cache hits while preserving isolation between callers, significantly reducing cache-hit latency and memory allocation for large cached objects.

### Why?

`st.cache_data` currently creates an independent copy of the cached value for each call. This provides isolation between callers, but for large objects such as Pandas DataFrames and NumPy arrays, repeatedly deserializing and copying cached values can introduce significant CPU time and memory allocation overhead.

This becomes particularly relevant for applications where large datasets are read repeatedly across multiple sessions, while mutations to returned values are relatively uncommon.

An opt-in copy-on-write mode can preserve the isolation guarantees of `st.cache_data` while avoiding unnecessary full-object duplication on cache hits. The existing behavior would remain unchanged for applications that do not opt into the new mode.

In benchmarks using Python 3.13.15, Pandas 3.0.6, and Streamlit 1.64.0, the prototype reduced observed cache-hit latency by approximately 2.7–3.2× for DataFrames ranging from 5,000 to 1,000,000 rows. In a separate allocation benchmark with 10 consecutive reads, observed allocation decreased from approximately 4.67 MB to 0.02–0.03 MB.

### How?

Introduce an optional `copy` parameter on `st.cache_data`:

```python
@st.cache_data(copy="cow")
def load_data():
    return pd.read_parquet("large_dataset.parquet")

### Additional Context

### Prototype

A working prototype is available in my fork:

https://github.com/Isllanrx/streamlit/tree/feature/cache-data-cow

The implementation is currently limited to the following areas:

- `st.cache_data` API support for `copy="cow"`
- Copy-on-write handling for supported cached return values
- Caller/session mutation isolation
- Integration with existing cache lifecycle and eviction behavior
- Unit tests for mutation isolation
- Static typing coverage for the public API

### Performance Benchmark

The prototype was benchmarked using Python 3.13.15, Pandas 3.0.6, and Streamlit 1.64.0.

| Dataset | Default copy | `copy="cow"` | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5,000 × 12 | 0.155 ms | 0.055 ms | 2.8× |
| 50,000 × 12 | 0.158 ms | 0.049 ms | 3.2× |
| 200,000 × 12 | 0.144 ms | 0.048 ms | 3.0× |
| 1,000,000 × 12 | 0.131 ms | 0.049 ms | 2.7× |

In a separate allocation benchmark using 10 consecutive cache reads, observed allocation decreased from approximately 4.67 MB with the existing behavior to approximately 0.02–0.03 MB with `copy="cow"`.

### Stress Testing

The implementation was also tested under concurrent mutation and cache lifecycle pressure:

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 50 concurrent threads mutating the same 100,000-row DataFrame | Passed |
| Nested dictionaries containing DataFrames, Series, and lists | Passed |
| 200 concurrent cache entries with `max_entries=5` | Passed |
| Concurrent readers while repeatedly calling `.clear()` | Passed |
| 1,000,000-row (~100 MB) DataFrame with mutation isolation | Passed |

The concurrent mutation test completed in approximately 0.046 seconds. The cached DataFrame remained unchanged and no cross-caller mutations were observed.

The 1,000,000-row test also preserved mutation isolation, with subsequent reads completing in approximately 0.08 ms.

These tests were specifically designed to validate both the performance characteristics and the isolation guarantees of the proposed copy-on-write behavior.
issues.title: [feature] Add copy="cow" option to st.cache_data

issues.body:
## Summary

Let a cached data source declare a cheap "has the source changed?" probe, so
Streamlit re-runs the expensive query (and updates dependent fragments) **only
when the underlying data actually changed** — instead of on a blind timer. This
is the event-driven counterpart to timer-based refresh.

## Why?

Timer-based refresh (`@st.fragment(run_every=…)`, or a server-side scheduled
refresh) fires on a fixed clock regardless of whether anything changed. For an
expensive query that forces a bad tradeoff:

- **Poll fast** → the heavy query re-runs every interval even when the data is
  identical, wasting warehouse/API cost.
- **Poll slow** → users stare at stale data between ticks.

Sources usually expose something *cheap* that reveals whether they changed — a
version token, an ETag, a `MAX(updated_at)`, a Snowflake stream or
change-tracking timestamp. There's no built-in way to poll that cheap signal
often and re-run the expensive work only when it moves.

## How?

Attach a cheap freshness function to a cached data source. Streamlit checks the
freshness token; when it changes, it invalidates the cache and re-runs the
fragments that read it. When it's unchanged, the cached value is served and no
expensive work runs.

Sketch (names illustrative):

```python
def orders_version():
    # Cheap probe — cache invalidates when this value changes.
    return conn.query("SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM orders")

@st.cache_data(freshness=orders_version)
def load_orders():
    return conn.query("SELECT * FROM orders")   # expensive; runs only on change

@st.fragment(run_every="5s")
def orders_panel():
    df = load_orders()      # cheap probe each poll; heavy query only when changed
    st.line_chart(df, x="ts", y="orders")

orders_panel()
```
issues.title: Freshness signal: refresh cached data only when the source actually changes

issues.body:
## Summary

Provide a way to refresh a data source on a **server-side schedule** — computed
once for the whole app and pushed to every session currently viewing it —
instead of each session running its own `run_every` timer and recomputing the
same query independently. This is the shared "the dashboard refreshes every
minute and everyone sees the latest" pattern that live/ops dashboards need.

## Why?

`@st.fragment(run_every=…)` already gives time-driven updates, but the timer and
the computation are **per session**: with _N_ viewers on the same dashboard you
get _N_ timers and _N_ executions of the same query every interval. A refresh
that is cheap for one user becomes _N×_ load on the warehouse/API for a shared
internal tool.

`@st.cache_data` dedupes the *computation* across sessions, but nothing *drives*
a periodic refresh or *wakes* the sessions when a new value lands — today
`run_every` is the driver, and it's per session. The missing piece is a refresh
that runs once for the whole app and updates every session viewing it.

## How?

Mark a cached data source to refresh on a fixed interval, centrally for the
whole app. Any fragment that reads it shows the current value and re-renders when
a new one lands.

Sketch (names illustrative):

```python
# The value refreshes centrally every 60s; sessions read the current value and
# rerun when a new one lands — no per-session timer, one shared computation.
@st.cache_data(refresh_every="60s")
def latest_metrics():
    return run_warehouse_query()

@st.fragment
def kpis():
    df = latest_metrics()          # returns the current cached value immediately
    st.metric("Orders", len(df))
    st.line_chart(df, x="ts", y="orders")

kpis()
```

## Additional Context

- Split out from [#12980](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12980)
  ("real-time chart updates without rerunning the entire script"), which is being
  closed now that fragments (`run_every`), `st.rerun(scope=…)`, and element
  diffing cover the original per-session/live-update and flicker concerns.
- Related in-flight work: the non-blocking background execution spec
  ([#17067](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17067)) covers shared,
  off-thread cached computation; scheduled/recurring refresh is called out there
  as not-yet-built.
- Companion gap: a **freshness signal**
  ([#17141](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/17141)) — a cheap "did
  the source change?" probe (e.g. Snowflake change-tracking / `LAST_ALTERED` /
  `MAX(updated_at)`) to drive **event-driven** invalidation instead of a blind
  timer. That's the push counterpart to this timer-based one.
issues.title: Periodic server-driven data refresh shared across sessions (vs. per-session run_every)

issues.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

The Core Idea

Streamlit's greatest strength is also one of its defining architectural characteristics: Python execution is the primary mechanism through which application state and UI are updated.

This works exceptionally well for data applications where an interaction naturally maps to a Python computation.

However, highly interactive applications expose a different requirement:

A browser event is not necessarily a Python execution event.

A mouse move, drag, hover, resize, crosshair movement, animation frame, realtime tick, or temporary UI state change may occur dozens or hundreds of times per second and may require data and state stored in the frontend.

The proposal is therefore not simply to add more widgets or more rerun options.

The deeper proposal is to introduce a lightweight event/state runtime between the browser and Python execution model.

Instead of treating every interaction as:

UI event → Python → rerun → UI

Streamlit could support:

                         UI EVENT
                             │
                 ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                 │                       │
                 ▼                       ▼
          Client-side state        Event routing
                 │                       │
                 │              ┌────────┼────────┐
                 │              │        │        │
                 ▼              ▼        ▼        ▼
             UI update       Client   Fragment   App
                              only      rerun    rerun

Python would remain the primary application and business-logic layer, but it would no longer have to participate in every interaction.

This is the architectural distinction behind the rest of this proposal.

The objective is not to turn Streamlit into React.

The objective is to make Streamlit capable of supporting both:

Traditional Streamlit
interaction → Python rerun

and:

Highly interactive Streamlit
interaction → client/state/event layer → Python only when needed

The existing programming model would remain intact. The new model would simply provide a second level of control for applications that need it.

Streamlit has made significant progress toward more granular execution control, fragments, background execution, and real-time UI updates.

The next step could be to provide a frontend interaction model that allows Streamlit applications to handle high-frequency client-side events and state changes without requiring a Python script rerun for every interaction.

This would make Streamlit much more suitable not only for dashboards and data applications, but also for highly interactive applications such as trading terminals, monitoring systems, visual editors, control panels, and real-time operational interfaces.

The goal is not to replace Streamlit's existing rerun model, but to add a second, more granular interaction layer alongside it.

---

# The Core Problem

Today, Streamlit provides an excellent Python-first programming model:

User interaction
      ↓
Widget event
      ↓
Python execution
      ↓
UI update

This model is extremely productive for traditional data applications.
However, highly interactive applications often have a different event profile:

Mouse movement
Drag
Resize
Hover
Crosshair movement
Keyboard shortcut
Realtime market tick
Chart event
Component state change
      ↓
potentially dozens or hundreds of events per second

Not every one of these events should require a Python rerun.

For example, dragging a trading order line from one price to another may generate many intermediate browser events, while the application may only need to execute Python logic when the user releases the mouse button.

Similarly, a chart crosshair can move continuously without requiring Python execution at every pixel.

A more explicit separation between **client-side interaction**, **application state**, and **Python execution** would make Streamlit considerably more powerful.

# Proposed Model
Introduce an event/state layer that allows developers to explicitly define what happens when a client-side event occurs.

Conceptually:

                    ┌─────────────────────┐
                    │      Browser        │
                    │                     │
                    │ UI / Chart / Input  │
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │
                    Client-side events
                               │
              ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
              │                │                │
              ▼                ▼                ▼
          Client state     Event stream     Python event
              │                │                │
              ▼                ▼                ▼
       No rerun needed    Optional rerun    Fragment/App

The important idea is that **an event should not automatically imply a Python rerun**.

# 1. True Client-Side State

Allow components to maintain state that can change frequently on the client without immediately triggering Python execution.

For example:

chart_state = st.chart(
    symbol="BTCUSDT",
    client_state=True
)

Client-side state could include:

* cursor position
* selected item
* drag position
* zoom level
* viewport
* temporary form state
* hover state
* drawing state
* component-local UI state

Python could explicitly request the current state when needed.

This would preserve Streamlit's Python-first model while allowing components to behave more like native browser applications.

# 2. Event Channels

Introduce a generic event mechanism for high-frequency or transient browser events.
For example:

[python]
chart.on("mousemove", handler)
chart.on("drag", handler)
chart.on("crosshair", handler)
chart.on("resize", handler)
chart.on("selection", handler)

Events should be distinguishable from persistent state.
A useful distinction could be:

State
→ "What is the current value?"

Event
→ "What just happened?"
```
This distinction is particularly important for transient events such as mouse movement, clicks, keyboard shortcuts, and drag operations.

# 3. Fire-and-Forget Events

Allow events to be processed entirely on the client without invoking Python.
For example:

[python]
chart.on(
    "mousemove",
    client=True
)
or conceptually:

[python]
chart.on("drag", rerun=False)

This would allow extremely frequent UI interactions without overwhelming the Streamlit execution engine.
Python could still receive the final result:

drag start
   ↓
client-side movement
   ↓
client-side movement
   ↓
client-side movement
   ↓
drag end
   ↓
Python event

This is especially useful for:

* chart interactions
* sliders
* drawing tools
* drag-and-drop
* resizing
* visual editors
* canvas applications

# 4. Explicit Rerun Policy

Allow developers to explicitly define the execution scope of an event.
For example, conceptually:

[python]
widget(
    on_change="client"
)

or:

[python]
widget(
    on_event="fragment"
)

or:

[python]
widget(
    on_event="app"
)

or:

[python]
widget(
    on_event="none"
)

The exact API is open for discussion.
The important principle is that the developer should be able to specify:

No Python execution
        OR
Component/client update
        OR
Fragment rerun
        OR
Full application rerun

This would complement Streamlit's existing progress toward selective reruns.

# 5. Shared Reactive State

Provide a lightweight mechanism for multiple components to observe the same application state without requiring a full application rerun for every update.
For example:

[python]
price = st.reactive_state("BTCUSDT.price")

chart.bind(price)
price_panel.bind(price)
order_panel.bind(price)

A state update could then propagate selectively:

             BTC price
                 │
       ┌─────────┼─────────┐
       ▼         ▼         ▼
     Chart     Metric    Order UI

This would be particularly useful for real-time applications where many UI elements depend on the same rapidly changing state.

The mechanism should ideally support:

* selective subscriptions
* batching
* throttling
* debouncing
* immutable snapshots
* explicit synchronization boundaries

# 6. High-Frequency Event Streams

Provide first-class support for event streams that may produce many updates per second.

Examples:

market ticks
sensor data
telemetry
mouse movement
chart crosshair
audio/video state
live logs
simulation output

Instead of:

event → rerun → render → event → rerun → render

the model could support:

event stream
     ↓
buffer / throttle / batch
     ↓
selected subscribers
     ↓
UI update

Developers should ideally be able to control:

[python]
throttle=50      # milliseconds
debounce=100
batch=True
max_rate=20

This would make realtime applications much easier to build while protecting the Python execution engine from excessive event traffic.

# 7. First-Class JavaScript / TypeScript Components

Streamlit's custom component architecture is extremely valuable, but highly interactive applications often require developers to move a significant amount of application logic into JavaScript/TypeScript.

A future component API could make this boundary more seamless.
Ideally, a component should be able to expose:

Python API
     │
     ├── persistent state
     ├── transient events
     ├── client-side actions
     └── server-side callbacks

without forcing developers to effectively build a separate frontend application.

For example:

[python]
chart = st.interactive_component(...)

chart.state
chart.events
chart.call("zoom_to", ...)
chart.emit("selection", ...)

The goal would be to make JavaScript/TypeScript an **extension of Streamlit**, rather than a parallel application architecture.

# 8. A Unified Event → State → Rerun Model

The eight ideas above could ultimately form one coherent programming model:

                 CLIENT
                   │
        ┌──────────┴──────────┐
        │                     │
      Events                State
        │                     │
        ▼                     ▼
   Event routing       State synchronization
        │                     │
        └──────────┬──────────┘
                   ▼
             Execution policy
                   │
        ┌──────────┼──────────┐
        ▼          ▼          ▼
      Client     Fragment     App
       only       rerun      rerun

This would preserve the simplicity that makes Streamlit attractive while giving developers much more control when building complex interactive applications.

# Example Use Case: Real-Time Trading Interface

A real-time trading terminal is a useful stress test for this model.
Consider a chart with draggable Entry, Stop Loss, and Take Profit levels.
During dragging:

Mouse movement
      ↓
Client-side chart update
      ↓
No Python rerun

When the user releases the mouse:

Drag end
      ↓
Event
      ↓
Python
      ↓
Risk calculation
      ↓
Order validation
      ↓
UI update

At the same time, market data could arrive independently:

WebSocket
    ↓
price event
    ↓
shared reactive state
    ↓
chart + position panel + P/L

This type of application currently requires a significant amount of custom frontend logic.

A more granular Streamlit event model could make such applications much more natural to implement while retaining Python as the primary application language.

# Why This Could Be Valuable Beyond Trading

The same architecture would benefit:

* real-time monitoring dashboards
* industrial control panels
* IoT interfaces
* scientific visualization
* financial terminals
* simulation environments
* visual editors
* workflow builders
* interactive maps
* multimedia applications
* operational dashboards
* collaborative applications

In other words, this would not be a trading-specific feature.

It would expand the category of applications that can be built naturally with Streamlit.

# Compatibility With the Existing Streamlit Model

This proposal does not require removing or fundamentally changing Streamlit's current execution model.

The existing model would remain the default:

Widget → Python → rerun

The new model would simply provide additional levels of control:

Client event
     ↓
   ┌───────────────────────────────┐
   │                               │
Client only → Fragment → App rerun


Developers building traditional data applications would not need to use any of this.

Developers building highly interactive applications could opt into it where necessary.

# Design Principle

The key principle could be summarized as:

> **Not every UI event should be a Python execution event.**

And similarly:

> **Not every state change needs to become a full application rerun.**

Streamlit has already been moving toward more granular execution and real-time interaction. A unified event/state model could provide the architectural layer that connects these improvements into a coherent system.

# Suggested Discussion Questions

Some questions that would be useful for the Streamlit team and community:

1. Should transient events and persistent component state be first-class, separate concepts?
2. Should client-only events be able to bypass Python entirely?
3. Should developers be able to explicitly select the rerun scope of an event?
4. Could shared reactive state be implemented without introducing a React-like programming model?
5. How should high-frequency events be throttled, debounced, or batched?
6. Could custom components expose a standardized event/state interface?
7. How far should Streamlit go toward supporting desktop-class interactive applications while retaining its Python-first simplicity?

---

## Conclusion

Streamlit's Python-first development model is one of its strongest advantages.

The goal should not be to turn Streamlit into React.

Instead, Streamlit could provide a **small, explicit event/state layer** that allows developers to build applications where:

* Python remains the application and business-logic layer;
* the browser handles high-frequency interaction locally;
* state can be synchronized selectively;
* events can be routed to client, fragment, or application scope;
* realtime streams can be throttled and batched;
* custom components can participate in the same model.

That would preserve Streamlit's simplicity while significantly expanding the class of interactive applications it can support.

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Please make AppTest's widget interaction API synchronize query parameters for widgets using `bind="query-params"`. Currently, `.set_value(...).run()` changes the widget value but leaves both `at.query_params` and the app's `st.query_params` unchanged, so tests observe a different state from the browser.

### Why?

Native query-param binding lets apps replace manual URL callbacks. After that change, AppTest tests that verify shareable filters or inspect `st.query_params` can no longer reproduce the state reached by the same user interaction in the browser. Each test must manually mirror the binding's serialization into `at.query_params`.

The following self-contained example demonstrates the gap on Streamlit 1.65.0; it also occurs on 1.64.0:

```python
from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest

at = AppTest.from_string("""
import streamlit as st

st.selectbox("FC", ["A", "B"], key="fc", bind="query-params")
st.session_state["seen_query"] = dict(st.query_params)
""").run()

at.selectbox[0].set_value("B").run()
assert not at.exception
print("Widget:", at.selectbox[0].value)
print("AppTest query params:", at.query_params)
print("App query params:", at.session_state["seen_query"])
```

Save as `repro_query_binding.py` and run `python repro_query_binding.py` with `streamlit==1.65.0` installed. No pytest or app-specific dependencies are required.

Observed:

```text
Widget: B
AppTest query params: {}
App query params: {}
```

In a browser, selecting B in the app string above updates the URL to `?fc=B` and the script sees `{"fc": "B"}`. The same AppTest gap occurs with `st.text_input(..., key="fc", bind="query-params")` and `at.text_input[0].set_value("B").run()`.

### How?

Use the existing interaction API to model the bound query-param update when a widget commits a value. For the example above, the desired result after `.set_value("B").run()` is:

```text
Widget: B
AppTest query params: {'fc': 'B'}
App query params: {'fc': 'B'}
```

The interaction should send a coherent widget-state/query-string pair using the widget's binding semantics, including serialization and clearing of the bound parameter. Unrelated query parameters should remain intact. This can be supported in the existing browserless AppTest API; a new browser runner is not requested.

A current workaround is to set the query params manually in the test before the run:

```python
at.selectbox[0].set_value("B")
at.query_params["fc"] = "B"
at.run()
assert at.session_state["seen_query"]["fc"] == "B"
```

This works, but the test must duplicate application binding logic. Keeping explicit `on_change` callbacks that write `st.query_params` also works, at the cost of retaining the application glue that native binding could replace.

### Additional Context

#### Environment and controls

- Streamlit: 1.65.0, also reproduced on 1.64.0.
- Python: 3.14.8.
- OS: macOS 27.0.1, arm64.
- Browser: Not required for the AppTest example. Browser comparisons used the Codex in-app browser on macOS and confirmed correct binding on both versions.
- The tested Streamlit Python files match their wheel RECORD hashes; no installed source was modified.
- Initial URL values correctly seed a bound widget in AppTest.
- Programmatically changing `st.session_state["fc"]` before rendering the bound widget correctly updates query params.
- Manual URL-writing callbacks work in AppTest.

#### Related work checked

- [#16906](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/16906) requests a first-party browser-testing API. This request targets bound-widget query serialization during existing AppTest interactions.
- [PR #17191](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17191), included in 1.65.0, fixes single-value/list representation in `at.query_params`. The example still returns an empty dict after that fix.
- [PR #16998](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16998) fixes browser back/forward restoration. This example changes a widget through AppTest and performs no history navigation.

I did not find an existing issue requesting this specific AppTest behavior. I am using the feature-request form because this extends the test simulation; the runtime binding itself works in the tested browser examples.

[LocalScriptRunner.run](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/ac7fffe6cf8474a258b2f64c96604137cfbbb37e/lib/streamlit/testing/v1/local_script_runner.py#L170) constructs the query string from the query params passed by AppTest. The current widget interaction path does not generate the corresponding query-param update that a browser would send.
issues.title: AppTest: synchronize query parameters when interacting with query-bound widgets

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

Starting with Streamlit 1.62.0, a button inside **st.container(horizontal=True)** (or placed directly in a column) gets an HTML **title** attribute on its label when **help** is not set. Hovering the label then shows the browser's native tooltip.

According to the **wrap** docstring, this is meant to "reveal the full label" when it's truncated with an ellipsis. However, the **title** is added even when the label fits and nothing is truncated. The result is an unexpected, unstyled tooltip on every short button in a horizontal layout. It also looks inconsistent next to Streamlit's own **help** tooltip, which has a different style and position.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

LONG_LABEL = "This is a very long button label " * 6

# 1. Unexpected: native tooltip although the label is not truncated
with st.container(horizontal=True):
    st.button("Short label")

# 2. Truncated label: here the native tooltip is useful
with st.container(horizontal=True):
    st.button(LONG_LABEL)

# 3. wrap=True: label wraps, no native tooltip
with st.container(horizontal=True):
    st.button(LONG_LABEL, wrap=True, key="wrapped")

# 4. Vertical container: no native tooltip
with st.container(horizontal=False):
    st.button("Short label", key="vertical")

# 5. help set: Streamlit tooltip only
st.button("With help", help="This is a button with a tooltip")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app above with **streamlit run app.py**.
2. Hover the mouse over the text of the first button ("Short label") and wait about one second.

### Expected Behavior

No tooltip should appear, because the label is fully visible and **help** is not set. The native **title** tooltip should appear only when the label is actually truncated, as in case 2.

### Current Behavior

The browser's native tooltip (rectangular, below and to the right of the cursor) shows the label text even though nothing is truncated. The button in the vertical container (case 4) does not show it.

### Is this a regression?

- [x] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.65.0 (also reproduced on 1.62.0)
- Python version: 3.12.8
- Operating System: Windows 11
- Browser: Chrome 154.0.8037.95 (64-bit)

### Additional Information

**Button** passes **addTitleTooltip = !wrap && !help** to the label component. In the 1.65.0 bundle, the hook that handles this flag (minified, in **StreamlitMarkdown.*.js**) always sets **title** to the label's text content. It does not check whether the text overflows (for example **el.scrollWidth > el.clientWidth**).

A possible fix is to set **title** only when the label is truncated, and re-check it with a **ResizeObserver** alongside the existing **MutationObserver**. The same hook appears to be used by **st.checkbox**, **st.popover** and markdown with **wrap=False**, so these may be affected too.

Workaround: pass **wrap=True** to the button.
issues.title: Button in horizontal container shows native browser title tooltip even when the label is not truncated

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

The element toolbar above an `st.dataframe` (Show/hide columns, Download as CSV, Search, Fullscreen) is in the Tab order, but `[data-testid="stElementToolbar"]` keeps `opacity: 0` while one of its buttons has keyboard focus. It only becomes visible on mouse hover. A keyboard user therefore tabs through four buttons they cannot see, which fails WCAG 2.4.7 (Focus Visible).

Related but distinct: #13332 (keyboard access to the column-header menu) and #17127 (toolbar target size, fixed).

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st


def home():
    st.title("Home")
    st.button("First button")
    st.dataframe(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": ["x", "y", "z"]}))
    st.button("Last button")


pg = st.navigation(
    {
        "": [st.Page(home, title="Home")],
        "Group": [
            st.Page(lambda: st.write("B"), title="Page B", url_path="b"),
            st.Page(lambda: st.write("C"), title="Page C", url_path="c"),
        ],
    },
    position="top",
)
pg.run()
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app above.
2. Click the page background, then press Tab until focus passes "First button".

### Expected Behavior

The toolbar is visible whenever focus is inside it, as it is on hover.

### Current Behavior

The next four Tab stops are the toolbar buttons. `document.activeElement` is the button, and `getComputedStyle(toolbar).opacity` is `"0"` for all four.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.65.0 (also reproduced on 1.61.1)
- Python version: 3.11
- Operating System: Linux (RHEL 8)
- Browser: Chromium (headless, Playwright 1.63.0)


### Additional Information

Workaround we use in our app:

```css
[data-testid="stElementToolbar"]:focus-within { opacity: 1; }
```
issues.title: `st.dataframe` toolbar stays invisible (opacity 0) while its buttons have keyboard focus

### Summary

`section[data-testid="stMain"]` is a Tab stop, which is right for keyboard scrolling (axe `scrollable-region-focusable`). But when it has focus it shows no indicator: `outline-style: none` and `box-shadow: none`. On every page, the Tab stop after the header is invisible, which fails WCAG 2.4.7 (Focus Visible).

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st


def home():
    st.title("Home")
    st.button("First button")
    st.dataframe(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": ["x", "y", "z"]}))

pg = st.navigation(
    {
        "": [st.Page(home, title="Home")],

            st.Page(lambda: st.write("B"), title="Page B", url_path="b"),
            st.Page(lambda: st.write("C"), title="Page C", url_path="c"),
        ],
    },
    position="top",
)
pg.run()
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app above.
2. Press Tab from the top of the page. Stops 1–4 are the top-nav items, Deploy and Main menu (Main menu shows a box-shadow ring).
3. Press Tab once more.

### Expected Behavior

A `:focus-visible` indicator on the main region, such as the ring other controls use.

### Current Behavior

Stop 5 is `stMain`, with `outline: none` and `box-shadow: none`. Nothing on screen shows where focus is.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.65.0 (also reproduced on 1.61.1)
- Python version: 3.11
- Operating System: Linux (RHEL 8)
- Browser: Chromium (headless, Playwright 1.63.0)


### Additional Information

[data-testid="stMain"]:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid <primary>; outline-offset: -2px; }

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

With `st.navigation(..., position="top")`, a section ("Group") opens on Enter and closes on Escape. But focus doesn't move into the open menu, and arrow keys do nothing. Each menu item is reached only after Tab has passed every other focusable element on the page. This fails WCAG 2.4.3 (Focus Order) and differs from the WAI-ARIA menu button pattern.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st


def home():
    st.title("Home")
    st.button("First button")
    st.dataframe(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": ["x", "y", "z"]}))
    st.button("Last button")


pg = st.navigation(
    {
        "": [st.Page(home, title="Home")],
        "Group": [
            st.Page(lambda: st.write("B"), title="Page B", url_path="b"),
            st.Page(lambda: st.write("C"), title="Page C", url_path="c"),
        ],
    },
    position="top",
)
pg.run()
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app above.
2. Tab to "Group" and press Enter (the menu opens).
3. Press ArrowDown.
4. Press Tab repeatedly.

### Expected Behavior

Enter, Space or ArrowDown opens the menu and moves focus to its first item; arrow keys move between items; Escape returns focus to the trigger. (Alternatively, the menu could be rendered right after its trigger in DOM order, so the next Tab reaches its items.)

### Current Behavior

- ArrowDown leaves focus on "Group".
- Tab goes to Deploy, Main menu, then the page content (both buttons, the dataframe toolbar, the grid).
- "Page B" is reached on the 14th Tab press, even in this tiny app.
- ArrowDown on the closed section doesn't open it.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.65.0 (also reproduced on 1.61.1)
- Python version: 3.11
- Operating System: Linux (RHEL 8)
- Browser: Chromium (headless, Playwright 1.63.0)

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Streamlit’s app shell should expose clear page landmarks and a way to skip repeated chrome, so keyboard and screen-reader users can move straight to the main content (WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks).

Today the shell has a semantic `<header>` and a labeled sidebar region, but the primary content area (`stMain`) is a `<section>` rather than `<main>`, sidebar/page navigation is not exposed as a `navigation` landmark, and there is no skip link.

### Why?

Without a main landmark and a skip mechanism, assistive-tech users often have to tab through header, toolbar, and sidebar controls on every page load or navigation. This was called out as part of the “page structure” ask in #8399 (now closed/triaged). Our theme a11y inventory also leaves WCAG **2.4.1** unscored.

### How?

Suggested shell improvements (exact shape TBD):

1. **Main landmark** — Render the primary app content as `<main>` (or give `stMain` an equivalent landmark role), without breaking existing layout/scroll behavior or `data-testid="stMain"` consumers.
2. **Navigation landmark** — Expose sidebar page nav and/or top nav as `<nav>` (or `role="navigation"`) with an accessible name when present.
3. **Skip link** — Add a keyboard-focusable “Skip to main content” link (visually hidden until focused) that moves focus into the main landmark.

Out of scope for this issue: author-controlled heading hierarchy inside app content; document language (`lang`) which is tracked in #15726; focus-indicator bugs on `stMain` which are tracked separately in #17338.

### Summary

Streamlit 1.65.0 pins `pyarrow>=7.0,!=25.0.0,<26` (and `develop` still has `<26`). pyarrow 26.0.0 was released on 2026-10-09 and is the first release with CPython 3.15 wheels; pyarrow 25.x has no `cp315` wheels.

uv add streamlit

2. Install `streamlit==1.65.0`.

Streamlit installs using the pyarrow 26.0.0 `cp315` wheel.

issues.body:
**Problem (user experience)**

When a page uses `@st.fragment(parallel=True)` for slow, independent work, interacting with a control *inside* one fragment feels unresponsive **while the rest of the page is still loading**. The interaction doesn't take effect until the slow parallel work elsewhere on the page finishes — so a quick control (a filter, a toggle, a view switcher) appears frozen even though it only affects its own fragment.

This is specific to the *in-progress* window — typically initial load, or just after a full rerun, while slow parallel fragments are still filling in. Once the page is idle, the same in-fragment control responds immediately.

**Reproduction**

```python
import time
import streamlit as st

@st.fragment(parallel=True)
def slow_panel():
    time.sleep(3)          # unrelated slow work
    st.write("slow done")

@st.fragment(parallel=True)
def controls():
    choice = st.radio("View", ["A", "B"], horizontal=True)
    st.write(f"selected {choice}")

slow_panel()
controls()
```

On initial load, change the radio while `slow_panel` is still running. The selection doesn't apply until `slow_panel` finishes (~3s), even though the control and its output live entirely in the `controls` fragment. Moving the control to the main script makes it respond immediately — but that forces an awkward layout and defeats the point of co-locating a control with the fragment it drives.

**Expected experience**

A control inside a fragment should stay responsive during a long load: changing it should update its own fragment promptly, without waiting for unrelated slow fragments elsewhere on the page to finish. Today's sequential, deterministic behavior for fragment reruns should be preserved — the goal is responsiveness during an in-progress load, not a change to how state is applied or a way to interrupt a fragment mid-execution (see #11030 for that).

**Related:** #14968, #11030, #12799
issues.title: Controls inside a fragment stay unresponsive while the rest of the page is still loading

### Summary

Add a `scope` parameter to `st.stop()`, mirroring `st.rerun(scope=...)`:

```python
st.stop(scope="app")       # default: current behaviour, halts the whole script run
st.stop(scope="fragment")  # halts only the currently executing fragment
```

With `scope="fragment"`, Streamlit would stop running the current fragment function. If the fragment is running as part of a full-app run, the rest of the script would continue from the statement after the fragment call.

### Why?

`st.stop()` is a common "guard clause" pattern: check a precondition, show a message, stop. Inside a fragment, though, `st.stop()` stops the *entire* script run when the fragment executes during a full-app run. Everything rendered after the fragment call is skipped, even though only the fragment's own precondition failed.
It would be useful when you have a called child function in the fragment that has st.stop in with its own conditions that you'd want to stop the flow of the parent.

Example:

```python
import streamlit as st

def some_stop_condition():
     now = datetime.now()
     if now < datetime.combine(now.date(), time(16, 45)):
           st.warning("You can't use this service before 4:45pm")
           st.stop(scope="fragment")

@st.fragment
def upload_panel():
    some_stop_condition()
    file = st.file_uploader("Upload a CSV")
    if file is None:
        st.info("Upload a file to see a preview.")
        st.stop()  # intent: stop this panel only
    st.dataframe(load(file))

st.title("Dashboard")
upload_panel()
st.header("Other section")  # skipped on full-app runs when no file is uploaded
render_other_stuff()
```

The usual workaround is `return`, but that only works at the top level of the fragment function. When the guard lives in a helper called from the fragment, you have to thread return values or flags back up through every layer, or raise and catch a custom exception. `st.stop(scope="fragment")` would give fragments the same clean early-exit that `st.stop()` gives scripts.

This also fits with the existing API. Since `st.rerun` already supports `scope="fragment"`, users reasonably expect the same option on `st.stop`. It would also be useful inside `@st.dialog` functions, which are built on fragments.

### How?

- Add `scope: Literal["app", "fragment"] = "app"` to `st.stop`.
- `scope="app"`: unchanged behaviour.
- `scope="fragment"`: end execution of the current fragment function only.
  - During a **fragment rerun**: equivalent to the fragment finishing early. Elements already written by the fragment in this run stay displayed.
  - During a **full-app run**: the fragment ends early and the script continues after the fragment call. (Unlike `st.rerun(scope="fragment")`, this is well defined during a full-app run, so it doesn't need to be disallowed there.)
  - Called **outside a fragment**: raise `StreamlitAPIException`, consistent with `st.rerun(scope="fragment")`.
- Nested fragments: stop the innermost executing fragment.

Possible implementation: raise a distinct `FragmentStopException` (or a `StopException` carrying a scope), which the fragment wrapper catches and swallows. The script runner would then continue normally.

### Additional Context

- `st.rerun` scope docs: https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/execution-flow/st.rerun
- Related but different: #11030 (interrupting an in-progress fragment run from a button click)

### Why?

_No response_

### How?

_No response_

### Additional Context

_No response_
issues.title: Add scope to st.stop()

### Summary

Provide a managed API for starting one-shot background work in response to an explicit signal, such as a button click or form submission.

Unlike background cache refresh, each start is an intentional action and the result should not be memoized.

```python
task = st.task(key="generate_report")

if st.button("Generate report"):
    task.start(generate_report, uploaded_data)

if task.running:
    st.info("Generating report...")
elif task.done:
    st.download_button("Download report", task.result)
elif task.error:
    st.error(task.error)
```

### Why?

Some work should:

- start only after an explicit user action;
- continue without blocking the app;
- survive script reruns;
- expose its running, completed, and error states; and
- execute exactly once per explicit start.

Examples include generating a report, sending an email, writing to a database, triggering a pipeline, or running an LLM request.

### Related

- #6687 — broader background execution request, closed after the cached-computation pattern became available
- #10578 — work interrupted by reruns
- #14524 — rerun-resilient UI streaming, a distinct use case
issues.title: Support on-demand, rerun-resilient background tasks

## Summary

Please update Streamlit's published Pillow requirement from `pillow>=9.2.0,<13` to `pillow>=9.2.0,<14` and regenerate the lockfile so Streamlit can resolve Pillow 13.0.0.

## Why?

Pillow 13.0.0 was released on 2026-10-16 and contains security fixes. Streamlit 1.66.0 currently caps Pillow below 13, which prevents downstream applications from receiving the patched release. ## How?

I prepared the minimal change locally:

```diff
- pillow>=9.2.0,<13
+ pillow>=9.2.0,<14
```

The lockfile resolves successfully to Pillow 13.0.0. Existing Streamlit Pillow usage is covered by the image, hashing, and write-path tests.

### Summary

Add a `streamlit deploy` CLI command for headless, non-interactive deployment and updates of Streamlit apps directly from the terminal. Ideally, it works out of the box with **Streamlit Community Cloud**, **Streamlit in Snowflake (SiS)**, and at least one external cloud target (e.g. **Cloudflare**), and provides a way to inspect server logs (e.g. `streamlit deploy --logs`).

### Why?

AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) can already scaffold, run (`streamlit run`), and test Streamlit apps locally, but there is no unified, headless way for an agent to **deploy an app, push updates, and read remote server logs** to verify the deployment or debug startup crashes.

Today, deploying requires browser-based flows (Community Cloud), separate ecosystem CLIs with their own project layouts (`snow streamlit deploy`, `wrangler`, etc.), or manual container setups. A built-in, agent-friendly `streamlit deploy` command closes the loop from local authoring to a live shareable URL.

### How?

Introduce a `streamlit deploy` CLI command modeled after `streamlit run`:

```bash
# Deploy or update an app (uses detected/configured target)
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py

# Explicitly select a deployment target
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py --target community-cloud
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py --target snowflake
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py --target cloudflare

# Inspect or stream server logs of the deployed app
streamlit deploy --logs
```

Key capabilities & design patterns:

- **Out-of-the-box targets (pluggable provider model):**
  - **Streamlit Community Cloud** (e.g. via GitHub repo coordinates / API or direct bundle upload).
  - **Streamlit in Snowflake (SiS)** (e.g. delegating to `snowflake-cli` / `snow streamlit` or native connection config).
  - **External provider (e.g. Cloudflare Workers / Containers)** for quick standalone hosting (potentially building on `streamlit dockerize`, #16307).
- **Idempotent create-or-update with persisted project state:**
  - Persist non-secret deployment metadata (target provider, app ID/slug, entrypoint, deployed URL) in the project (e.g. `.streamlit/deploy.toml` or `config.toml`) so subsequent `streamlit deploy` and `streamlit deploy --logs` calls work with zero arguments.
- **Server log access & closed-loop verification:**
  - Support fetching/streaming build and runtime logs (e.g. `streamlit deploy --logs [--follow]` or `streamlit deploy logs`).
  - Automatically surface startup errors / tracebacks and exit non-zero if the deployed app fails its initial health check or boot run, so agents can self-correct.
- **Headless & agent-friendly UX:**
  - Non-interactive execution (`--yes` / env var / token auth) with a one-time login flow (`streamlit deploy --login` or reusing `gh` / `snow` / `wrangler` credentials).
  - Structured output option (`--json`) returning the deployed URL, status, and app identifier.
  - Sync `.streamlit/secrets.toml` / environment variables safely when requested (e.g. `--secrets`).

### Additional Context

- Related:
  - #13635 — Allow Cursor or other AI agents to deploy to Community Cloud
  - #16307 — Add a `streamlit dockerize` CLI command to package an app into a Docker image
  - [PR #16843 — Agent-app interface spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16843)
issues.title: Add a `streamlit deploy` CLI command for headless app deployment
