### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Allow configuring a headless AI agent / model backend in Streamlit (e.g. Cortex in SiS, an ACP-compatible agent, or a CLI agent like `coco`, `claude`, `cursor`, `gemini`, `codex`) that operates the app internally via the [Agent Interaction API (`/_stcore/agent/interact`, PR #16843)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16843) to unlock built-in, **viewer-facing** agentic capabilities — such as a built-in "chat with app" assistant, standalone HTML/PDF report generation (#611), and AI-assisted widget/chart interactions (#12991, #12992).

Developer-facing workflows (debugging, profiling, test generation) should be kept separate, as most of them are better served by extending Streamlit's **embedded agent skills (`streamlit skills`)** and CLI tools rather than embedding a coding agent into the app runtime.

### Why?

We have several long-standing requests for rich, viewer-facing capabilities in deployed apps:
- Exporting an app (or a synthesis of multiple filter states) as a standalone HTML or PDF report (#611).
- Asking a dashboard natural-language questions or co-browsing ("Chat with app").
- Natural-language / voice / smart filling for widgets and forms (#12992, #6717) and ad-hoc chart building (#12991).

Building bespoke engines or deterministic compilers for each of these inside core Streamlit is complex and brittle. Meanwhile, `/_stcore/agent/interact` ([#16843](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16843)) already exposes the app as a safe, structured semantic tree (elements, Markdown explanations, Arrow tables, Vega/Plotly specs, and legal widget actions) bounded by what the viewer is allowed to see. Pairing that endpoint with a configurable headless agent unlocks all of these viewer features through a single, safe runtime loop.

### How?

#### 1. Viewer-facing runtime features (powered by a configured app agent + `/_stcore/agent/interact`)

Allow configuring an agent/model backend for the running app (e.g. `[agent]` in `config.toml`, `st.App`, or pre-configured on SiS via Cortex), scoped strictly to `/_stcore/agent/interact` (no filesystem or code-execution access) and the viewer's identity (`st.user`):

- **Built-in "Chat with app" / Co-browsing UI:**
  - Viewers can ask questions about the dashboard or ask the assistant to set filters/forms.
  - The agent runs in an isolated `/_stcore/agent/interact` session seeded from the viewer's current widget state ([#17394](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17394), [#17401](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17401)), drives filters across one or more runs, reads Arrow tables/metrics, and returns cited answers (or syncs state changes back to the browser).
- **Export app as a standalone HTML or PDF report (#611):**
  - The agent reads the structured snapshot, prose, metrics, Arrow data, and Vega/Plotly specs via `/_stcore/agent/interact` (optionally sweeping across multiple filter states on request) and compiles a self-contained interactive HTML file or formatted PDF report.
- **AI-assisted widgets, forms, and chart builder (#12991, #12992, #6717):**
  - **AI chart builder (#12991, #10257):** Viewers describe a chart on a dataframe or existing chart; the agent inspects the Arrow schema/preview and generates a Vega-Lite/Plotly spec.
  - **Smart widget & form input (#12992, #6717):** Translate natural language (e.g. `"first to last day of Q2 2023"` in `st.date_input`), pasted unstructured text into an `st.form`, or transcribed voice input (#6717) into typed widget values validated against the snapshot's `value_schema`.

#### 2. Developer-facing workflows (keep separate — prioritize `streamlit skills` + CLI/dev hooks)

Developer tasks require source-code and shell access and happen where a coding agent (`coco`, `claude`, `cursor`, `codex`) is **already running outside Streamlit**. Instead of mixing them into the viewer runtime agent:
- **Extend embedded skills (`streamlit skills`) + `/_stcore/agent/interact`:** Teach the developer's existing coding agent how to use `/_stcore/agent/interact`, `streamlit deploy --logs` (#17619), and profiling/state endpoints to debug, profile (#373), and generate `AppTest` / `streamlit.testing.e2e` tests (#16906).
- **Lightweight dev-mode UI bridges (#16730, #12990, #16306):** If a local coding agent is configured/detected in development mode, `st.exception` (#12990) and the debug pane (#16730) only need a lightweight bridge (e.g. *"Copy context for agent"* or *"Send to local agent"*) rather than a separate built-in dev agent.

### Additional Context

- Foundation spec: [PR #16843 — `[spec] Agent-accessible Streamlit apps`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16843) (`specs/2026-08-28-agent-app-interface/product-spec.md`), plus [#17394](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17394) and [#17401](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17401).
- Related viewer-facing issues:
  - #611 — Export to standalone HTML file (and PDF report generation)
  - #6717 — Input widgets to accept voice and convert it to text
  - #12991 — AI-assisted chart builder (and #10257)
  - #12992 — AI-assisted `st.date_input`
- Related developer-facing issues (better addressed via `streamlit skills` + thin dev-mode bridges):
  - #373 — Implement an easy to use profiler for Streamlit
  - #12990 — AI-generated summary/help text in `st.exception`
  - #16730 — Add a developer debug pane for inspecting state, cache, memory, and profiling (and #16306)
  - #16906 — Add a first-party Playwright-based e2e testing API (`streamlit.testing.e2e`) alongside AppTest
issues.title: Allow configuring a headless agent to unlock built-in agentic app features

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Allow apps to clear a chart's selection from Python for `st.altair_chart`, `st.vega_lite_chart`, `st.plotly_chart`, and `st.pydeck_chart`. Today, chart selection state is read-only: assigning to `st.session_state[key]` raises `StreamlitValueAssignmentNotAllowedError`, so the only way to clear a selection is to change the chart's `key`, which remounts the chart.

### Why?

Cross-filtered dashboards usually have a "Clear filters" button, or per-filter chips that remove one filter. The filter state lives in Python, but the chart that produced it keeps showing the old selection, and the selection reappears in `st.session_state[key]` on the next rerun.

The current workaround is to bump a generation counter in the chart's key:

```python
st.session_state.setdefault("gen", 0)

if st.button("Clear all"):
    st.session_state.gen += 1

event = st.altair_chart(chart, on_select="rerun", key=f"region_{st.session_state.gen}")
```

This works, but it:

- remounts the chart, which re-creates the view and costs a full re-render;
- forces apps to track per-chart key generations and to ignore stale selections from the old key; and
- is not discoverable.

`st.dataframe` already supports this since #13594: assigning `{"selection": {"rows": []}}` to its key clears the selection.

### How?

Mirror the `st.dataframe` design from #13594, limited to clearing:

- Allow assigning an empty selection to the chart's key, for example `st.session_state["region"] = {"selection": {}}`, or `None`. Non-empty values can keep raising until setting selections is supported (#17627).
- Send the clear to the frontend once, through a proto field, so the chart resets its visual selection and widget state without a remount.
- Clear the frontend's saved selection view state, so the selection does not come back after a remount or in fullscreen.

Things to define:

- Whether a programmatic clear triggers `on_select` callbacks. Widgets generally don't fire callbacks for programmatic changes.
- Behavior inside forms and fragments.
- Applying the same API to `st.echarts_chart` once its selection support lands.

### Additional Context

- Related: #12395 (easier cross-filtering between charts and dataframes), #10308 (an Altair `selection_point` default value is ignored with `on_select="rerun"`).
- Precedent: #10128 and #13594 (setting `st.dataframe` selections programmatically).
issues.title: Allow clearing chart selections programmatically

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Allow apps to set a chart's selection from Python, through session state and a `selection_default` parameter, for `st.altair_chart`, `st.vega_lite_chart`, `st.plotly_chart`, and `st.pydeck_chart`. This is the chart equivalent of what #13594 added for `st.dataframe`.

### Why?

- **Initial selections:** show a chart with a value already selected, for example the current region, or a filter restored from query parameters or a saved view.
- **Syncing views:** when a filter changes elsewhere (a widget, a dataframe selection, another chart), the chart that owns that dimension should show the same selection.
- **Undo and history:** restore a previous filter state.

Today, chart selection state is read-only, so none of this is possible. Even a selection default defined in the chart spec is ignored once `on_select="rerun"` is set (#10308).

### How?

Mirror the `st.dataframe` design from #13594:

- Accept a selection in the same schema the chart returns. For example, `st.session_state["region"] = {"selection": {"region": [{"region": "EUROPE"}]}}` for an Altair point selection, or point indices per trace for Plotly.
- Add a `selection_default` parameter for the first render.
- Validate against the chart's data and selection parameters, filtering or rejecting entries that don't apply.

Feasibility differs by chart type:

- **Plotly:** point indices per trace, plus box and lasso shapes, map well to Plotly's own selection APIs.
- **PyDeck:** object indices per layer, likely feasible.
- **Altair / Vega-Lite:** the selection Streamlit returns is simplified. A point selection carries field values, and an interval selection carries `[min, max]` per field. Vega's internal selection record needs more: which panel of the chart a selection belongs to, and the type of each field. That can be rebuilt for single-view charts with selections that declare `fields` or `encodings`. Composite charts (layer, concat, facet) and point selections without `fields`, whose values are Vega's internal row IDs, may need to stay unsupported, with a clear error.

Things to define:

- Whether a programmatic set triggers `on_select` callbacks.
- What happens when the data changes and a selected value is no longer present.
- Behavior inside forms and fragments.
- Applying the same API to `st.echarts_chart` once its selection support lands.

Clearing a selection is simpler and tracked separately in #17626.

### Additional Context

- Related: #10308, #12395 (easier cross-filtering between charts and dataframes).
- Precedent: #10128 and #13594 (setting `st.dataframe` selections programmatically).
issues.title: Allow setting chart selections programmatically and with a selection_default parameter

### Summary

Clicking “Edit with Codespaces” in Community Cloud automatically added .devcontainer/devcontainer.json to my repository’s main branch, with the commit attributed to my GitHub account. The action should preview the proposed change and require explicit consent before writing to the repository.

### Why?

I expected “Edit with Codespaces” to open a development environment. I didn’t expect it to create a commit on my default branch under my name without showing me the file or asking for confirmation.

The generated config also broke my CI since it didn't conform to my project's validation hooks.

The unexpected commit initially made me question whether someone else had accessed my account. Its attribution made it harder to identify what had actually created it.

Reviewing a repository change is useful friction. I would prefer to see the configuration the app needs and add it myself. Authorizing repository access should not replace clear consent at the point where an action modifies the repository.

### How?

Before creating a devcontainer configuration:
1. Show the exact file contents, target repository, and branch.
2. Offer a copy/download option so users can review and commit the file themselves. 
3. If automated setup is offered, require explicit confirmation and create a pull request instead of committing directly to the default branch.
4. Clearly identify Streamlit as the source of automated changes rather than attributing them solely to the user.

https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/why-is-there-impersonation-with-added-dev-container-folder-commit/92371

### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Custom components v2 can reference JS and CSS files by path only when the component is an installed package that declares `asset_dir` in its `pyproject.toml`. A component defined inside an app has to pass its HTML, CSS and JavaScript as inline strings. Allow `st.components.v2.component()` to take an `asset_dir` resolved relative to the calling script, so app authors can use real files without packaging. This especially helps JavaScript-only custom components, whose Python side is just the `component()` definition and whose code is written and built with JavaScript tooling.

### Why?

Inline strings work for small snippets, but they get in the way as soon as a component is built with a bundler or grows beyond one file:

- **One file only.** Inline JS can't import other files with relative paths, so there are no code-split chunks.
- **No other assets.** Fonts, images, or WASM can only be embedded as data URIs.
- **Awkward workflow.** The build output has to be read into a Python string, and editors and devtools see one long string instead of files.

The only way to use files today is to turn the component into an installed Python package. Streamlit finds a component's `asset_dir` by scanning installed distributions at startup, so a `pyproject.toml` next to the app isn't enough. For a component used in one app, that means:

- **A separate package.** It needs its own `pyproject.toml` with build-system config, a name and version, package-data rules so the JS and CSS files are included, and a `[[tool.streamlit.component.components]]` entry.
- **An install step everywhere the app runs**, for example `pip install -e ./my_component`, on every developer machine, in CI, and in every deployment. Without it, the app fails at startup.
- **Deployment workarounds.** Hosted environments install from a requirements file, so a local package needs a path dependency or publishing to a package index.

Packaging is the right model for components meant to be shared or published. For a component that belongs to one app, and especially for a JavaScript-only component with no Python code to package, it's a lot of machinery just to serve files from a folder next to the script.

### How?

Add an `asset_dir` parameter to `st.components.v2.component()`:

```python
my_component = st.components.v2.component(
    "my_component",
    js="index.js",          # relative to asset_dir
    css="styles.css",
    asset_dir="frontend",   # relative to this script
)
```

Possible rules:

- The path resolves against the file that calls `component()`, not the working directory.
- It must be an existing directory. It can't contain the calling script, so `.` and parent directories are rejected, and it can't contain `.streamlit`. This keeps app code and secrets from being served.
- If the component's package already declares an `asset_dir`, raise an error rather than guessing which to use.
- Files under the folder are watched in development, so editing them reloads the app like editing the script does.
- `asset_dir` can point straight at a bundler's output folder, such as Vite's `dist/`, so code-split chunks, fonts and images load relative to the entry file. Optionally, Streamlit could read the entry file and CSS from the bundler's manifest, so `js=` and `css=` can be left out.

### Additional Context

- The current docstring says paths and globs are "only possible for installed components".
- Related: [#15484](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/15484) (AppTest discovery of installed CCv2 components).

**If you'd use this, please react with a 👍 so we can gauge interest.**
issues.title: Let `st.components.v2.component` serve files from a local `asset_dir` without packaging

### Summary

`st.dataframe` still truncates most unevaluated inputs to 10,000 rows and shows a "showing only …" warning. Polars `LazyFrame` already loads on demand; the other types we treat as unevaluated should do the same out of the box, with no cutoff and no manual `to_pandas()` / `collect()` / `compute()`.

### Why?

These objects are used because the data lives on the backend (Snowflake, Spark, DuckDB, …) and is too large to materialize. The cutoff forces a full collect or hand-rolled pagination, which defeats passing a Snowpark table or similar straight into `st.dataframe`.

### How?

Reuse the existing lazy path: above the current 10k cutoff, fetch rows from the backend as the user scrolls. `lazy=False` keeps today's preview.

```python
orders = session.table("orders")  # Snowpark Table
st.dataframe(orders)
```

Still cut off today (`is_unevaluated_data_object`):

- Snowpark DataFrame / Table
- Snowpark pandas DataFrame / Series / Index
- PySpark DataFrame
- Dask DataFrame / Series / Index
- Modin DataFrame / Series
- DuckDB relation
- DB-API 2.0 cursor
- Generator functions

Where a type can't report a row count or serve a stable range (generators, some cursors), use sequential server-side loading instead of the cutoff.

### Additional Context

- Cutoff is `_MAX_UNEVALUATED_DF_ROWS = 10000` in `convert_anything_to_pandas_df`. `lazy=True` on these types currently raises `lazy-no-adapter-available`.
- Polars `LazyFrame` already has an adapter.
- Lazy dataframe spec: #15092. Implementation: #15756.
- Adjacent: #11701 (only evaluate required columns for unevaluated frames in charts).
issues.title: Lazy-load unevaluated data objects in `st.dataframe` instead of cutting them off

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add `required: bool = False` to `st.file_uploader`, `st.camera_input`, and `st.audio_input`, so a form can't be submitted until a file or recording is provided. This is a follow-up from the [required-widgets spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-08-18-required-widgets/product-spec.md) (#16555), which shipped `required` on the text, number, date/time, and selectbox widgets (#7165).

### Why?

Upload forms usually can't continue without a file ("upload a CSV, then ingest it"). Today an empty uploader submits the form. Checking for `None` afterwards in Python costs a rerun, and with `clear_on_submit=True` the other fields are already wiped by the time the app rejects the submit. These widgets also commit empty today: deleting the last file or clearing a recording reruns the app with `None`.

### How?

Proposed behavior, from the spec's "File-like widgets" section:

- **Empty** means `None`, or `[]` with `accept_multiple_files`. An upload still in flight is not empty.
- **Form submit:** blocked while the widget is empty (no rerun, no `clear_on_submit`). The widget shows `This field is required.` with the same error chrome as the other required widgets: red outline, error icon with tooltip, and a visually hidden `role="alert"` linked by `aria-describedby`. The submit button is not disabled.
- **`st.file_uploader`:** deleting the last remaining file is locked, so the widget can't go back to empty. Dropping a new file still replaces it.
- **`st.camera_input` / `st.audio_input`:** keep the Clear button, because it is how the user recaptures, but Clear no longer commits `None`. The next capture commits.
- **Label and accessibility:** a muted `(required)` marker when the label is visible. The dropzone, camera, and audio roots don't honor `aria-required`, so `(required)` also goes into the accessible name (`aria-label` / `aria-labelledby`).
- **Same as the shipped widgets:** the return type does not narrow, `required` is part of the widget ID only when there is no `key`, and the check runs in the browser only.

```python
with st.form("upload"):
    f = st.file_uploader("CSV", type="csv", required=True)
    if st.form_submit_button("Ingest"):
        ingest(f)
```

### Additional Context

- Spec: [required-widgets product spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-08-18-required-widgets/product-spec.md), sections "Enforcement styles" (file-like widgets) and "Accessibility".
- Umbrella request: #7165.
- The existing behavior that disables the form submit button while an upload is in flight stays as it is.
issues.title: Add `required` parameter to `st.file_uploader`, `st.camera_input`, and `st.audio_input`

### Summary

`st.pills` and `st.segmented_control` have had `required` since 1.56 (#14414), but it only stops the user from deselecting a single-select option. Align it with the `required` parameter the other input widgets now have from the [required-widgets spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-08-18-required-widgets/product-spec.md) (#16555): a `(required)` label marker, form-submit gating, and multi-select support.

### Why?

`required` should mean the same thing on every widget. Today a required pills or segmented control that starts empty (no `default`) still lets a form submit with `None`, shows no `(required)` marker, and `required=True` with `selection_mode="multi"` raises an error (#14900).

### How?

From the spec's "Pills and segmented_control" section:

| Today | Proposed |
| --- | --- |
| Can't deselect once a value is selected | Unchanged |
| May start empty when `default` is unset | Unchanged; don't auto-select the first option |
| No `(required)` label | Add the marker when the label is visible; keep `aria-required` |
| An empty required widget can still submit a form | Block the submit and show `This field is required.` with the shared error chrome (red outline, error icon with tooltip, visually hidden `role="alert"`) |
| `required=True` with `selection_mode="multi"` raises | Allow it: at least one selection, and the last selected option can't be deselected |

Also:

- **Widget identity:** `required` is not part of the widget ID today. Match the other required widgets: include it only when there is no `key`.
- **Typing:** keep the existing overloads that narrow the return type when `required=True` and `default` is set. Multi-select with `required` still returns `list[V]`.
- **Behavior change:** an empty required pills or segmented control inside a form will start blocking the submit. Call this out in the changelog.

### Additional Context

- Spec: [required-widgets product spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-08-18-required-widgets/product-spec.md), section "Pills and segmented_control (existing `required`)".
- This includes #14900 (`required` for multi-select pills).
- #9870: the original single-select request, shipped in 1.56.
- Umbrella request: #7165.
issues.title: Align `required` on `st.pills` and `st.segmented_control` with other input widgets

### Summary

Add `required: bool = False` to `st.multiselect`, meaning at least one option must be selected. This is a follow-up from the [required-widgets spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-08-18-required-widgets/product-spec.md) (#16555), which shipped `required` on the text, number, date/time, and selectbox widgets (#7165).

### Why?

Many forms need "pick at least one" (tags, regions, recipients). Today an empty multiselect submits the form, and outside a form, removing the last option reruns the app with `[]`.

### How?

Proposed behavior, from the spec:

- **Empty** means `[]`. `required=True` doesn't change the default.
- **Form submit:** blocked while nothing is selected (no rerun, no `clear_on_submit`). The widget shows `This field is required.` with the same error chrome as the other required widgets: red outline, error icon with tooltip, and a visually hidden `role="alert"` linked by `aria-describedby`. The submit button is not disabled.
- **Can't return to empty:** once at least one option is selected, the last one can't be removed. The remove button on the last chip and the clear-all button are hidden, and Backspace doesn't remove it either. Users can add another option first and then remove the old one.
- **`max_selections=1` with `required=True`:** the last-option lock plus the existing "Remove an option first" limit means the user can't swap the only selection. The spec keeps the same lock here (no swap shortcut and no error); call it out in the changelog. `st.selectbox(..., required=True)` is the alternative for a single required choice.
- **Label and accessibility:** a muted `(required)` marker when the label is visible, and `aria-required="true"`.
- **Same as the shipped widgets:** the return type stays `list[V]` (no non-empty guarantee, since the widget returns its default until the user picks), `required` is part of the widget ID only when there is no `key`, it works with `on_change="ignore"`, and the check runs in the browser only.

```python
with st.form("share"):
    recipients = st.multiselect("Recipients", team, required=True)
    if st.form_submit_button("Share"):
        share(recipients)
```

### Additional Context

- Spec: [required-widgets product spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-08-18-required-widgets/product-spec.md), sections "Enforcement styles" (selection widgets) and "Edge cases".
- `min_selections` (#9977) stays separate. `required=True` is the `min_selections=1` case.
- Umbrella request: #7165.
issues.title: Add `required` parameter to `st.multiselect`

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add `required: bool = False` to `st.radio`, so a form with a radio that starts empty (`index=None`) can't be submitted until the user picks an option. This is a follow-up from the [required-widgets spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-08-18-required-widgets/product-spec.md) (#16555), which shipped `required` on the text, number, date/time, and selectbox widgets (#7165).

### Why?

Radio groups without a preselected option are common in forms (survey questions, "Choose a plan"), because a preselected answer biases the result. Today `st.radio(..., index=None)` lets the form submit `None`, and the app has to reject it after the rerun.

### How?

Proposed behavior, from the spec:

- **Empty** means `None` (`index=None`). `required=True` doesn't change the default: a radio still starts on the first option unless you pass `index=None`.
- **Form submit:** blocked while nothing is selected (no rerun, no `clear_on_submit`). The radio group shows `This field is required.` with the same error chrome as the other required widgets (error icon with tooltip and a red outline; exact placement on the group to be settled in design), a visually hidden `role="alert"` linked by `aria-describedby`, and `aria-invalid` on the `radiogroup`. The submit button is not disabled.
- **Outside a form:** users can't deselect a radio, so `required` adds the muted `(required)` label marker and `aria-required="true"` on the `radiogroup`.
- **Same as the shipped widgets:** the return type stays `V | None`, `required` is part of the widget ID only when there is no `key`, it works with `on_change="ignore"`, and the check runs in the browser only.

```python
with st.form("survey"):
    plan = st.radio("Plan", ["Free", "Pro", "Team"], index=None, required=True)
    if st.form_submit_button("Continue"):
        st.write(f"Selected {plan}")
```

### Additional Context

- Spec: [required-widgets product spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-08-18-required-widgets/product-spec.md), sections "Enforcement styles" (selection widgets), "Design", and "Accessibility".
- Umbrella request: #7165.

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

`st.metric(format=...)` applies one format to both `value` and `delta`. A metric whose value and delta have different units, such as a dollar amount with a percent change, therefore can't use numeric inputs. Add a `delta_format` parameter so the delta can have its own format.

### Why?

KPI cards usually mix units: revenue with a percent change, a rate with a change in percentage points, a count with a "vs. last period" percent. While building a BI demo ([feature-demos/bi-dashboard](https://github.com/streamlit/feature-demos/tree/main/bi-dashboard)), none of the four KPI cards could use `format`. Each one formats both strings by hand:

```python
st.metric(
    "Annual recurring revenue",
    money(arr),  # "$21.44M"
    f"{arr_change:+.1%}",  # "+40.6%"
    delta_description="vs. 12 months ago",
)
st.metric(
    "Net revenue retention",
    f"{nrr:.1f}%",  # "125.5%"
    f"{nrr_change:+.1f} pts",  # "+13.0 pts"
)
```

Passing pre-formatted strings gives up the numeric handling of `delta`. Only the number `0` and the string `"0"` count as zero, so a change that rounds to zero still gets a colored arrow. The app needs a helper to turn those strings back into `0`; see #17835.

### How?

Add a keyword-only `delta_format` parameter that accepts the same values as `format` (`"percent"`, `"dollar"`, `"compact"`, printf-style strings, and the others). When it's `None` (default), the delta keeps using `format`, so existing apps don't change.

```python
st.metric("Revenue", 1_240_000, 0.084, format="dollar", delta_format="percent")
st.metric("Net revenue retention", 125.5, 13.0, format="%.1f%%", delta_format="%+.1f pts")
```

With numeric deltas, the existing zero, sign, and color rules keep working while the text shows the right unit.

### Additional Context

- Related: #12284 (precision for `"compact"` formatting), #17835 (zero-valued string deltas).
- Found while building [feature-demos/bi-dashboard](https://github.com/streamlit/feature-demos/tree/main/bi-dashboard) against `develop`.
issues.title: Add a separate delta_format to st.metric

issues.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

`st.metric` treats only the number `0` and the string `"0"` as a zero delta. A formatted string that is numerically zero, such as `"+0.0 pts"` or `"0.0%"`, gets a colored arrow. Treat a string delta as zero when its leading number is zero.

### Why?

The current rule is intentional (#15790 kept zero-looking strings positive, and #17029 documented it). It's still easy to hit in real dashboards:

- Formatted strings are the only way to show units on a delta today, because `format` is shared with `value` (see #17834). So most KPI cards pass strings.
- Rounding produces zero strings all the time. In a BI demo, the gross churn card showed a red up arrow (with `delta_color="inverse"`) for a change of about `+0.04` points, formatted as `"+0.0 pts"`.
- The documented workaround (pass the number `0`) requires a helper next to every formatting call, and the formatting code usually sits far from the `st.metric` call.

```python
import streamlit as st

st.metric("Monthly gross churn", "1.2%", f"{0.04:+.1f} pts", delta_color="inverse")
# Shows "+0.0 pts" with a red up arrow instead of a gray, arrow-less delta.
```

### How?

When `delta` is a string, read its leading signed number (after optional currency symbols and whitespace, for example `"+0.0 pts"`, `"0%"`, `"-0.00"`, `"$0"`). If that number equals zero, use the existing zero treatment: gray, no arrow. Other strings keep today's rules (a leading minus is negative, otherwise positive).

This changes behavior for zero-valued strings such as `"0%"`, which are green today. It updates `test_zero_like_strings_keep_positive_direction` and `test_negative_zero_string_is_negative`. A gray zero seems to be what authors expect, but if the change is too risky, #17834 (`delta_format`) would let apps pass numeric deltas with units, which avoids most of these strings.

### Additional Context

- Related: #15005 and #15790 (neutral zero delta), #17029 (documentation of the string rule), #17834 (`delta_format`).
- Found while building [feature-demos/bi-dashboard](https://github.com/streamlit/feature-demos/tree/main/bi-dashboard) against `develop`.

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

`st.echarts_chart` selections and `st.column_config.ButtonColumn` clicks report only positions (`data_indices` and `click.row`). To act on them, an app has to rebuild the exact order Streamlit received and map each position back to an entity. Include the selected item's name (and `id` when set) in ECharts selections, and the row's index label in `ButtonColumn` clicks.

### Why?

In a BI demo ([feature-demos/bi-dashboard](https://github.com/streamlit/feature-demos/tree/main/bi-dashboard)), every interactive element maps positions back to entities by hand:

- **Donut of revenue by industry** (click a slice to filter a table): `INDUSTRIES[i]` only works because the spec's `data` list was built in exactly that order.
- **Scatter with one series per plan** (brush to filter): indices are series-local, so the page rebuilds each plan's subset in the same row order as the spec.
- **Bars sorted by value** (click to filter): `totals.index[i]` from the same sorted Series that built the spec.
- **ButtonColumn row actions**: `table.index[click.row]`. In an `on_click` callback, the whole table has to go through `args=` so the callback can resolve the row.

```python
event = st.echarts_chart(spec, on_select="rerun")
selected = [
    INDUSTRIES[i]  # Must match the order used to build spec["series"][0]["data"].
    for group in event.selection.selected
    for i in group["data_indices"]
]
```

This mapping is easy to get subtly wrong, and the docstring warns that indices "are not revalidated against the new data" when `key` keeps a selection across spec changes. The other chart commands already return values: `st.plotly_chart` points include `x`, `y`, and `customdata`, and Vega-Lite selections report field values.

### How?

**ECharts:** Add `names` (and `ids` when data items set `id`) to each entry in `selection.selected`, aligned with `data_indices`:

```python
{
    "series_index": 0,
    "series_name": "Industry",
    "data_type": "main",
    "data_indices": [2],
    "names": ["Retail"],
}
```

ECharts already resolves this name: it's the `{b}` value in templates and `params.name` in events (the data item's `name`, or the category for category-axis series). The frontend could read it with `seriesData.getName(dataIndex)` when it builds the payload. For graph `edge` entries, the link's `source`/`target` might be more useful than a name.

**ButtonColumn:** Add `index` to `ButtonColumnClickState`, holding the clicked row's index label (a tuple for a `MultiIndex`, if serializable):

```python
click = st.session_state.deal_click
deal_id = click.index  # Instead of table.index[click.row].
```

The same idea could apply to `st.dataframe` row selections (`event.selection.rows` is positional too), but that can be a follow-up.

### Additional Context

- Related: #12395 (easier cross-filtering between charts and dataframes), #8914 (confusion over Plotly selection indices), #17627 (setting chart selections programmatically).
- Found while building [feature-demos/bi-dashboard](https://github.com/streamlit/feature-demos/tree/main/bi-dashboard) against `develop`.
issues.title: Return item names in st.echarts_chart selections and index labels in ButtonColumn clicks

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Chart colors from `theme.chartCategoricalColors` are assigned by position, not by category. When a filter removes a category, the remaining ones can change color, so "Enterprise is indigo" holds on one rerun and not the next. Add a theme-aware way to pin a category to a palette slot, shared by charts and colored badge columns.

### Why?

Dashboards filter all the time, and readers learn colors as identities. Today the color a category gets depends on where it lands:

- **`st.echarts_chart`:** palette colors follow series order, and data order for pies and funnels. Removing the first series shifts every later series to a new color.
- **Built-in charts with `color=<column>`:** Vega-Lite picks colors from the values present in the data ("let Vega-Lite auto-assign colors" in `built_in_chart_utils.py`), so the mapping changes when a filter removes a value.
- **`MultiselectColumn(color="auto")`:** colors follow the position in `options`. That's stable only while every chart orders its categories the same way.

The only stable alternative is explicit hex colors, which ignore the light/dark theme palettes. Built-in charts and badge columns accept theme color names (`"red"`, `"blue"`, …), but not slots of `chartCategoricalColors`. ECharts specs accept neither.

In a BI demo ([feature-demos/bi-dashboard](https://github.com/streamlit/feature-demos/tree/main/bi-dashboard)), keeping plan colors stable under a plan filter meant keeping every plan's series in every chart, with null data when filtered out:

```python
series = [
    {
        "name": plan,
        "type": "line",
        "stack": "mrr",
        # A filtered-out plan keeps its series (and color slot) but draws nothing.
        "data": values[plan].tolist() if plan in active_plans else [None] * len(months),
    }
    for plan in PLANS  # Fixed order = fixed colors.
]
```

### How?

Some options, from smallest to largest:

1. **Palette slot references** wherever Streamlit resolves colors: built-in chart `color` lists, `MultiselectColumn(color=[...])`, `ProgressColumn` and the chart columns, and `st.echarts_chart` specs. For example, `"chart:1"` (exact syntax open) would resolve on the frontend to the active theme's first categorical color, so it's correct in light and dark mode.
2. **A value-to-color mapping** for built-in charts and `MultiselectColumn`, for example `color={"Enterprise": "chart:1", "Pro": "chart:2", "Starter": "chart:3"}`, accepting slots, theme color names, or CSS colors.
3. **An app-wide category map**, set once (in config or a command) and applied to every chart and badge that colors by category.

Option 1 alone would fix ECharts specs and keep everything theme-aware. Option 2 would make the built-in charts stable without reshaping data.

### Additional Context

- Related: #12805 (theme colors in `st.map` and `st.pydeck_chart`), #11974 (`chartCategoricalColors` needs a reload for Plotly).
- Found while building [feature-demos/bi-dashboard](https://github.com/streamlit/feature-demos/tree/main/bi-dashboard) against `develop`.
issues.title: Keep category colors stable across charts and badge columns when data is filtered

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Start downloading the Material Symbols icon font while the page loads, instead of waiting until the first icon renders. Icons are part of the app's own UI and of many apps, so on a first (uncached) visit they often appear late, with visible loading artifacts until the font has downloaded.

### Why?

Material icons are now a common part of most apps:

- Streamlit's own UI uses them: the sidebar collapse and expand buttons, the main menu items, and the status widget.
- Many apps use them for page icons in `st.navigation` / `st.Page`, `icon=` on buttons, expanders, alerts and toasts, and `:material/...:` in Markdown.

The font is declared in `frontend/app/src/assets/css/fonts.css` with `font-display: block` and is about 375 KB. Browsers request an `@font-face` font only once text using it is laid out, so the download starts only after the JS bundle has run, the websocket has connected and the first icon has rendered. Until the font arrives, icons render as blank space. On slow connections, once the browser's block period (about 3 seconds) ends, the fallback font shows the icon's ligature name (for example `keyboard_double_arrow_left`) instead. Later visits hit the browser cache, so this mostly affects first loads, which is what new users see.

### How?

Start the download from the app's entry script with the CSS Font Loading API, instead of waiting for the first icon to render:

```ts
document.fonts.load('1em "Material Symbols Rounded"')
```

This needs no file name, so it can't go stale, and because it runs once the entry bundle has loaded, it doesn't compete with the JS the app needs for its first render.

Alternatives considered:

- **A `<link rel="preload">` in `index.html`**, as we do for Source Sans. That preload hard-codes the font's hashed file name, which works because Source Sans rarely changes. The `update-emojis-material-icons` workflow replaces the Material Symbols font every few weeks (28 times in 2026 so far), and each update changes its hash. Only the Vite build can compute that name, so a hard-coded preload would silently go stale. Keeping it current would need a build-time `index.html` transform or a frontend build inside the update script.
- **`fetchpriority="low"` on such a preload** would start the download even earlier, but it can't keep the font from competing with the JS. Over HTTP/1.1, the hint only delays when the request is sent, and the download then shares bandwidth.

The trade-off: every first visit downloads the font, even for apps that never show an icon.
issues.title: Preload the Material Symbols icon font so icons don't show loading artifacts on first load

### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add an `icon` parameter to `st.selectbox` that shows an emoji or Material icon inside the input field, to the left of the selected value. `st.text_input` (#10761) and `st.number_input` (#10711) already support this, which came from #8787.

### Why?

An icon hints at what the field is for (a globe for a country, a person for an assignee, a calendar for a reporting period) and lets a selectbox line up visually with text and number inputs that already have icons in the same form.

Today the only workaround is prefixing every option with an emoji via `format_func`. That repeats the icon in every dropdown row, changes the displayed value, and can't use Material icons (#12151).

### How?

Match the existing `icon` parameter on `st.text_input` and `st.number_input`:

```python
country = st.selectbox("Country", countries, icon=":material/public:")
assignee = st.selectbox("Assignee", people, icon="👤", placeholder="Pick someone")
```

- `icon: str | None = None`. Accepts a single-character emoji, `":material/icon_name:"`, or `"spinner"`, validated with `validate_icon_or_emoji` and documented with the same docstring as the other inputs.
- The icon renders at the start of the input field, before the selected value or placeholder. It stays visible while the user types to filter options, with `accept_new_options=True`, and when the widget is disabled.
- Size, spacing, and color match the start icon of `st.text_input` / `st.number_input` (`StyledStartEnhancer`), so the three widgets align when stacked.
- As with the other inputs, `icon` is part of the widget ID only when no `key` is set.

### Additional Context

- Original request for input icons: #8787.
- Related but separate: icons and Markdown inside option labels (#12151, #7466).
- `st.multiselect`, `st.date_input`, and `st.time_input` could get the same parameter later; this issue covers `st.selectbox` only.
issues.title: Add `icon` parameter to `st.selectbox`

issues.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

When `sys.modules` changes, [`update_watched_modules()`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L276) rebuilds the path set for every loaded module rather than for the names that were added, so importing one module re-resolves all of them.
For a better performance removing the bottleneck, it should scan only the difference, which the method already has in hand.

### Why?

The rebuild runs inline on the event loop, from `AppSession._handle_scriptrunner_event_on_event_loop` ([`:843`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/runtime/app_session.py#L843), [`:867`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/runtime/app_session.py#L867)), so nothing is served while it runs. Each path goes through [`realpath()` plus `_is_valid_path()`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L348), which [stats it](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L353), and the cost therefore follows the size of the dependency tree and the latency of the filesystem rather than the size of the change.

[#4491](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/4491) fixed the case where `sys.modules` is unchanged, by [caching the set of names](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L280). What remains is the cache miss, which any lazy import causes, and in an app that loads models on demand those keep happening long after startup.

The work beyond the new names is discarded anyway: [`_file_is_new()`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L266) is `filepath not in self._watched_modules`, so already-watched paths are rejected right after being stat'd. Removals are not handled either way, since [`_deregister_watcher()`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L255) is only called from [the pages path](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L119).

Measured on an app with the environment on a network filesystem, polling `/_stcore/health` ten times a second (median 1.3 ms) while one module is imported mid-session:

| event | latency |
| --- | --- |
| scan after the startup import of 3000 modules | 580 ms |
| scan after the later import of **one** module | 550 ms |
| ~950 modules loaded instead of ~3950, one module imported | 229 ms |

One module costs what three thousand do, and the figure follows the total rather than the change. On a local disk the same scan is far cheaper, so a small app will not notice it.


### How?

Resolve paths only for `set(sys.modules) - self._cached_sys_modules`, which the method computes already as part of its cache check. No change to where the work runs and no new concurrency. The only behavior given up is noticing that an already-imported module mutated its own `__path__` in place without its name changing.

Moving the sweep off the event loop would bound the worst case regardless of tree size or filesystem latency, but running it there after a script run is presumably what keeps watcher state off a second thread, and [#4491](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/4491) already noted multi-threading concerns here. With an incremental scan the remaining window is one module's paths, so that may not be worth the risk.

### Additional Context

This came out of our real use case, where we do suffer from it. The app runs for hours streaming audio and video to the browser, carries `torch` and `transformers` (1700 to 3900 loaded modules), and its environment sits on a network filesystem. Models load on demand, so `sys.modules` keeps changing mid-session, and each rescan stopped the server sending anything for **0.3 to 3.7 seconds**, long enough for the browser to conceal all audio and freeze video. A watchdog dumping thread stacks mid-stall put six of eight dumps in this path:

```
File "streamlit/runtime/app_session.py", line 714 in _handle_scriptrunner_event_on_event_loop
File "streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py", line 272 in update_watched_modules
File "streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py", line 340 in get_module_paths
File "streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py", line 346 in _is_valid_path
File "<frozen genericpath>", line 30 in isfile
```

(1.58.0 line numbers, where it was captured; verified unchanged in 1.66.1.) Scanning that dependency tree (1682 paths) in a plain Python process took 340 ms to 13666 ms depending on attribute cache state, the high reading seen once and not reproducible on demand. We now disable file watching to keep sessions usable.

A standalone app that shows the stall, needing no third party packages:

```python
import pathlib
import sys
import tempfile
import time

import streamlit as st

MODULES = 3000  # set to 0 for the control
# Outside the script folder on purpose: files under it are watched
# individually, which is a separate cost and not what this reproduces.
PKG = pathlib.Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "fake_deps_pkg" / "fake_deps"


@st.cache_resource
def build_and_import() -> int:
    PKG.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    (PKG / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    for i in range(MODULES):
        (PKG / f"mod{i}.py").write_text(f"value = {i}\n")
    sys.path.insert(0, str(PKG.parent))
    for i in range(MODULES):
        __import__(f"{PKG.name}.mod{i}")
    return len(sys.modules)


st.write(f"{build_and_import()} modules loaded at startup, {len(sys.modules)} now")


# A button click would do as well; this just triggers the one rerun unattended.
@st.fragment(run_every="3s")
def import_one_more() -> None:
    if st.session_state.get("imported"):
        st.write("idle")
        return
    st.session_state["imported"] = True
    (PKG / "extra.py").write_text("")
    __import__(f"{PKG.name}.extra")
    st.write(f"imported ONE module at {time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}")


import_one_more()
```

Run it, open it in a browser so a session exists, and poll an endpoint the event loop serves while the single extra module is imported a few seconds in:

```sh
while true; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{time_total}\n" http://localhost:8501/_stcore/health
  sleep 0.1
done
```

Verified against 1.66.1 by reading the source at that tag, after measuring on 1.58.0. Python 3.12.2, Linux 5.15.0.
issues.title: Efficient re-scan of module paths upon `sys.modules` changes

### Checklist - [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests. - [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue. ### Summary `st.echarts_chart` tooltips can't format individual fields without JavaScript. `{@column}` placeholders in a tooltip `formatter` template insert raw values, and `tooltip.valueFormatter` applies one number format to every value of a series. Support per-field number and date formats in tooltips, so a tooltip can show `9.5 MiB`, `3.8%`, and `Jan 03` side by side. ### Why? Moving an internal dashboard app (about 85 charts) to `st.echarts_chart`, the biggest source of friction was tooltips with extra fields, such as a commit SHA, a date, and a size. Every coding agent working on it hit this independently. - **Templates insert raw values.** `"formatter": "{@sha}
size: {@size}
date: {@date}"` renders `size: 11000000.5` and `date: 2026-01-02T00:00:00.000`. `valueFormatter` doesn't apply to template placeholders, and the docstring says so: "Values are inserted as escaped text without a number format". - **One format per series.** `valueFormatter: "percent"` formats every numeric value of the series as a percent, so a tooltip can't show a percentage next to a byte size or a count. - **No date formats.** Printf-style formats and the named number formats don't cover dates, so dates in templates show as full ISO strings. The workaround was to round columns or add pre-formatted string columns to the dataframe. Those extra columns also show up in the chart's **Show data** table and in the agent API's data. A separate fix ([#17883](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17883)) labels each `encode.tooltip` field in the default tooltip and shows dataframe datetimes readably there. Per-field formats in the default tooltip and in templates are still missing. ### How? These are the options considered so far, from smallest to most expressive. They aren't mutually exclusive. **A. Apply the existing formatting to placeholders.** `{@column}` values would use the tooltip's `valueFormatter` when set, and the Streamlit theme's number shortening and date formatting otherwise. It's the smallest change and needs no new syntax, but there is still only one number format per tooltip. **B. A format per placeholder.** For example `{@size|bytes}`, `{@pct|%.1f%%}`, or `{@date|MMM DD}`: ```python "tooltip": {"formatter": "{@sha}
{@size|bytes} · {@date|MMM DD}"} ``` - Number formats would be the ones `st.metric(format=...)` and `valueFormatter` already accept. Date formats could reuse the momentJS formats of `st.column_config.DatetimeColumn(format=...)`. - It's flexible, but it's syntax only Streamlit understands. The original product spec rejected a similar `{@[2]:compact}` suffix for that reason. - `|` already means rich text in ECharts label templates (`{style|text}`), so the separator needs care. **C. A per-field format mapping.** ```python "tooltip": {"valueFormatter": {"size": "bytes", "pct": "percent", "date": "MMM DD"}} ``` - This would apply in both the default tooltip and templates, and keeps templates portable. - ECharts calls `valueFormatter` without saying which dimension a value belongs to, so the frontend would have to match values to fields through `encode.tooltip`. That makes it more work than A or B. Open questions: - Should per-item tooltips in `series.data` be covered too? - Should Python validate the formats and log a warning, as it does for `valueFormatter` today? ### Additional Context - Product spec: `specs/2026-07-06-echarts-chart/product-spec.md`, "Tooltip formatting". It lists "per-dimension formats" and "date/time formats for tooltip values" as not included. - Related: [#17128](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/17128) (JavaScript callback support, the JavaScript route to the same result).
issues.title: Per-field number and date formats in st.echarts_chart tooltips

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

`st.echarts_chart` axis labels can't use Streamlit's number formats. `axisLabel.formatter` accepts only ECharts string templates such as `"{value} MB"`, so a byte axis shows `10,000,000` instead of `9.5 MiB`, and a fraction axis shows `0.05` instead of `5%`. Accept the same number formats that `tooltip.valueFormatter` already supports (`"bytes"`, `"compact"`, `"percent"`, `"dollar"`, printf strings) in `axisLabel.formatter`.

### Why?

Moving an internal dashboard app (about 85 charts) to `st.echarts_chart`, axis labels were the second biggest formatting gap after tooltips:

- **Bundle size chart:** the y axis reads `2,000,000 … 12,000,000` (bytes) while its tooltip, using `"valueFormatter": "bytes"`, reads `9.5 MiB`. The axis and the tooltip disagree.
- **Rates stored as fractions:** a template can append a unit (`"{value}%"`) but can't multiply by 100, so the axis reads `0.05%`.
- **Large counts or currency:** there's no compact (`1.2M`) or currency format without a JavaScript callback, which `st.echarts_chart` doesn't support.

The workaround is to rescale the data in pandas (for example, divide by 1,048,576 and append " MiB" in a template). That changes the values in tooltips, in the **Show data** table, and in the agent API's data, and it doesn't pick a unit per tick the way `"bytes"` does.

### How?

Treat a string `axisLabel.formatter` as a Streamlit number format when it is one, the same rule `tooltip.valueFormatter` uses today:

```python
st.echarts_chart(
    {
        "dataset": {"source": df},
        "xAxis": {"type": "time"},
        "yAxis": {"type": "value", "axisLabel": {"formatter": "bytes"}},
        "series": [{"type": "bar", "encode": {"x": "date", "y": "size"}}],
        "tooltip": {"trigger": "axis", "valueFormatter": "bytes"},
    }
)
```

- **Detection.** A named format (`"bytes"`, `"compact"`, `"percent"`, ...) or a printf string with a placeholder (`"%.1f s"`) that has no `{...}` template placeholder. Templates such as `"{value} MB"` or `"{value}%"` keep ECharts' meaning.
- **Backward compatibility.** In ECharts, a string without `{value}` prints literally on every tick, so no working spec uses `"bytes"` or `"%.1f"` as an axis formatter. Existing charts wouldn't change.
- **Validation.** As with `valueFormatter`, the frontend would ignore a malformed printf string, and Python would log a warning.

Open questions:

- Which other label formatters should accept the formats? Candidates are `axisPointer.label.formatter`, series `label.formatter` (bar and point labels show raw values like `10545470.237731934` today), and `visualMap` / `dataZoom` labels.
- Should value axes under the Streamlit theme shorten long numbers by default, like the theme already does in tooltips?
- Time axes already have ECharts' `{yyyy}`/`{MM}` templates. Do they need date formats here, or only numbers?

### Additional Context

- Product spec: `specs/2026-07-06-echarts-chart/product-spec.md`, "Tooltip formatting". It lists "number formats for axis labels" as not included, and "Tradeoffs" says axis labels still need pre-formatted strings.
- Related: [#17128](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/17128) (JavaScript callback support, the JavaScript route to the same result).
issues.title: Streamlit number formats for st.echarts_chart axis labels

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

`st.column_config` columns accept `alignment` ("left" / "center" / "right") for cell content, but column headers are always left-aligned. Please let headers be aligned too, either by following the column's `alignment` or through a separate header alignment option.


### Why?

Centring a column's cells leaves its header pinned to the left edge, so on wide columns the header no longer sits over its data. That looks broken in business dashboards, where centred numeric columns are a common house style.

There's no workaround: the grid is canvas-rendered, so custom CSS can't reach the header text, and pandas `Styler` header styles are ignored (#6958). The only option today is to drop `st.dataframe` for an HTML table and lose sorting, resizing, search and virtualisation.

Theming already covers the header's *colours* (`dataframeHeaderBackgroundColor`, `dataframeHeaderTextColor`), so alignment is the main header property that still can't be controlled.

Minimal example (Streamlit 1.67.0):

```python
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

df = pd.DataFrame({"Name": ["Alpha", "Bravo", "Charlie"], "Count": [10, 20, 30], "Score": [1.5, 2.5, 3.5]})
st.dataframe(
    df,
    hide_index=True,
    column_config={c: st.column_config.Column(c, alignment="center", width="medium") for c in df.columns},
)
# Cells are centred; headers stay left-aligned.
```


### How?

Either of these would work:

1. **Header follows the column:** when `alignment` is set on a column, apply it to the header as well. This is the simplest option and matches what most people expect from "align this column".
2. **Explicit parameter:** add `header_alignment: Literal["left", "center", "right"] | None = None` to `st.column_config.Column` and its subclasses. `None` keeps today's behaviour or follows `alignment`.

An optional theme-level default (e.g. `[theme] dataframeHeaderAlignment = "center"`) would avoid repeating it for every column, the same way the header colour options work today.


### Additional Context

- Related: #12106 (cell/content alignment, closed), #11110 (`alignment="center"` not applied to cells; fixed April 2025), #6958 (header styling from pandas `Styler` isn't kept, open).
- Use case: internal dashboards running on Streamlit in Snowflake (container runtime). Header alignment would only reach those apps through a Streamlit release, so a built-in option matters more than a workaround.
issues.title: Support column header alignment in st.dataframe / st.data_editor

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the existing issues for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Could Streamlit clarify the intended parameter-order convention for widgets that accept a value and minimum/maximum bounds? In 1.67.0, `st.date_input` places `value` before the bounds, while `st.slider` and `st.number_input` place it after them. This is an API consistency discussion, not a report of incorrect widget behavior.

### Why?

The leading parameters are:

```python
st.date_input(label, value, min_value, max_value, ...)
st.slider(label, min_value, max_value, value, ...)
st.number_input(label, min_value, max_value, value, ...)
```

Switching between these widgets requires remembering two positional conventions for similar concepts. This also comes up when writing application wrappers that present a consistent interface.

### How?

Is there a historical or design reason for this difference? It would be helpful to establish a convention for future APIs and consider how existing APIs could align if a backward-compatible path becomes available.

I am not proposing an immediate reorder: that would change the meaning of existing positional calls. Using explicit keyword arguments is a workable approach today.

### Additional Context

Compared the implementation signatures in Streamlit 1.67.0:

- [date_input](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.67.0/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/time_widgets.py#L1847)
- [slider](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.67.0/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/slider.py#L529)
- [number_input](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.67.0/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/number_input.py#L353)
issues.title: API consistency: parameter order of date_input versus slider and number_input

issues.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Let viewers rearrange the cells of an `st.grid` with drag and drop. If the grid has a `key`, save the order in the browser's `localStorage` so the layout is still there after a reload or a later visit.

### Why?

`st.grid` is designed for metric walls, card galleries, and dashboard panels. On dashboards, different viewers often care about different panels. Today the order is fixed by the script, so the only way to personalize it is to build settings widgets and store preferences in a database, which is a lot of work for a small win.

Dashboard tools like Grafana, Datadog, and Power BI, and layout libraries like [React Grid Layout](https://github.com/react-grid-layout/react-grid-layout), let users move panels around. The `st.grid` product spec (`specs/2026-05-14-grid-layout`) listed "draggable, resizable, or user-persisted layouts" as out of scope for the first version, so this request proposes the reordering part as a follow-up.

### How?

Add an opt-in parameter:

```python
grid = st.grid(3, reorderable=True, key="kpis")
grid.metric("Revenue", "$1.2M", "+8%", border=True)
grid.metric("Pipeline", "$4.8M", "+12%", border=True)
grid.metric("Conversion", "12.4%", "+1.1%", border=True)
```

Proposed behavior:

- **Drag handle:** A handle appears when the pointer is over a cell, or when the cell has keyboard focus. Only the handle starts a drag, so charts, dataframes, and inputs inside the cell work as usual.
- **Client-side only:** Reordering doesn't trigger a rerun, and Python doesn't see the new order, the same way the sidebar width works (the sidebar width is also kept in `localStorage`). The order survives reruns within the session.
- **Persistence:** If `key` is set, the order is saved in `localStorage`, scoped to the app, page, and grid key. Without a `key`, the order lasts only for the current session (or, alternatively, `reorderable=True` requires a `key`; see open questions).
- **Changes in the script:** If the script adds cells, they go at the end of the saved order. If it removes cells, they are dropped from the saved order. If the grid's structure changes too much (for example, a different number of cells), the saved order is discarded.
- **Reset:** A way to go back to the order in the script, for example a "Reset layout" entry in the app menu or a toolbar action on hover.
- **Accessibility:** Keyboard reordering (pick up with Space/Enter, move with arrow keys, drop with Space/Enter) with screen-reader announcements. The DOM order should change along with the visual order, unlike CSS `order` or `dense`, so keyboard and screen-reader order match what users see.
- **Spans:** Cells that span several columns (`grid.cell(column_span=2)`) move as one unit and keep their span.

Open questions:

1. **Cell identity:** Matching saved positions to cells by index breaks when cells are conditional or come from a loop over changing data. Should `grid.cell()` accept a `key` for a stable identity, with index-based matching as the fallback?
2. **Without a `key`:** Should reordering keep the order for the session only, or require a `key`?
3. **Reading the order in Python:** Is there a later need to read the order back (for example, through `st.session_state[key]`), or to set it from Python to save it per user on the server? That would need a widget-like value and is probably a separate follow-up.
4. **Name:** `reorderable`, `draggable`, or `sortable`?

Out of scope for this request: resizing cells, moving cells between grids, and server-side persistence.

### Additional Context

- `st.grid` feature request: #11101
- Related drag-and-drop request: #6700 (`st.multiselect`)
- Related discussion on client-side state: #17242
- Existing `localStorage` example: sidebar width (`frontend/app/src/components/Sidebar/Sidebar.tsx`)
issues.title: Drag-and-drop cell reordering for `st.grid`, saved in localStorage

issues.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Charts, maps, and dataframes each use a different default height: 350px for Vega-based charts and `st.echarts_chart`, up to 400px for `st.dataframe`, 450px for `st.plotly_chart`, and 500px for `st.map` and `st.pydeck_chart`. Placed side by side, they only line up if the author passes the same `height` to each. This request proposes one shared default height of **400px** (`25rem` at the default font size) for all of them. The frontend would resolve it from a single theme token.

### Why?

Dashboards place charts, maps, and tables next to each other in `st.columns`, `st.grid`, and cards. With today's defaults, a line chart next to a Plotly chart is 100px shorter, and a map next to a dataframe is 100px taller, so the bottoms of the row don't line up. The workaround is to pass the same integer `height` (or `height="stretch"`) to every element in the row. Our own examples do this: the `st.grid` docstring passes `height=220` to a line chart, a bar chart, and a dataframe, and the embedded skill's `dashboards.md` passes `height=260`. The embedded skill also tells agents to use Vega or ECharts for ordinary charts and Plotly for 3D and scientific charts, so agent-built dashboards mix libraries by design.

The defaults also scale differently with `theme.baseFontSize`. Vega charts and dataframes use rem values from the frontend theme. ECharts (350), Plotly (450), and maps (500) send fixed pixel values from Python. With a 14px base font, a line chart is 306px and a dataframe is 350px, but an ECharts chart stays at 350px.

Current defaults on `develop`:

| Element | Default height | Source | Scales with base font size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `st.line_chart`, `st.area_chart`, `st.bar_chart`, `st.scatter_chart`, `st.altair_chart`, `st.vega_lite_chart` | 350px | `theme.sizes.defaultChartHeight` (`21.875rem`), used as Vega-Lite `continuousHeight` | Yes |
| `st.echarts_chart` | 350px | `_DEFAULT_CONTENT_HEIGHT` in `echarts_chart.py` (copies the Vega token) | No |
| `st.dataframe`, `st.data_editor` (`height="auto"`) | Up to 400px (header + ~10 rows) | `defaultTableHeight` (`25rem`) in `DataFrame/hooks/useCustomTheme.ts` | Yes |
| `st.plotly_chart` | 450px | Plotly.js default; `_resolve_content_height` in `plotly_chart.py`, `DEFAULT_PLOTLY_HEIGHT` in `PlotlyChart.tsx` | No |
| `st.map`, `st.pydeck_chart` | 500px | `height=500` in the Python signatures | No |
| `st.table` | All rows | Content height | – |
| `st.graphviz_chart`, `st.mermaid_chart` | Natural diagram size | Content height (`st.mermaid_chart` has no `height` parameter) | – |
| `st.pyplot` | Figure aspect ratio at the column width (about 530px for a default 6.4×4.8in figure in the centered layout) | Image | – |

The `height="stretch"` fallback, used when the parent has no definite height, also differs. It is 350px for Vega and ECharts, the figure height or 450px for Plotly, and the auto height for dataframes. Maps get only 100px (`minHeight: "6.25rem"` in `DeckGlJsonChart/styled-components.ts`).

### How?

Use one theme token, set to `25rem` (400px at the default 16px base font), wherever a chart, map, or dataframe has no explicit height:

| Element | Today | Proposed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vega-based charts (built-in charts, `st.altair_chart`, `st.vega_lite_chart`) | 350px | 400px |
| `st.echarts_chart` | 350px | 400px |
| `st.plotly_chart` (figure without `layout.height`) | 450px | 400px |
| `st.dataframe`, `st.data_editor` (`height="auto"`) | Up to 400px | Up to 400px (unchanged) |
| `st.map`, `st.pydeck_chart` | 500px | 400px |
| `height="stretch"` fallback for all of the above | 100px to 450px | 400px (dataframes keep their auto height) |

Why 400px:

- `st.dataframe` is one of the most used Streamlit commands and already uses 400px. That shows the header, ten rows, and part of an eleventh row, which hints that the table scrolls. Aligning on 400px leaves dataframes unchanged, while aligning on 350px would cut them to about nine rows.
- 400px is in the middle of today's values, so no element changes by more than 100px. Vega and ECharts charts grow by 50px, Plotly charts shrink by 50px, and maps shrink by 100px.
- The centered layout's content is 704px wide, so a 400px chart is close to 16:9. A 350px chart is 2:1, which gets flat once the legend and axis labels take their share. Vega's `autosize: fit` fits them inside the 350px.
- Highcharts uses the same 400px default.

What stays the same:

- An explicit size always wins: an integer `height`, Altair `.properties(height=...)`, Plotly `layout.height`, or pyecharts `InitOpts(height=...)`.
- Content-sized elements keep their content height:
  - `st.table` shows all its rows.
  - `st.graphviz_chart` and `st.mermaid_chart` render at their natural size, because a fixed default would add empty space or shrink the labels.
  - `st.pyplot` and `st.image` keep the image's aspect ratio.
- Vega-Lite charts with a discrete y axis, such as horizontal bar charts over categories, keep Vega-Lite's step-based height of 20px per category, because the Streamlit theme only sets `continuousHeight`.

Implementation notes:

- Resolve the default in the frontend from the theme token, instead of the pixel values hard-coded in Python: `_DEFAULT_CONTENT_HEIGHT = 350` in `echarts_chart.py`, the 450 fallback in `plotly_chart.py`, and `height=500` in `map.py` and `deck_gl_json_chart.py`. This follows the rule in `lib/streamlit/AGENTS.md` that layout calculations belong in the frontend. It also keeps the elements in sync when the token changes and makes every default scale with `theme.baseFontSize`. The ECharts product spec already lists this as a deferred follow-up ("Resolve content size from the frontend theme token").
- Three tokens exist today: `defaultChartHeight` (`21.875rem`) and `defaultMapHeight` (`31.25rem`) in `frontend/lib/src/theme/primitives/sizes.ts`, and `defaultTableHeight` (`25rem`) in `DataFrame/hooks/useCustomTheme.ts`. Replace them with one shared token.
- An untitled Plotly figure keeps about 100px of empty top margin: Plotly.js defaults `margin.t` to 100, and the Streamlit theme only overrides `l`, `r`, and `pad`. At 400px, that leaves the plot less room than a Vega chart gets. Consider trimming the default top margin for figures without a title.
- Update the docstrings that state 350px, 450px, or 500px, add charts and dataframes to the "Default heights" list in the embedded skill's `references/layouts.md`, and update the e2e snapshots of every chart and map. This is a visible change and needs a release note.

Open questions:

1. Should maps also use 400px, or keep 500px because they often need more height?
2. Should `st.map` and `st.pydeck_chart` keep an integer default in their signatures (changed to `400`), or accept `"content"` as the default so the frontend resolves it like the other charts?
3. Should the Plotly top margin be trimmed in the same change or separately?

### Additional Context

- Layout optimization findings in the [agent wiki](https://issues.streamlit.app/agent_wiki_explorer?file=references/2026-10-13-layouting-optimization.md): G11 (mixed-library default heights), S4 (the current workaround), P3.6 (the open decision, which leaned toward documentation only), and B3 / P0.3 (the 100px map stretch fallback).
- ECharts product spec, "Sizing" section: `specs/2026-07-06-echarts-chart/product-spec.md`.
- Stretch fallbacks: #17410 (Vega and Plotly charts) and #17662 (dataframes).
- Related: #4799 (chart aspect ratio), #9518 and #12304 (dataframe height in rows), and #16308 (relative stretch heights).
issues.title: Unify the default height of charts, maps, and dataframes
